docs.title: MARLEM clean
docs.text:
MARLEM rebuilt step by step on SimBench networks: configure a local energy market, then step through it by hand and watch the network's power flow. The market and reinforcement-learning layers now share this repository, with the RL layer in core/rl/. They are validated separately.

Section Start with marlem-v1 The working solution: the market and the RL layer wired together, what changed, how to train, and the validation results. Code structure Every folder and script: what it does and how far it is built. MARLEM Methodology: the market as the paper states it (clearing, pricing, DSO fees, reputation, agents, batteries, grid, one market step), without the reinforcement-learning parts. Learning layer: observation, action, paradigms, algorithms, hyperparameters, population-based training and the 3 × 3 experiment as the papers state them, with the original code's settings where the papers are silent. RL Code and running instructions. Training cycle: the math of one training iteration for PPO, APPO and SAC in each paradigm (CTCE, CTDE, DTDE), and how many steps each takes. One iteration, step by step: every calculation from the agents' observation to the weight update, with what each paradigm changes. Worked examples: the same cycle with numbers, for the parts our own code defines (grouping, CTDE's per-agent actor, settings, evaluation). Validation Market layer: everything that was wrong in the original market (code or paper) and what changed. RL layer: what is wrong in the original training paradigms, trainer and inference, and what the tests in tests/rl/ show. The two papers: where the MARLEM paper and the implicit-cooperation paper agree and differ. SimBench Overview: what SimBench is, its codes, grids, scenarios and study cases. Network catalogue: every network's size, load, PV and load mix. Profiles: the time series of every load and generator class, and where they come from. API Reference One page per module, generated from the docstrings, one section per top-level folder. About these docs How the site is built: where the source is, how the API pages are made, how to use the diagrams.

docs.title: Source and build
docs.text:
The Markdown source is docs/ in the repository, readable on its own in VS Code and on GitHub. The site is built with MkDocs Material from docs_site/:

pip install -r docs_site/requirements.txt        # once, in the marlem env
mkdocs serve -f docs_site/mkdocs.yml -a 127.0.0.1:8001   # live preview
mkdocs build -f docs_site/mkdocs.yml             # static site in site/

run_all.py docs-clean starts the preview at http://127.0.0.1:8001. A new document appears on the site once it is added to nav in docs_site/mkdocs.yml. After editing docs_site/hooks.py, restart mkdocs serve; changes to the docs, the code and docs_site/overrides/ are picked up while it runs.

What the site does differently from the Markdown files happens at build time in docs_site/hooks.py: it generates the API pages, and turns links to code and other non-Markdown files into links to the repository on GitHub, keeping #L line anchors. Those links point at the clean branch, so they work once it is pushed.

docs.title: The API reference
docs.text:
The API pages are generated from the code, never written by hand:

  • One section per top-level folder (core.grid, core.market, core.config, studio, core.rl), in API_SECTIONS in docs_site/hooks.py. A package becomes a section with an index page; its subpackages become subsections.
  • One page per module, with its classes and functions, their signatures, type annotations and source. The module index lists each module with the first line of its docstring, so that line should say what the module is for.
  • Private names are hidden: anything starting with _ does not appear.
  • Docstrings are Google style (Args:, Returns:, Raises:, Attributes:), rendered by mkdocstrings. A class's __init__ arguments are shown with the class. Members appear in source order.
  • A section can link to its design document: the reasons behind the code live in the docs, the API pages say what the code is.

So documenting the code means writing its docstrings well; the API pages follow on the next build.

docs.title: Diagrams
docs.text:
Diagrams are written as Mermaid code blocks (```mermaid) and drawn by docs_site/overrides/assets/diagrams.js instead of Material, which renders them where they cannot be zoomed. On every diagram:

Control Does Drag pan Ctrl + mouse wheel, or the + / − buttons zoom Double-click zoom in fit back to the whole diagram ⛶ fill the browser window (Esc closes; F11 as well for the whole screen)

Diagrams fit themselves again when the window size changes. docs_site/overrides/assets/diagrams.css also widens the page on large screens.

docs.title: Formulas
docs.text: LaTeX between $…$ (inline) or $$…$$ (display), rendered by MathJax.

docs.title: Code structure
docs.text:
The repository folder by folder, down to each script: what it is for and how far it is built. Keep this page current when files are added, moved or built.

The market has three layers: core/grid/ models the network, core/market/ models the market on it (LocalEnergyMarket runs both, step by step), and core/config/ describes a scenario. notebooks/ call core/ directly to validate it. The NiceGUI Studio is in studio/: pages and components call studio/adapters/, a thin layer over core/. core/ never imports studio/ or notebooks/, so anything that looks wrong in the Studio can be reproduced in a notebook to tell a core problem from a UI one. core/env/ makes the market an RL environment; core/rl/ is the RL layer, which imports no market module (the environment arrives as a class), so its probes test it alone. core/runner/ is the one place that knows both: it starts, watches and stops training experiments (specs in experiments/, results in runs/).

docs.title: core/config/: the scenario
docs.text:
Everything the user sets before stepping the market, as plain data.

Script What it does State scenario.py Scenario: the network (GridSetup), the participants with their batteries, the market rules with the reputation weights and decay, and the DSO's tariffs, fee factors and loss factor; each setup lists its own problems (problems()), shown on the Summary page data and its checks store.py Save and load a scenario as JSON done placement.py Placing participants on the scenario's network: one on a bus, or one on every bus of the chosen kinds (load, load+pv, load+storage, ...); taken-over SimBench storage becomes the participant's battery, fixed in size (set_battery); SimBench-sized battery presets; imports core/grid/ done

docs.title: core/grid/: the SimBench network
docs.text:
The only place that imports pandapower and simbench. It hands out plain records, never pandapower objects.

Script What it does State contract.py The plain records that cross the grid seam: networks, topology, elements, profiles, power-flow results, the path between two buses (GridPath) done simbench.py Lists, loads and caches networks; topology, elements, profiles, the profile catalogue; a one-hour power flow done powerflow.py SimBenchGrid: one power flow per market step; owned elements switched off, each participant's net injection at its bus; the path between two buses (distance, lines, zones = feeders) done

docs.title: core/market/: the MARLEM market
docs.text:
The market of the paper (methodology). lem.py is the one class that runs it (LocalEnergyMarket, as in the original); clearing.py, bidding.py, clearing_price.py and reputation.py are its rebuilt pieces, and the remaining original files (ledger, profiles) are the reference.

Script What it does State lem.py LocalEnergyMarket: the participants (Participant), the DSO (Dso) and the reputation rule, one step in the paper's phases (validate, orders, the three stages, settle, power flow, rate, advance), one stage at a time or all at once; the history of the day done clearing.py The three clearing stages as separate functions: preferences, double auction, DSO; every trade assessed by the DSO (distance, loss, fee) done bidding.py The rule that writes orders: battery first, then sell the surplus or buy the deficit between the DSO's tariffs done clearing_price.py Pricing mechanisms with one fixed signature (fixes the seller price) done order.py Order, Trade (stage, distance, loss, fee and who pays it) and GridFees (the parts of eq. 8) done reputation.py The original's ReputationHandler, all reputation dials in one place (weights, decay): eq. 12 from reliability, price fairness and grid contribution, blended with the decay; reads a StepRecord; fixed where it disagreed with [P1] (see its docstring); ReputationScore done validation.py Hash-chained trade ledger with proof of work; seal_block closes a market period's block original, public seal_block added agent/der.py Participant: profiles from its elements, feasibility (eq. 15a-b), partner choice by reputation and distance, settlement (eq. 13, 14 less its fees, battery eq. 16), its reputation (decay blend), its bus injection; ParticipantOutcome done agent/battery.py Battery: its energy, what it can still take or give (eq. 15c-d), charging and discharging (eq. 16); the market only calls it done dso/dso.py Dso: tariffs, market price (their midpoint), the lines' loading of the last power flow, transmission losses (eq. 18), grid fees (eq. 8) and who pays them, stage 3 clearing (§3.3.2), its balance (eq. 7) and money; DsoOutcome, DSO_ID done profile/ Synthetic or CSV generation, demand and tariff profiles original, imports

docs.title: core/env/: the market as an RL environment
docs.text:
MarketEnv is the RLlib MultiAgentEnv over LocalEnergyMarket: one agent per participant, one episode per market day. It only translates actions to orders and the step's record to observations and rewards; the market rules stay in core/market/.

Script What it does State market_env.py MarketEnv: 16 normalised observations per agent (OBS_NAMES), 2 actions (signed quantity with a dead zone, price between the feed-in tariff and the utility price), reward = scaled net energy bill (profit less untraded imports at the utility price), episode = one day drawn from days, terminated at the day end; baselines zero_policy, net_position_policy. The module docstring documents the interface done __init__.py Public imports: MarketEnv, OBS_NAMES, net_position_policy, zero_policy done

docs.title: core/rl/: the reinforcement-learning layer
docs.text:
The three paradigms (CTCE, CTDE, DTDE) on RLlib's own PPO, APPO and SAC. It imports no market module: the environment is passed in as a class. Each file's docstring names the issues it fixes (validation/rl.md). The original code and its annotations live on the clean branch.

Script What it does State grouping.py GroupedEnv (CTCE: joint observations and actions, summed reward); CentralStateEnv (CTDE: own observation plus the global state, own reward) done ctde_modules.py CTDE: one RLlib module per agent, actor on its own observation, critic on the global state done config.py Algorithms, paradigms and configuration (build_config, SETTINGS) done policy.py Policy actions, baselines, rollout and evaluation done train.py train(Run(...)): training budgets, metrics, run records and saved policies; load_policy done benchmark.py Build, training and sampling timings done envs/probes.py Five probe tasks with known answers done envs/toy.py Individual and team toy tasks done envs/spread.py MPE2 simple_spread and visualisation helpers done envs/shapes.py Cheap environment with the market's observation and action sizes done __init__.py, envs/__init__.py Public imports done

docs.title: core/runner/: experiments
docs.text:
Start training runs that outlive the terminal, the Studio and the Claude session, and watch them from files only. The one place that imports both core/env/ and core/rl/ (inside a job; the rest stays light). An experiment is a spec in experiments/; start copies it to runs/<name>/experiment.json, writes a status.json per run and spawns one detached worker, which keeps max_parallel job processes training (one run each, then a held-out evaluation).

Script What it does State spec.py Experiment: the JSON spec (validated early), expanded to one RunSpec per algorithm x paradigm x variant x seed, each building a core.rl.Run done launch.py start (queue, detached worker), work (the worker loop), job (train, held-out evaluation, status), stop (kill worker and process trees, checked by pid and start time) done registry.py Read-only view of runs/: experiments(), runs(experiment) with a RunState per run (state, progress, ETA, last and held-out score); detects lost runs done __main__.py python -m core.runner start / status / stop, plus the internal work and job done

docs.title: experiments/: what to train
docs.text: File What it is State smoke.json Two tiny PPO-DTDE runs, to check the runner end to end (a few minutes) done sac_alpha.json SAC-DTDE on the market with initial temperatures 1, 0.1 and 0.01 done, not run market_3x3.json Three algorithms x three paradigms on the market, one seed done, not run

docs.title: studio/: the user interface
docs.text:
NiceGUI, port 8090. A page is one file in pages/; code goes to components/ only when more than one place uses it.

Script What it does State app.py Registers the pages and starts the server done layout.py, navigation.py, theme.py, static/ Page frame, left navigation, colours and styles; the header names the current scenario and opens another from a scenario file (scenarios/ or an upload) done state.py The adapters (services()), built once done pages/inspect.py Inspect: any network in depth, all SimBench profiles, two networks compared done pages/settings.py Workspace folder, network cache and its coverage, dark mode done pages/grid_participants.py Network, day, step length, background, limits; participants placed by clicking buses or per load or prosumer bus; batteries done pages/market_dso.py Pricing mechanism, bounds, preferred partners, ledger; the bidding rule; the DSO's tariffs done pages/summary.py Summary before running: readiness checks; tab Settings (every grid, market, DSO and battery setting once, the participants' day, the network) and tab Day profiles done pages/runs.py Runs: the training experiments in runs/, refreshed every 2 s. One card per experiment (newest first): runs per state, worker alive or not, Stop experiment (with confirmation); a table of its runs with state badge, progress bar, env steps / budget, elapsed, ETA, last evaluation and held-out return, a Stop button per queued or running run, and the error of a failed run in a tooltip done pages/step.py One click per part of a step (orders, the three stages, settle and power flow): order book, network with trades and voltages, trades, participants, the day so far done components/network.py Network picker with filters, summary, topology plot, element table, profile inspector done components/profiles.py, charts.py, cards.py, tables.py Profile class tiles, Plotly figures (also the day's curves), cards, tables done components/day_profiles.py The Summary's Day profiles tab: every element on the scenario's day, participants (they trade) apart from the background; summed curves, single curves by row selection done components/labels.py The names shown for mechanisms, background modes and step lengths, shared by the settings and summary pages done

docs.title: scenarios/: saved scenarios
docs.text: File What it is State validate_market.json The market notebook's scenario, saved by it in the Studio's format: open it from the Studio's header (Scenario: ... → Open) to play the same scenario there. Also the scenario of tests/market/ and of the market environment's examples done

docs.title: notebooks/: the core without the Studio
docs.text:
Notebooks import core/ only. Run them with the marlem conda env as kernel; their setup cell finds the repository root from wherever they run. Runs go to runs/ in the root.

Notebook What it does State market/validate_market.ipynb Scenario, inputs per step, one step part by part, the whole day, rule checks, experiments side by side done market/benchmark_market_step.ipynb Time per market step on SimBench LV networks of 13 to 118 participants (random orders), split into market logic, grid preparation and the power flow; the floor under a training run on the market done market/results/market_step.csv That notebook's summary, read by the RL speed benchmark (notebooks/rl/benchmark_speed.ipynb) done rl/probe_paradigms.ipynb The probe environments on every combination of algorithm and paradigm: run these first after any change to core/rl/ done rl/probe_playground.ipynb Inspect learning iteration by iteration done rl/simple_spread.ipynb MPE2 simple_spread, the second test after the probes done rl/benchmark_speed.ipynb Compare RL timing with notebooks/market/results/market_step.csv done

docs.title: tests/: market and RL checks
docs.text:
Run with python -m pytest from the root in the marlem conda env (pytest.ini sets testpaths = tests and pythonpath = .).

Test What it checks State market/test_studio_matches_core.py validate_market.json read by ScenarioService and stepped part by part by MarketService gives the same StepRecords as LocalEnergyMarket.run_to_end done market/test_market_env.py MarketEnv on validate_market.json: spaces, a zero-action day, the reward as the scaled net bill, action decoding (quantity, price, dead zone), reproducible day draw, net_position_policy against zero_policy, RLlib's multi-agent environment check done market/test_powerflow_recycle.py pandapower's recycle in the step power flow gives the same grid results done rl/test_0_every_probe.py to test_5_obs_action_probe.py Deterministic checks of the probe environments done rl/test_6_ctde_structure.py The CTDE modules' structure: what the actor and the critic read done rl/probe_helpers.py, rl/conftest.py Shared assertions and readable test output (each test's docstring is printed) done runner/test_runner.py Experiment specs (grid names, budgets, variants, date ranges, validation errors) and the registry's run states (queued, running, lost, completed, failed, legacy, progress and ETA); no training done runner/test_run_service.py The Studio's RunService over a temporary runs/ (MARLEM_RUNS): experiments newest first, runs, spec, stopping queued runs done

docs.title: studio/adapters/: what the pages call
docs.text:
Translates between the Studio and the layers below, so pages never touch the market or pandapower directly.

Script What it does State container.py Builds the adapters once done workspace.py Where the Studio keeps its data: the network cache, the scenario file, per-browser state (C:\MARLEM here) done grid_catalog_service.py Networks, their facts, topology, elements as the grid contract's records; the network cache and its background warming done profile_service.py A network's profiles and SimBench's whole catalogue; every element's power on the scenario's day (day_profiles) done profile_classes.py SimBench's profile classes and how a profile name is classified done models.py The data types only the Studio needs: profile classes, profile types, chart series, a day's element profiles done scenario_service.py The scenario being edited, saved on every change; calls core/config/placement.py to place participants; lists, reads and opens scenario files done run_service.py The experiments in runs/ and their runs, as the runner's registry reports them (RunState), newest folder first; stops an experiment or one run through core.runner.launch.stop done market_service.py Builds and holds the LocalEnergyMarket the Step page plays; build, next part, step, run to the end, clear (when another scenario is opened) done

docs.text: Path What it is docs/ This documentation (Markdown); docs/networks.py generates the network catalogue docs_site/ The MkDocs site built from docs/: config, build hooks, diagram assets run_studio.py Starts the Studio with auto-reload run_all.py Starts the dev servers (both branches' docs and Studios) in their own windows AGENTS.md Rules for working in this repository pytest.ini Discover the market and RL tests together from the root (tests/) runs/ Training runs, checkpoints and benchmark results; ignored by Git. Experiments started by the runner: runs/<name>/{experiment.json, worker.json, worker.log, <run>/{status.json, log.txt, run.json, metrics.csv, evaluation.csv, heldout.csv, checkpoint/}} .vscode/ Launch entries and the Python interpreter

docs.title: Choices in the rebuilt market step
docs.text:
Where the rebuilt step differs from the paper or the original code, for now:

Topic Here Orders Written by the bidding rule (core/market/bidding.py); no learning Orders preferring the DSO Skip stages 1 and 2 and are cleared in stage 3 (the original cleared them first) Distance d_ij Line length along the shortest path between the two buses (km); for a trade with the DSO, the path to the transformer's low-voltage busbar, where its energy enters Losses (eq. 18) Recorded on every trade as d · q · κ (κ = 0.03 per km); not taken off the delivered energy, since the power flow has the physical losses Grid fees (eq. 8) Calculated by the DSO for every trade and charged (fees_charged). Congestion C_t is the highest line loading on the trade's path in the previous step's power flow (0 at step 0). F_trans, which has no formula in [P1], is the lost energy at the trade price, κ · d · q · p (the form quantity × distance × price factor is set; the factor and the distance measure are open). Zones are feeders. Trades with the DSO pay the fees of their path to the transformer, without a zone bonus. F_imb applies only to trades with the DSO that worsen the market's balance. No trade is blocked for grid reasons: the fees penalize (I-55). Peer fees split 50/50 between buyer and seller; a DSO trade's fee is paid by the participant. Factor values are the original code's DSO balance (eq. 7) Energy sold minus bought per step and over the day, plus the DSO's revenue and fees; money adds up to 0 with the participants' profits Market balance B_grid (eq. 20) Energy offered minus energy asked in the step's orders (before stage 3) Reputation (eq. 12) ReputationHandler.update_reputation for every participant after each step, as in the original: reliability = order volume matched by peers / order volume, fairness = its peer trade prices against the peer clearing price, grid = its trades against B_grid (DSO trades neutral). Weights 0.3/0.2/0.5 (the original's); decay a constant, r ← 0.8 r + 0.2 score (the original used the time of day; still open). Start 0.5 Partner choice (§3.4) Weighted score: 0.5 · standing + 0.5 · closeness, both rescaled over the candidates (closeness 1 = nearest, 0 = farthest; standing 1 = highest reputation, 0 = lowest) Tariffs Constant over the day Submitted orders Never changed by the clearing (the original changed them in place) Batteries (eq. 15–16) Efficiencies and the power limit included; partial charges allowed. A participant taking over a SimBench storage unit gets its capacity and power; other batteries take their power limit by hand (none by default), or SimBench's capacity ÷ 2 h through simbench_battery and its presets Demand satisfied / deferred (§3.4.1) Per step on each outcome; deferred = what the participant's orders and battery left uncovered, exchanged with the upstream grid untraded

docs.title: marlem-v1: the working solution
docs.text: Branch marlem-v1 (worktree workspace/marlem-v1), built from clean on 14 Oct 2026. The market (core/) and the RL layer (core/rl/) wired together: agents trained with PPO, APPO or SAC in the three paradigms play the SimBench market. Core API only; the Studio is untouched.

docs.title: 1. What is new
docs.text: Part Where What CTDE rebuilt core/rl/ctde_modules.py, grouping.py MAPPO / MASAC with one module per agent: own reward, own critic, own PPO clip and SAC temperature; actor on the agent's own observation, critic on the global state Value cap lifted core/rl/config.py PPO vf_clip_param 1e6 instead of RLlib's 10 Market environment core/env/market_env.py MarketEnv: the market as an RLlib multi-agent environment, plus two baseline policies Reputation decay core/market/lem.py per hour, applied as decay ** step_hours (I-38b decided) Tests tests/market/test_market_env.py, tests/rl/test_6_ctde_structure.py 10 market-environment tests, 4 CTDE structure tests (plus the 17 probe-environment tests)

docs.title: 2. The three paradigms now
docs.text:
Environment the algorithm sees Modules Objective DTDE the market as it is one per agent, RLlib's default own bill CTDE CentralStateEnv: agent i observes [o_i, o_1 … o_N] one per agent; actor reads o_i, critic reads everything own bill CTCE GroupedEnv: one agent, joined observations and actions one, RLlib's default the sum of all bills (social planner)

DTDE and CTDE now optimise the same thing (each agent its own bill) and differ only in what the critic sees, so a difference between them is the central critic's effect. CTCE is a different question by design: what one controller of all households would achieve. The paper's CTDE summed the rewards (a team objective); that is changed here because the market's prosumers are self-interested.

What this fixes, compared with the grouped CTDE of clean:

  • the PPO and APPO clip is per agent (it was on the product of all agents' ratios, which clips more and more as the number of agents grows);
  • rewards, values and advantages are per agent (it was one team value);
  • SAC's temperature and entropy target are per agent.

Known deviation: SAC's CTDE critic is Q_i(s, a_i), the global state and the agent's own action. MADDPG / MASAC also give it the other agents' actions; that needs the joint action in each agent's training batch, which RLlib does not provide. PPO and APPO are unaffected (their critic is a state value).

Not done (not needed for correctness): parameter sharing between similar agents, value normalisation (PopArt), separate actor and critic optimisers.

docs.title: 3. The market as an environment
docs.text:
Full definition in the module docstring of market_env.py. In short:

  • Agents: one per scenario participant.
  • Episode: one market day, drawn at each reset from the configured days. The day's end terminates the episode (the hour is in the observation, so no bootstrap past midnight is needed).
  • Observation (16 per agent, scaled to about [-1, 1]): hour (sin, cos); own generation, demand, net; battery (has one, state of charge, room to charge and discharge); own reputation; last clearing price within the tariff range; last step's peer and DSO volumes, grid balance, own reward and own net trade.
  • Action (2 per agent, in [-1, 1]): a signed quantity, as a share of what the agent may sell or buy this step (eq. 15a-b; a small dead zone means "no order"), and a price between the feed-in tariff and the utility price. The quantity is feasible by construction, so no action is ever rejected.
  • Reward: the agent's net bill for the step, scaled: (profit − p_utility · deferred_demand) / reward_scale. Settlement leaves energy that no trade covers unpriced, so profit alone would make not buying free; untraded imports are therefore charged at the utility price and untraded exports earn nothing.
  • Baselines: zero_policy (never trade) and net_position_policy (the market's own bidding rule: offer the surplus, ask for the deficit, battery first).

Choices made here that the papers leave open, with the reason:

Choice Decision Why Objective individual bill per agent self-interested prosumers; CTCE keeps the welfare objective as the planner benchmark Reward net bill, not the paper's five-part weighted reward the economic outcome itself; no hand-tuned weights; the paper's reward has three inconsistent versions (papers.md) Action 2 numbers: signed share of the feasible quantity, price in [FiT, utility] no infeasible or rejected orders (I-10, I-39); no discrete parts decoded from continuous numbers; prices outside the tariffs are dominated Partner preference β not learned the stage-1 preference adds a discrete choice per step; left for later Scaling fixed scales in the environment the same in training and evaluation; returns of order 1-10 Day end termination a market day settles; the hour is observed Days drawn from a list per episode train on some days, evaluate on held-out ones (I-72)

docs.title: 4. How to use it
docs.text:
from core.env import MarketEnv, net_position_policy, zero_policy
from core.rl import Run, evaluate, load_policy, train

config = {"scenario": "scenarios/validate_market.json",
          "days": [f"2016-06-{d:02d}" for d in range(1, 31)]}
record = train(Run("ppo", "ctde", MarketEnv, config, budget=24_000, eval_every=4_800,
                   training={"lr": 3e-4, "train_batch_size_per_learner": 2400,
                             "minibatch_size": 240, "num_epochs": 10}))

held_out = {"scenario": config["scenario"], "days": [f"2016-07-{d:02d}" for d in range(1, 15)]}
env = MarketEnv(held_out)
policies = {"trained": load_policy(record["out_dir"])[0],
            "zero": zero_policy(env), "net_position": net_position_policy(env)}
evaluate(MarketEnv, held_out, policies, seeds=list(range(2000, 2014)))

Run from the worktree root (the RL code is imported as core.rl, the market as core.*). Each run writes run.json, metrics.csv, evaluation.csv and a checkpoint to runs/ (not in git).

docs.title: Running experiments
docs.text:
For more than one run, or one that should outlive the terminal, describe the runs in experiments/<name>.json (algorithms x paradigms x seeds x variants, budget, train and test days; see core/runner/spec.py for the fields) and use the runner:

python -m core.runner start experiments/smoke.json   # returns at once
python -m core.runner status                          # one line per experiment
python -m core.runner status smoke                    # table: state, progress, ETA, scores
python -m core.runner stop smoke [run]                # kill the worker and jobs (or one run)

A detached worker keeps up to max_parallel runs training; each run ends with heldout.csv (trained policy and baselines on the test days). Everything is in files under runs/<name>/, so status works from any terminal, and the Studio can read the same files. start on an existing experiment resumes it: completed runs stay, failed, stopped and lost runs (process gone) start again.

docs.title: Probes (RL layer, before the market)
docs.text:
The five probe environments, all nine combinations, fast settings (2 × 64 network, learning rate 1e-3). A run passes when every value and action is within tolerance of the exact answer; DTDE and CTDE values are checked per agent, CTCE's against the group sum; SAC's discount-probe value includes its entropy bonus.

CTCE CTDE DTDE PPO 1-5 pass 1-5 pass 1-5 pass (probe 4: 1.04 on seed 0, a marginal miss; passes at twice the budget, 0.76, and on seed 1, 0.37) APPO 1-5 pass 1-5 pass 1-5 pass SAC 1-2 pass; 3-5 pass at three times the budget same same

SAC's action probes need more steps in every paradigm, DTDE included (RLlib's own module): its entropy bonus and tanh squashing pull the actions toward 0 until the temperature has fallen. That is SAC's behaviour, not a paradigm defect.

docs.title: Market
docs.text:
Scenario scenarios/validate_market.json (5 households on 1-LV-rural1--0-sw, two with batteries and PV, two pure consumers). Trained on the 30 days of June 2016, 24,000 environment steps (1,000 days); evaluated on 14 held-out days (1-14 July 2016) with the most likely action. Team return = sum of the five agents' scaled daily bills (higher is better).

Policy Steps (days) CTCE CTDE DTDE zero (never trade) – −12.64 −12.64 −12.64 PPO 24,000 (1,000) −11.43 −10.30 −9.04 APPO 24,000 (1,000) −12.43 −10.51 −10.72 SAC 6,000 (250) −11.26 −12.35 −12.50 net position (the market's rule) – −8.47 −8.47 −8.47
  • Every combination learns something: all nine end above never trading on days they were not trained on. PPO and APPO in CTDE and DTDE are clearly better; APPO-CTCE, SAC-CTDE and SAC-DTDE only just (they mostly learned to trade P1's surplus).
  • None beats the market's own bidding rule yet, and no training curve had levelled off: PPO-DTDE went from −12.0 to −7.4 on training days. These are single runs, one seed, short budgets; the ordering between paradigms is not a result.
  • SAC had a quarter of the budget: each SAC step costs far more (a gradient update per sampled batch), so 6,000 steps took about 40 minutes per paradigm, as long as 24,000 PPO steps. Its runs say "it learns", not how it compares.
  • Wall time per run: PPO and APPO about 30-35 min, SAC 15-40 min, three in parallel.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
python -m pytest tests          # market environment + Studio check
cd RL; python -m pytest         # probe environments + CTDE structure

docs.title: 6. Open points
docs.text:
• Longer training and several seeds per combination before any comparison is read as a result (the market curves were still rising at the end).
  • Hyperparameters for the market are a first choice (learning rate 3e-4, PPO batch of 100 days), not tuned.
  • Partner preference β, the paper's KPIs as observations, and forecast errors are not in the observation or action yet.
  • Ray's start-up occasionally fails when memory is short (several runs in parallel each start their own Ray); run fewer in parallel if it happens.

docs.title: MARLEM: the learning layer as stated in the papers
docs.text:
The reinforcement-learning half of the MARLEM method, the counterpart of the market as stated in the paper: what the agents observe and do, the three training paradigms, the three algorithms, their hyperparameters, population-based training, and the 3 × 3 experiment. Each section says what the papers say. Where they leave out something needed to run it, a folded section titled In the original code (click to open) gives how the original implementation (salazarna/marlem, commit 15d6715) configures it, so every setting has a reference value. Those sections describe the code as it is; what is wrong in it is recorded separately, in RL layer: what is wrong, and only linked here.

Sources

  • [P1] Salazar-Peña, Tabares, González-Mancera. MARLEM: A multi-agent reinforcement learning simulation framework for implicit cooperation in decentralized local energy markets. Applied Energy 412 (2026) 127546. doi:10.1016/j.apenergy.2026.127546. §3.2 (the Dec-POMDP) and §3.7 (paradigms and algorithms, in words). [P1] trains nothing; it defers "the full mathematical and implementation specifics" of MARL to [P2].
  • [P2] Same authors. Harnessing Implicit Cooperation: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Approach Towards Decentralized Local Energy Markets. SSRN preprint 6685504, not peer reviewed. §3.3 (algorithms, eq. 11-15), §3.4 (paradigms, eq. 16-20), §4 (the case study and training setup, Tables 6-8), §5 (results, Tables 9-10).
  • The original code: src/environment/ (lem.py, action.py, observation.py, train.py, ctce.py, ctde.py, inference.py) and the notebook notebooks/case6_implicit_cooperation.ipynb, which sets up [P2]'s experiment. It is built on Ray RLlib 2.x (new API stack) and Ray Tune.

Equation numbers are the papers' own and marked with the paper. The reward and the KPIs are compared paper against paper against code in The two papers and are only summarised here.

Notation

Symbol Meaning \(i \in \mathcal{I}\), \(I = \lvert\mathcal{I}\rvert\) agent, number of agents \(t \in \{0, \dots, \tau\}\) trading period (step) of an episode \(o_i\), \(a_i\), \(R_i\) agent \(i\)'s observation, action and reward \(s\), \(\mathbf{a}\) global state, joint action \(\pi_\theta\), \(Q_\phi\), \(V\) policy (actor), action-value critic, state-value critic \(\psi\) discount factor ([P2]'s symbol; \(\gamma\) in RLlib)

docs.title: 1. The learning problem ([P1] §3.2, [P2] §3.1)
docs.text: The market is a decentralised partially observable Markov decision process (Dec-POMDP) \(\langle \mathcal{I}, \mathcal{S}, \mathcal{A}, \mathcal{P}, \mathcal{R}, \Omega, \mathcal{O} \rangle\): each agent \(i\) sees only its own observation \(o_i\), chooses its own action \(a_i\) and receives its own reward \(R_i\); the transition \(\mathcal{P}(s' \mid s, \mathbf{a})\) is one market step (methodology §3). An episode is one day of \(\tau = 24\) hourly steps ([P2] Table 7).

docs.title: 1.1 Action ([P1] eq. 2)
docs.text:
\[ a_i = \left\langle p_{\text{bid}},\ q_{\text{bid}},\ \alpha,\ \beta \right\rangle \tag{[P1] 2} \]

Price, quantity, order type (0 sell, 1 buy) and preferred partner (another agent, the DSO, or none), as in methodology §2. [P1] calls the action space continuous.

In the original code

ActionHandler (action.py L35-L44) gives every agent one continuous Box of 4 numbers; the discrete parts are decoded from it in step (lem.py L351-L381):

Dimension Bounds Decoded as \(p_{\text{bid}}\) [min_price, max_price] clipped to the bounds \(q_{\text{bid}}\) [min_quantity, min(max_quantity, agent capacity)] clipped to [min_quantity, max_quantity] \(\alpha\) [0, 1] buy if \(> 0.5\) \(\beta\) [0, \(I + 1\)] int(β): \(0 \dots I-1\) an agent (in list order), \(I\) the DSO, \(I + 1\) no preference

With enable_partner_preference=False the learned \(\beta\) is ignored and a rule picks the partner. With enable_asynchronous_order=True each order's time gets a random offset within the step. In [P2]'s case, 8 agents × 4 = 32 action numbers for the group.

The policy outputs a Gaussian over these 4 numbers; RLlib rescales its sample from \([-1, 1]\) to the Box bounds before step sees it.

docs.title: 1.2 Observation ([P1] Table 2, [P2] Table 5)
docs.text:
Three blocks, the same 42 signals in both papers (listed in The two papers §1):

Block Signals Visible to Market signals 16: step, time of day, clearing price and volume, grid balance, DSO volumes and prices, P2P volume, local prices all agents (public) Agent signals 16: generation and demand (forecasts), demand and supply satisfied and deferred, profit, reputation, battery state the agent only (private) Implicit-cooperation KPIs 10: welfare, liquidity, spread, volatility, imbalance, congestion, coordination score and convergence, self-consumption, flexibility use all agents (shared)

When partner preference is on, the observation adds every agent's reputation. The KPIs are the "stigmergic" signals of [P2]: they are what lets independent learners see the others' aggregate effect (§2, DTDE). Forecasts carry up to 30 % error ([P2] Table 7).

In the original code

ObservationHandler (observation.py L65-L176) builds one Box per agent: the 42 signals, plus \(I\) reputations when enable_partner_preference=True, so \(42 + 8 = 50\) numbers per agent in [P2]'s case and \(8 \times 50 = 400\) for the group in CTCE and CTDE. Each signal has its own bounds (prices in the market's price range, volumes up to max_quantity × \(I\), the step up to max_steps, ...). The values are passed to the networks as they are: neither the environment nor the trainer normalises them.

docs.title: 1.3 Reward ([P1] eq. 3-6, [P2] eq. 3)
docs.text:
Every agent gets its own reward each step: a base reward of five weighted parts (grid balance, resource allocation, trading, stability, economic efficiency), raised by a cooperation bonus \(f_{\text{coop}} \cdot f_{\text{contrib},i}\) built from the KPIs, minus penalties for DSO reliance and unmet demand. The two papers write the overall form differently, and the code is a third version; all three, with the weights, are in The two papers §3.

What matters for training: the reward is per agent. How it becomes a paradigm's learning signal is the paradigm's choice (§2).

docs.title: 1.4 Episodes and seeds
docs.text:
[P2]: 24 steps of one hour; a global seed (42) controls "all stochastic processes within the simulation", so that "environmental conditions are identical across all experimental runs" (§4.3). DSO price profiles are kept fixed between episodes.

In the original code
  • Episode end (lem.py L443-L453): all agents are terminated (and "__all__" set) once the step counter reaches max_steps − 1.
  • Seeding (lem.py L258-L311): every reset calls np.random.seed(seed) with the seed from env_config (42) unless one is passed, so every episode starts from the same random state.
  • enable_reset_dso_profiles=False keeps the DSO prices of the first day.

docs.title: 2. Training paradigms ([P1] §3.7.1, [P2] §3.4)
docs.text:
Paradigm Training Execution Objective CTCE One policy on the global state \(s\) (all observations concatenated) The same policy outputs the joint action Sum of all agents' returns, [P2] eq. 17 CTDE Each agent's actor, guided by a centralised critic \(Q_\phi(s, \mathbf{a})\) on the global state and joint action Each actor on its own \(o_i\); the critic is dropped [P2] eq. 18 DTDE Each agent learns alone from its own \(o_i\) and \(R_i\) Local Own return, [P2] eq. 19 \[ \pi_ heta(a_1, \dots, a_I \mid s) = \prod_{i=1}^{I} \pi_{ heta,i}(a_i \mid s) ag{[P2] 16} \] \[ J_{ ext{CTCE}}( heta) = \mathbb{E}\left[ \sum_{t=0}^{ au} \sum_{i=1}^{I} \psi^t R_i(s_t, \mathbf{a}_t) ight] ag{[P2] 17} \] \[ abla_{ heta_i} J( heta_i) = \mathbb{E}\left[ abla_{ heta_i} \log \pi_{ heta_i}(a_i \mid o_i)\; Q_\phi(s, a_1, \dots, a_I) ight] ag{[P2] 18} \] \[ J_{ ext{DTDE}}( heta_i) = \mathbb{E}\left[ \sum_{t=0}^{ au} \psi^t R_i(o_{i,t}, a_{i,t}) ight] ag{[P2] 19} \] \[ P_i(s' \mid s, a_i) = \sum_{a_{-i}} P(s' \mid s, a_i, a_{-i}) \prod_{j e i} \pi_j(a_j \mid o_j) ag{[P2] 20} \]

Eq. 20 is the non-stationarity an independent learner faces: the others' policies are part of its environment. The papers' answer is the shared KPIs in the observation, which make that environment "quasi-stationary". [P1] calls CTCE "a theoretical upper bound for system performance" and [P2] uses it as the benchmark the other paradigms are measured against.

In the original code

The paradigm is chosen with TrainingMode and set up in _setup_training_config (train.py L296-L353).

DTDE. The market environment as it is, one RLlib policy per agent (policy_mapping_fn maps agent \(i\) to policy \(i\)), each with RLlib's default module for the algorithm (DefaultPPOTorchRLModule, DefaultAPPOTorchRLModule, DefaultSACTorchRLModule) and default network settings. Nothing is shared between agents; each learns from its own reward.

CTCE and CTDE: the grouped environment. GroupedLEM (train.py L623-L705) wraps the market with RLlib's with_agent_groups into one agent, "grouped_agents", whose observation and action are Tuples of the agents' and whose reward is the sum of the agents' rewards (as [P2] eq. 17). The episode ends for the group when it ends for all.

CTCE: CTCEModule (ctce.py), a custom RLlib module, with embeddings_dim = 128:

Part Network Encoder all observations concatenated → Linear(128) → ReLU → Linear(128) → ReLU Actor head pi Linear(128 → 2 × all action dims): a mean and a log-std per action number Critic head vf_head Linear(128 → 1), on the same encoder SAC only twin Q encoders (same shape) on observations and actions, each with a Linear(128 → 1) head; target copies of actor and critics Distribution one diagonal Gaussian per agent (TorchDiagGaussian), combined

CTDE: CTDEModule (ctde.py): the same central encoder, actor head and critic head as CTCE, plus one network per agent, pi_heads[i]: \(o_i\) → Linear(128) → ReLU → Linear(128) → ReLU → Linear(2 × \(\dim a_i\)). Acting (data collection, evaluation, inference) uses pi_heads, each on its own agent's observation; the loss is computed from the central pi. That split is the defect I-48.

docs.title: 3. Algorithms ([P1] §3.7.2, [P2] §3.3)
docs.text:
All three are actor-critic methods for continuous actions:

PPO, on-policy: a clipped surrogate objective with GAE advantages.

\[ J^{\text{CLIP}}(\theta_i) = \mathbb{E}_t\left[ \min\left( r_t(\theta_i) A_t,\ \operatorname{clip}\left(r_t(\theta_i), 1 - \varepsilon, 1 + \varepsilon\right) A_t \right) \right], \qquad r_t(\theta_i) = \frac{\pi_{\theta_i}(a_t \mid o_t)}{\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(a_t \mid o_t)} \tag{[P2] 11-12} \]

APPO, asynchronous PPO: actors sample while the learner trains, and V-trace corrects for the lag between the two.

\[ V_t^{\text{target}} = V(s_t) + \sum_{k=0}^{l-1} \psi^k \left( \prod_{j=0}^{k-1} c_{t+j} \right) \rho_{t+k}\, \delta_{t+k}, \qquad \rho_t = \min\left( \bar\rho,\ \frac{\pi_{\text{target}}(a_t \mid o_t)}{\pi_{\text{behavior}}(a_t \mid o_t)} \right) \tag{[P2] 13-14} \]

SAC, off-policy with a replay buffer: maximises reward plus entropy, with twin Q-networks and a learned temperature \(\alpha\).

\[ J(\pi) = \sum_{t=0}^{\tau} \mathbb{E}_{(o_t, a_t) \sim \rho_\pi}\left[ r(o_t, a_t) + \alpha\, \mathcal{H}\left(\pi(\cdot \mid o_t)\right) \right] \tag{[P2] 15} \]

How each is computed step by step in RLlib is in One training iteration.

In the original code

RLAlgorithm selects RLlib's PPOConfig, APPOConfig or SACConfig (train.py L207-L262), with PyTorch, one learner, and RLlib's new API stack. Everything the code does not set is RLlib's default (§4).

docs.title: 4. Hyperparameters ([P2] Table 8)
docs.text:
[P2] gives the initial values; population-based training changes some of them during training (§5).

PPO APPO SAC Learning rate \(10^{-5}\) \(10^{-5}\) actor \(10^{-5}\), critic \(10^{-5}\) Discount \(\psi\) 0.99 0.99 0.99 Entropy coefficient 0.01 0.01 dynamic (target entropy*) Gradient clip 0.5 0.5 0.5 Clip parameter 0.2 – – Advantage GAE V-trace – Batch / buffer minibatch 128 – buffer capacity 1000

* "For centralized paradigms (CTCE/CTDE), the target entropy is set to the negative sum of all action dimensions (\(-\sum \dim A_i\)). For the decentralized mode (DTDE), it corresponds to the negative dimension of the individual agent's action space (\(-\dim A_i\))."

In the original code

What the code sets (train.py L215-L259), Table 8's values plus the ones [P2] does not list:

Setting PPO APPO SAC lr 1e-5 1e-5 actor_lr 1e-5, critic_lr 1e-5 gamma 0.99 RLlib default 0.99 0.99 lambda_ 0.95 0.95 – use_critic, use_gae True, True – – vtrace – True – num_epochs 30 – – minibatch_size 128 – – kl_coeff 0.0 0.0 – entropy_coeff 0.01 0.01 – clip_param 0.2 RLlib default 0.4 – grad_clip 0.5 0.5 0.5 twin_q – – True target_entropy – – \(-\sum_i \dim a_i\) (CTCE, CTDE), \(-\dim a_i\) of the first agent (DTDE) Replay buffer – – EpisodeReplayBuffer (CTCE, CTDE) or MultiAgentEpisodeReplayBuffer (DTDE), capacity 1000 batch_mode RLlib default truncate_episodes default complete_episodes

With [P2]'s 4 action numbers per agent and 8 agents, SAC's target entropy is −32 for the group and −4 per agent.

What comes from RLlib's defaults (Ray 2.51.1), which the code does not set:

PPO APPO SAC Batch per iteration 4000 environment steps (train_batch_size) fragments of 50 steps, learner batches of 500 256 transitions per gradient step Updates 30 epochs × minibatches of 128, ≈ 940 per iteration one per batch, each batch reused up to twice one per training step; starts after 1500 sampled steps Value loss coefficient 1.0, squared error capped at 10 coefficient 0.5 Huber loss on the twin Q-values Other use_kl_loss=True, kl_target 0.01 target policy refreshed every 2 × 4 × 2 batches, circular buffer of 4 batches tau 0.005, initial \(\alpha\) 1.0, \(\alpha\) learning rate 3e-4 Iteration length one training step at least 10 s at least 1 s and 100 sampled steps Actions rescaled from \([-1, 1]\) to the bounds (normalize_actions=True) the same the same

Networks. The papers do not describe them. In DTDE they are RLlib's defaults (for PPO and APPO: two hidden layers of 256, tanh, actor and critic on a shared encoder, log-std clipped at ±20); in CTCE and CTDE the custom modules of §2 (128, ReLU).

docs.title: 5. Population-based training ([P1] §3.7.2, [P2] §4.2)
docs.text:
Both papers name Population-Based Training (PBT, Jaderberg et al. 2017), which "jointly optimizes the neural network weights and hyperparameters of a population" ([P1]). [P2]: "10 tune samples for each of the nine configurations, resulting in 90 concurrent trials … PBT periodically clones the weights of the best-performing trials, while … the framework mutates the hyperparameters of low-performing trials." Which hyperparameters, over which ranges and how often are not given.

In the original code

RLTrainer.train (train.py L401-L460) runs every training through Ray Tune with PopulationBasedTraining, also for a single trial:

Setting Value Trials tune_samples (default 1) Score env_runners/episode_return_mean, maximised Perturbation interval every checkpoint_freq training iterations Mutated (PPO, APPO) lr ~ loguniform(1e-4, 1e-2), entropy_coeff ~ loguniform(0.01, 10), lambda_ ~ loguniform(0.8, 0.99) Mutated (SAC) actor_lr, critic_lr ~ loguniform(1e-4, 1e-2) Exploit, explore Ray Tune's defaults: the bottom 25 % of trials copy a top-25 % trial's weights and settings; each setting is then resampled from its range with probability 0.25, else multiplied by 1.2 or 0.8

The mutation ranges are in train.py L178-L198. How they relate to the starting values is I-49.

docs.title: 6. The training run ([P2] §4.2)
docs.text:
[P2]: "Each configuration is trained for a total of 10 000 episodes … Model checkpoints are saved every 10 iterations, and the evaluation is performed at each training iteration, with the duration automatically determined by the framework … based on the capacity of the evaluation workers." Hardware: a 12-core Ryzen 9 9900X, 128 GB RAM, an RTX 4090.

In the original code

RLTrainer (train.py L39-L460):

Setting Argument (default) What it does Budget iters (100) training stops after this many training iterations Checkpoints checkpoint_freq (10) every checkpoint_freq iterations and at the end; the 3 best by evaluation return are kept Evaluation evaluation_interval (1), evaluation_duration ("auto") every iteration, in episodes, in parallel with training, without exploration (exploration=False: the policy's most likely action) Workers cpus (cpu_count() − 4) that many sampling workers and as many evaluation workers GPUs gpus (all CUDA devices) for the one learner Output storage_path Tune experiment lem_<algorithm>_<paradigm>_<date>, plus the environment config

train_checkpoint continues from a checkpoint; restore_experiment resumes a Tune experiment.

[P2]'s experiment in the notebook. case6_implicit_cooperation.ipynb runs one combination at a time (ALGO, MODE) with:

Setting [P2] Notebook Budget 10 000 episodes iters=10000 (TRAINING_EPISODES), so 10 000 iterations Trials 10 per configuration TUNE_SAMPLES = 100 Checkpoints (and PBT interval) every 10 iterations CHECKPOINT_FREQ = 2 Evaluation every iteration, automatic duration EVALUATION_INTERVAL = 1, EVALUATION_DURATION = 3 Resources 12 cores, 1 GPU CPUS = 1, GPUS = 0 Network width – EMBEDDINGS_DIM = 128

docs.title: 7. The 3 × 3 experiment ([P2] §4-5)
docs.text:
Set-up. 8 agents on the IEEE 34-bus feeder ([P2] Table 6), each with PV and a battery (95 % efficiency, SoC 5-95 %):

Agent Node Capacity (kW) Battery (as printed, kW) Small industry 840 180 108 Community hospital 890 170 85 University campus 844 140 98 Shopping mall 816 130 78 Residential complex 800 80 64 Apartment building 830 75 52.5 Community solar farm 848 180 180 Parking lot 860 160 144

Environment ([P2] Table 7): 24 steps of 1 h, grid capacity 1800 kW, seed 42, prices 20-600, quantities 0-180 kWh, forecast error 30 %, asynchronous orders. Average pricing, \(p = (p_{\text{buy}} + p_{\text{sell}})/2\), and partner preference enabled (§4.1).

In the original code

The notebook builds a different population: 8 agents commercial_morning_001 … flexible_coordinator_002 of 150-400 kW, battery ratios 0.5-1.0 (SoC 5-95 %, efficiency 0.95), profiles from data/*_60min.csv, on GridTopology.IEEE34 with 8 nodes, and the proportional-surplus clearing mechanism. The rest matches Table 7: max_steps=24, capacity 1800 kW, seed 42, prices 20-600, quantities 0.1-180, max_error=0.3, num_anchor=4, enable_asynchronous_order=True, enable_reset_dso_profiles=False, enable_partner_preference=True.

Results ([P2] Table 9, mean episode reward over 10 000 training episodes; all nine runs converged before 300 episodes):

CTCE PPO CTCE APPO CTCE SAC CTDE PPO CTDE APPO CTDE SAC DTDE PPO DTDE APPO DTDE SAC Mean 3099.4 3143.9 3139.8 3004.8 3096.5 3158.2 2742.5 2998 54.5 Max 3123.3 3272.1 3189.7 3074.1 3181.4 3166.1 2935.2 3243.5 708.4

Final hyperparameters after PBT ([P2] Table 10, best trial of each configuration):

CTCE PPO CTCE APPO CTCE SAC CTDE PPO CTDE APPO CTDE SAC DTDE PPO DTDE APPO DTDE SAC Learning rate 9.2e-6 3.3e-4 4.6e-3 9.2e-6 1.2e-5 2.9e-3 4.4e-3 3.7e-5 1.0e-3 Entropy coefficient 5.72 0.01 – 0.04 0.01 – 0.24 0.02 –

Scalability test ([P2] §4.3): the same set-up with 1000 episodes per run, one PBT trial, the full 3 × 3 matrix, and 2, 20 or 34 agents; wall-clock time to convergence is measured.

docs.title: 8. Using a trained policy
docs.text:
The papers do not describe how a trained policy is run outside training.

In the original code

RLInference (inference.py) loads the module from a checkpoint and plays iters episodes (the notebook: ITERS_INFERENCE = 100). For each agent it takes the network's mean action (exploration=False) or samples from the Gaussian (exploration=True), clips it to the action bounds and steps the environment, collecting episode rewards and market metrics. DTDE runs on the market environment, CTCE and CTDE on the grouped one. How this differs from training's actions is I-61.

docs.title: 9. Points the papers leave unspecified
docs.text:
Needed to train MARLEM's agents but not given in [P1] or [P2]:

  • The network architectures (layers, sizes, activations, shared or separate actor and critic).
  • What "10 000 episodes" means in RLlib's terms, and the batch size of PPO and APPO.
  • PPO's number of epochs, \(\lambda\) and KL settings; APPO's buffer and target update; SAC's batch size, warm-up and target-network rate.
  • The PBT mutation ranges, perturbation interval and exploit rule.
  • How the observation is scaled before it reaches the networks.
  • How the action's discrete parts (\(\alpha\), \(\beta\)) come from a continuous policy.
  • The number of evaluation episodes and on which days or seeds evaluation runs.
In the original code Point In the code Networks DTDE: RLlib's defaults (PPO, APPO: 2 × 256 tanh, shared encoder). CTCE, CTDE: custom, 2 × 128 ReLU, shared encoder; CTDE adds per-agent 3-layer acting heads (§2) Budget iters training iterations; PPO samples 4000 environment steps per iteration (≈ 166 days of 24 steps) PPO 30 epochs, minibatches of 128, \(\lambda\) = 0.95, kl_coeff 0 APPO RLlib's defaults: batches of 500, buffer of 4 batches, clip 0.4, \(\lambda\) 0.95 set SAC RLlib's defaults: batch 256, warm-up 1500 steps, tau 0.005; uniform buffer of 1000, whole episodes PBT §5: lr, entropy_coeff, lambda_ (SAC: the two learning rates), every checkpoint_freq iterations, Ray Tune's 25 % quantile rule Observation scaling none: raw values Discrete action parts buy if \(\alpha > 0.5\); partner int(β) (§1.1) Evaluation in parallel with training, every iteration, "auto" duration, on the training environment and seed

docs.title: MARLEM: the market as stated in the paper
docs.text:
The part of the MARLEM method this rebuild implements: the market, its DSO, the agents' accounting and batteries, the grid, and the order of one market step. Everything about reinforcement learning is left out (the observation, the reward, the training paradigms and algorithms, the learning experiments): here orders come from scripted rules or from the user on the Step page, not from learned policies. The learning half is in the learning layer as stated in the papers. This file says what the paper says, not what the code does. Taken from the refactor branch's full summary of both papers and cut to the market. Where the paper leaves out what is needed to compute something, a folded section titled Not in [P1]: the original code (click to open) gives what the original implementation does (salazarna/marlem, commit 15d6715), so the gap can be read off; it describes that code, faults included, not what this rebuild does.

Source

  • [P1] Salazar-Peña, Tabares, González-Mancera. MARLEM: A multi-agent reinforcement learning simulation framework for implicit cooperation in decentralized local energy markets. Applied Energy 412 (2026) 127546. doi:10.1016/j.apenergy.2026.127546. This paper defines the environment.
  • [P2] Same authors, Harnessing Implicit Cooperation: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Approach Towards Decentralized Local Energy Markets (SSRN preprint), the learning study. Cited here only for the mean congestion (§6.3).

Equation numbers, at the right of each equation, are [P1]'s own; the one taken from [P2] is marked. Equations garbled in the PDF text extraction were reconstructed from the surrounding text and are marked (reconstructed).

Notation

Symbol Meaning \(i \in \mathcal{I}\) DER agent (prosumer) \(t \in \{1,\dots,\tau\}\) Trading period (time step) \(G_t,\ D_t\) Generation and demand of an agent at \(t\) \(E_{\text{bought},t},\ E_{\text{sold},t}\) Energy bought and sold by an agent at \(t\) \(p,\ q\) Price and quantity (of an order or trade) \(p_{\text{FiT}},\ p_{\text{utility}}\) DSO feed-in tariff (DSO buys) and utility price (DSO sells) \(C_{\text{nom}},\ SoC\) Battery nominal capacity and state of charge \(\mathcal{G} = \langle \mathcal{V}, \xi \rangle\) Grid graph: nodes \(\mathcal{V}\), lines (edges) \(\xi\) \(d_{ij}\) Electrical distance between agents \(i\) and \(j\) (shortest path)

docs.title: 1. Architecture ([P1] §3.1, Fig. 2)
docs.text:
The paper has three conceptual levels:

Level Content In this rebuild Level 0: Platform Marketplace Market Module (order matching, clearing, DSO, reputation, validation) and Grid Module (network, losses, congestion). Provides the physical and economic environment. built: the market, and a SimBench network with a power flow instead of the paper's graph model Level 1: MARL Agents Self-interested DER agents with generation and demand profiles and an optional battery. Each learns a bidding policy from local observations. the agents and their batteries, without learning: orders come from rules or the user Level 2: Implicit Cooperation The emergent coordination produced by shared KPIs in the observations and cooperation terms in the reward, also measured by those KPIs. left out

docs.title: 2. Orders ([P1] §3.2.3)
docs.text:
In the paper an agent's action is its order for the period. Without learning, the same four values describe what a participant submits:

\[ a_i = \left\langle p_{\text{bid}},\ q_{\text{bid}},\ \alpha,\ \beta \right\rangle \tag{2} \] Component Domain Meaning \(p_{\text{bid}}\) \([p_{\min}, p_{\max}]\) Bid price \(q_{\text{bid}}\) \([q_{\min}, q_{\max}]\) Bid quantity \(\alpha\) \(\{0, 1\}\) Order type: 0 = sell, 1 = buy \(\beta\) \(\{0, 1, \dots, \lvert\mathcal{I}\rvert + 1\}\) Preferred trading partner index (the other agents, the DSO, or no preference)

Two constraint layers are applied:

  1. \(p_{\text{bid}}\) and \(q_{\text{bid}}\) are clipped to the market bounds.
  2. \(q_{\text{bid}}\) is constrained for physical feasibility with the battery, using \(q_{\text{sell,max}}\) and \(q_{\text{buy,max}}\) from [P1] (15) (§5.2).

docs.title: 3. One market step ([P1] §3.9, Fig. 4)
docs.text:
The paper's period \(t\) runs eight phases. Phases 5 and 7 exist only for learning (the reward, the observation) and are not part of this rebuild; the KPI update of phase 5 belongs to Level 2 and is left out too.

# Phase Content Here 1 Action processing and validation Limit each order by current generation, demand and battery state (physical). Then validate that price, quantity, type and partner fall within market bounds (rule-based). yes 2 Order creation and submission Validated orders become formal orders. If no partner is given, a rule-based selection scores partners by reputation and grid distance. yes 3 Market clearing and trade execution Three-stage clearing (§4): mutual preferences → double auction (with reputation) → DSO for the residual. Output: all executed trades and summary statistics. yes 4 Energy tracking and battery updates Trades update each agent's physical state (energy tracking, battery SoC) and the grid state (balance, congestion). yes; the grid state comes from a power flow 5 Reward calculation and KPI updates System KPIs from trades, agent states and grid conditions, then every agent's reward. no (learning) 6 State transition Advance the clock. Update states that depend on the full market outcome, such as financial balances and reputation scores. yes 7 Observation update Build each agent's next observation. no (learning) 8 Episode management Stop after the last period \(\tau\); otherwise repeat for \(t+1\). yes: the last step of the day

docs.title: 4.1 Market operation workflow ([P1] Algorithm 1)
docs.text:
Input: agents I, joint action {a_1 … a_I}, market state S_t
Output: executed trades, updated market state S_t′

Phase 1 — Order collection and validation
  O_t ← ∅
  for each agent i:
      o_i ← ActionToOrder(a_i)
      if ValidateOrder(o_i, S_t): O_t ← O_t ∪ {o_i}

Phase 2 — P2P market clearing
  trades_pref,  O_rem ← PreferenceMatch(O_t)        # Stage 1: mutual preferences
  trades_price, O_rem ← PriceMatch(O_rem)           # Stage 2: continuous double auction
  trades_P2P ← trades_pref ∪ trades_price
  for each trade in trades_P2P: UpdateAgentStates(trade)   # energy, profit for buyer and seller

Phase 3 — DSO clearing and finalization
  trades_DSO ← DSOClear(O_rem)                      # Stage 3: residual cleared by the DSO
  for each trade in trades_DSO: UpdateAgentStates(trade)
  trades_t ← trades_P2P ∪ trades_DSO
  ValidateBlock(trades_t)                           # simulated blockchain validation
  S_t′ ← UpdateMarketState(trades_t, S_t)           # prices, volumes, reputations
  G_{t+1} ← UpdateGridState(trades_t, G_t)          # congestion on the affected edges
return trades_t, S_t′

docs.title: 4.2 Three-stage matching ([P1] §3.3.2, Fig. 3)
docs.text: Stage Rule 1 Preference-based Match agents that have mutually specified each other as preferred partners. Pre-arranged relationships take priority over the open market. 2 Price-based (double auction) Buys sorted by price descending, sells by price ascending. Trade every compatible pair with \(p_{\text{bid}} \ge p_{\text{ask}}\). Reputation is the secondary sort key (tie-breaker). 3 DSO clearing The DSO buys all residual supply at \(p_{\text{FiT}}\) and sells all residual demand at \(p_{\text{utility}}\), guaranteeing clearing. The prices satisfy \(p_{\text{FiT}} < p_{\text{P2P}} < p_{\text{utility}}\), which makes local trading attractive.

docs.title: 4.3 Clearing (pricing) mechanisms ([P1] §3.3.3)
docs.text:
The P2P trade price \(p_{ij}\) is set by a configurable mechanism.

Average:

\[ p_{ij} = \frac{p_{\text{buy}} + p_{\text{sell}}}{2} \tag{9} \]

Pay-as-bid (seller): \(p_{ij} = p_{\text{seller}}\).

Pay-as-offer (buyer): \(p_{ij} = p_{\text{buyer}}\). This favours the seller, since \(p_{\text{buy}} \ge p_{\text{sell}}\).

Nash bargaining, an equal split of the surplus:

\[ p_{ij} = p_{\text{sell}} + \frac{p_{\text{buy}} - p_{\text{sell}}}{2} \tag{10} \]

Proportional surplus (reconstructed): the surplus is split by each side's distance from a reference price \(p_{\text{ref}}\):

\[ p_{ij} = p_{\text{sell}} + \frac{p_{\text{buy}} - p_{\text{ref}}}{(p_{\text{buy}} - p_{\text{ref}}) + (p_{\text{ref}} - p_{\text{sell}})} \cdot \left(p_{\text{buy}} - p_{\text{sell}}\right) \tag{11} \]

The [P1] case study also uses a bid-ask spread mechanism, which is not defined in §3.3.3.

docs.title: 4.4 DSO: balance and fees ([P1] §3.3.1)
docs.text:
The DSO is the market maker of last resort and a proxy grid operator that collects grid fees.

DSO balance:

\[ B_{\text{DSO}} = \sum_{\text{trades}} \left( E_{\text{sold}} - E_{\text{bought}} \right) \tag{7} \]

Total fee for a trade between \(i\) and \(j\) with quantity \(q_{ij}\) and price \(p_{ij}\):

\[ F_{\text{total}} = F_{\text{cong}} + F_{\text{trans}} + F_{\text{imb}} + F_{\text{volt}} + F_{\text{thermal}} + F_{\text{zone}} \tag{8} \] \[ \begin{align*} F_{\text{cong}} &= f_{\text{cong}} \,(C_t - C_{\text{threshold}})\, q_{ij}\, p_{ij} \tag{8a} \\ F_{\text{imb}} &= f_{\text{imb}} \,\lvert B_{\text{impact}} \rvert\, q_{ij}\, p_{ij} \tag{8b} \\ F_{\text{volt}} &= \min(V_{\text{drop}},\, V_{\text{threshold}})\, q_{ij}\, p_{ij} \tag{8c} \\ F_{\text{thermal}} &= \min(f_{\text{thermal}},\, f_{\text{threshold}})\, q_{ij}\, p_{ij} \tag{8d} \\ F_{\text{zone}} &= -\, f_{\text{zone}}\, q_{ij}\, p_{ij} \quad \text{(same-zone bonus)} \tag{8e} \\ V_{\text{drop}} &= f_{\text{volt}}\, d_{ij} \tag{8f} \\ f_{\text{thermal}} &= \frac{C_t - T_{\text{threshold}}}{1 - T_{\text{threshold}}} \tag{8g} \end{align*} \] \[ B_{\text{impact}} = \begin{cases} \ \ \min\!\left(\dfrac{q_{ij}}{\lvert B_{\text{grid}} \rvert},\, 1\right) & \text{DSO buying during excess supply / selling during excess demand} \\[2ex] -\min\!\left(\dfrac{q_{ij}}{\lvert B_{\text{grid}} \rvert},\, 1\right) & \text{DSO buying during excess demand / selling during excess supply} \\[2ex] \ \ 0 & \text{balanced grid} \end{cases} \tag{8h} \] Parameter Meaning Default in paper \(C_t \in [0,1]\) Congestion level at \(t\) — \(C_{\text{threshold}}\) Congestion intervention threshold 0.8 (80 % utilization) \(V_{\text{threshold}}\) Voltage-drop threshold 0.05 (5 %) \(T_{\text{threshold}}\) Thermal instability threshold 0.2 (20 % utilization) \(B_{\text{grid}} \in [-1,1]\) Grid balance (\(>0\) excess supply, \(<0\) excess demand) — \(f_{\ast}\) Configurable fee factors not given

\(F_{\text{trans}}\) is named in (8), described as a charge for "usage per unit of distance of the transmission lines (predefined by the DSO)", but has no formula in the paper. Agents do not observe the topology; only the DSO computes distance fees and congestion.

Not in [P1]: the original code

DSOAgent.calculate_fees (dso.py) computes eq. 8 for every peer trade in stage 2, with these values:

Factor In the code \(f_{\text{cong}}\) 0.5 \(f_{\text{volt}}\) 0.15 per unit of graph distance \(f_{\text{zone}}\) 0.15 \(f_{\text{imb}}\) 0.15 \(f_{\text{threshold}}\) (eq. 8d) 0.3 \(C_{\text{threshold}}\), \(V_{\text{threshold}}\), \(T_{\text{threshold}}\) 0.8, 0.05, 0.2 (as the paper) Transmission factor distance_factor = 0.35 is defined but never used

Each part, with \(v = q_{ij}\, p_{ij}\) the trade's value:

\[ \begin{aligned} F_{\text{cong}} &= f_{\text{cong}}\,(C_t - C_{\text{threshold}})\, v && \text{if } C_t > C_{\text{threshold}} \text{, else } 0 \\ F_{\text{trans}} &= 0 && \text{always} \\ F_{\text{volt}} &= \min(0.2,\ V_{\text{drop}})\, v,\quad V_{\text{drop}} = f_{\text{volt}}\, d_{ij} && \text{if } V_{\text{drop}} > V_{\text{threshold}} \text{, else } 0 \\ F_{\text{thermal}} &= \min\!\left(0.3,\ \frac{C_t - T_{\text{threshold}}}{1 - T_{\text{threshold}}}\right) v && \text{if } C_t > T_{\text{threshold}} \text{, else } 0 \\ F_{\text{zone}} &= -f_{\text{zone}}\, v && \text{if buyer and seller share a zone} \\ F_{\text{imb}} &= f_{\text{imb}}\, \lvert B_{\text{impact}} \rvert\, v && \text{if } B_{\text{impact}} < 0 \text{, else } 0 \end{aligned} \]
  • \(C_t\), the congestion level, is the highest edge loading on the shortest path between buyer and seller, \(C_t = \max_{e \in \text{path}} \min(1,\ F_e / C_e)\). It falls back to the mean over all edges when no path is found.
  • \(d_{ij}\) is the shortest-path length on the topology graph.
  • \(B_{\text{impact}}\) follows eq. 8h, \(\pm\min(q_{ij} / \lvert B \rvert, 1)\). \(B\) is the DSO balance, not a normalised \(B_{\text{grid}} \in [-1, 1]\), and the impact of a peer trade is defined as 0.

So, against eq. 8:

  • \(F_{\text{trans}}\) is 0, although the distance is computed on the line above it (dso.py L297, L318).
  • \(V_{\text{threshold}}\) is used as a gate, not the cap of eq. 8c, and the cap is 0.2.
  • \(F_{\text{imb}}\) is always 0, because the fee is only computed for peer trades.
  • Trades with the DSO carry no fee at all, being created with distance, loss and fee 0.
  • The total is stored on the trade and added to dso.fees, but nobody is ever charged.

The DSO balance (eq. 7) in the code. dso.balance changes only for DSO trades made in stage 1 or 2, never for stage 3 where they normally happen, so it stays 0. It is also carried from one step to the next. The DSO's profit is kept separately, as \(p_{\text{utility}} \cdot \text{sold} - p_{\text{FiT}} \cdot \text{bought}\) per step.

These are faults against [P1]; see the market validation, §6.

docs.title: 4.5 Reputation and validation ([P1] §3.3.4)
docs.text:
Reputation \(r_i \in [0,1]\), updated after every trading period with a decay factor that weighs recent behaviour more:

\[ r_i = w_{\text{rel}}\, \delta_{\text{rel},i} + w_{\text{fair}}\, \delta_{\text{fair},i} + w_{\text{grid}}\, \delta_{\text{grid},i} \tag{12} \]
  • \(\delta_{\text{rel}}\): reliability, the ratio of matched to total order volume;
  • \(\delta_{\text{fair}}\): price fairness, the deviation from the market clearing price;
  • \(\delta_{\text{grid}}\): grid contribution, whether trades alleviate or worsen grid stress.

The weights \(w\) are not given. Reputation is the tie-breaker in the double auction.

Not in [P1]: the original code

[P1] names the three parts of eq. 12 but gives no formula, weight, decay value or starting value. The original computes them in ReputationHandler (reputation.py), after every step, for every agent, from that step's trades:

Part In the code Weights \(w_{\text{rel}} = 0.3\), \(w_{\text{fair}} = 0.2\), \(w_{\text{grid}} = 0.5\) Start \(r_i \sim U(0, 1)\), drawn at each reset Score \(r_i^{\text{new}} = \min\left(1, \max\left(0,\ w_{\text{rel}}\, \delta_{\text{rel},i} + w_{\text{fair}}\, \delta_{\text{fair},i} + w_{\text{grid}}\, \delta_{\text{grid},i}\right)\right)\) Decay \(r_i \leftarrow \tau_t\, r_i + (1 - \tau_t)\, r_i^{\text{new}}\), with \(\tau_t = (t \bmod T) / T\) the time of day

With \(n_i\) the number of agent \(i\)'s trades in the step (peer and DSO trades alike), \(u_i\) the number of its unmatched orders, \(\bar{p}\) the step's clearing price and \(B\) the grid balance:

\[ \delta_{\text{rel},i} = \frac{n_i}{n_i + u_i} \qquad \delta_{\text{fair},i} = 1 - \min\left(1,\ \frac{1}{n_i} \sum_{k} \frac{\lvert p_k - \bar{p} \rvert}{\bar{p}}\right) \qquad \delta_{\text{grid},i} = \frac{1}{2}\left(1 + \frac{1}{n_i} \sum_{k} \iota_k\right) \]

where the sums run over agent \(i\)'s trades \(k\), and each trade's grid impact \(\iota_k \in [-1, 1]\) is

\[ \iota_k = \begin{cases} 0 & \lvert B \rvert < 0.1 \\ 0.5 & \text{trade with the DSO} \\ +\min(1,\ q_k / \lvert B \rvert) & \text{buying when } B > 0 \text{, or selling when } B < 0 \\ -\min(1,\ q_k / \lvert B \rvert) & \text{selling when } B > 0 \text{, or buying when } B < 0 \end{cases} \]

A part with nothing to measure is neutral, 0.5: reliability with no trades and no unmatched orders, fairness and grid with no trades. A step without any trade leaves every reputation unchanged.

What feeds these formulas matters as much as the formulas:

  • \(u_i\) is always 0, because the matcher passes an empty list of unmatched orders (the DSO clears everything), so \(\delta_{\text{rel}} = 1\) for any agent with a trade.
  • \(\bar{p}\) is the volume-weighted price of all trades, the DSO's included.
  • \(B\) is the DSO balance (dso.balance), which stays 0, so every \(\iota_k = 0\) and \(\delta_{\text{grid}} = 0.5\).
  • The decay weight is the time of day, so the old reputation counts \(1/24\) in the first hour and \(23/24\) in the last.
  • The random start is drawn after reseeding the global generator with the same seed for every agent, so all agents start equal.

The decay weight comes from the environment, not from the reputation module (lem.py):

self.time_of_day = (self.current_step % self.max_steps) / self.max_steps
agent.reputation = self.reputation_handler.update_reputation(agent, matching_result, self.time_of_day)

These are faults against [P1]; see the market validation, §8.

Decentralized validation. After each period, all trades are hashed (SHA-256), aggregated into a block and validated with a simplified proof-of-work, then appended to an immutable ledger.

Not in [P1]: the original code

Validator (validation.py) collects trades and closes a block every 5 trades (block_size = 5), and the matcher forces one more at the end of each step. A block's hash is SHA-256 over the previous block's hash, a nonce, the block time (its earliest trade's) and, per trade, buyer, seller, price, quantity and time; distance, loss and fee are not included. Proof of work raises the nonce until the hash starts with difficulty zeros (default 2, so about 256 tries per block). The chain starts with an empty genesis block, and verify_chain recomputes every hash and link.

docs.title: 5.1 State and accounting
docs.text:
Each agent has an ID, a grid location, forecast profiles \(G_t\) and \(D_t\), a balance, profit, reputation, and cumulative demand satisfied and deferred.

Balance; positive means surplus, negative means deficit:

\[ B_t = (G_t - D_t) + (E_{\text{bought},t} - E_{\text{sold},t}) \tag{13} \]

Profit:

\[ \text{profit}_{t+1} = \text{profit}_t + \sum_{\text{trades}} \left( p_{\text{sell}}\, q_{\text{sell}} - p_{\text{buy}}\, q_{\text{buy}} \right) \tag{14} \]

Partner selection: learned through \(\beta\), or, if not RL-controlled, rule-based. The rule-based variant uses a weighted score of high reputation and short grid distance.

docs.title: 5.2 Physical feasibility ([P1] §3.4.2)
docs.text:
Before an order is submitted, the requested quantity is constrained by:

\[ \begin{align*} q_{\text{sell,max}} &= \max(0,\, G_t - D_t) + E_{\text{dischargeable}} \tag{15a} \\ q_{\text{buy,max}} &= \max(0,\, D_t - G_t) + E_{\text{chargeable}} \tag{15b} \\ E_{\text{dischargeable}} &= (SoC_t - SoC_{\min})\, C_{\text{nom}} \tag{15c} \\ E_{\text{chargeable}} &= (SoC_{\max} - SoC_t)\, C_{\text{nom}} \tag{15d} \end{align*} \]

docs.title: 5.3 Battery ([P1] §3.4.3)
docs.text:
Parameters: \(C_{\text{nom}}\), \(SoC_{\min}\), \(SoC_{\max}\), \(\eta_{\text{charge}} \in [0,1]\), \(\eta_{\text{discharge}} \in [0,1]\). The energy stays within \(SoC_{\min} C_{\text{nom}} \le E_{\text{bat},t} \le SoC_{\max} C_{\text{nom}}\) and evolves with the net flow from the agent's balance and trades:

\[ E_{\text{bat},t+1} = \begin{cases} \min\!\left(E_{\text{bat},t} + E_{\text{in}}\, \eta_{\text{charge}},\ SoC_{\max}\, C_{\text{nom}}\right) & \text{charging with } E_{\text{in}} \\[1.5ex] \max\!\left(E_{\text{bat},t} - \dfrac{E_{\text{out}}}{\eta_{\text{discharge}}},\ SoC_{\min}\, C_{\text{nom}}\right) & \text{delivering } E_{\text{out}} \end{cases} \tag{16} \]

Discharging depletes storage by more than the delivered energy. The text says the operations are also bound by "maximum charge/discharge rates", but no rate appears in (16).

docs.title: 5.4 Profiles ([P1] §3.4.4)
docs.text:
Profiles are loaded from files (real data) or generated procedurally, then smoothed.

Generation, solar PV:

\[ G_t = C_{\text{gen},i}\, I_t\, \left(1 + \varepsilon_{\text{noise}} + \varepsilon_{\text{cloud}}\right) \tag{17} \]

\(C_{\text{gen},i}\) is the nominal capacity (PV plus battery). \(I_t\) is irradiance, a Gaussian centred at noon. \(\varepsilon_{\text{noise}}\) is random noise. \(\varepsilon_{\text{cloud}}\) is correlated cloud-cover variation.

Demand: a typical pattern with morning and evening peaks, which creates the temporal mismatch with solar generation.

DSO prices: \(p_{\text{FiT}}\) and \(p_{\text{utility}}\) are step functions with higher prices at peak hours, generated by the same algorithm, always with \(p_{\text{utility}} > p_{\text{FiT}}\), and smoothed.

docs.title: 6. Grid ([P1] §3.5)
docs.text: The paper's grid is a graph model. This rebuild replaces it with a SimBench network and an AC power flow (SimBench); the paper's model is kept here because its distances, zones and congestion feed the DSO fees (§4.4) and the partner choice (§5.1).

docs.title: 6.1 Topology
docs.text:
The network is a weighted undirected graph \(\mathcal{G} = \langle \mathcal{V}, \xi \rangle\) with agents at nodes.

  • Predefined topologies: IEEE 13-node and IEEE 34-node feeders.
  • Procedural topologies: mesh, ring and line.

The electrical distance \(d_{ij}\) is the shortest-path length through the graph, not a Euclidean distance.

Zones ([P1] §3.5.4): the graph can be partitioned into connected zones \(\mathcal{Z} = \langle \mathcal{V}, \xi \rangle \subseteq \mathcal{G}\). By default a same-zone trade gets a bonus (the negative fee \(F_{\text{zone}}\)); cross-zone trades can carry extra fees or constraints.

docs.title: 6.2 Constraints
docs.text:
Transmission losses, linear, with loss factor \(\kappa\). The loss derates the delivered quantity and is included in the DSO fees:

\[ l_{ij} = d_{ij}\, q_{ij}\, \kappa \tag{18} \]

Congestion. Total grid capacity is distributed over the edges, with more capacity for shorter (lower-impedance) edges. The congestion of edge \(e\) is:

\[ \zeta_e = \frac{F_e}{\max(C_e)} \tag{19} \]

docs.title: 6.3 State updates ([P1] §3.5.3)
docs.text:
Power-flow update: after each period, for every executed trade, find the shortest path between buyer and seller, then increase the flow \(F_e\) on every edge of that path by \(q_{ij}\) (considering losses). Trades that would violate capacity "can be penalized or disallowed by the DSO".

Grid balance; close to 0 means a self-sufficient market:

\[ B_{\text{grid}} = \sum_{i \in \mathcal{I}} \left( G_i - D_i + E_{\text{bought},i} - E_{\text{sold},i} \right) \tag{20} \]

Mean congestion, from [P2]:

\[ \bar{\zeta} = \frac{1}{\lvert \xi \rvert} \sum_{e \in \xi} \frac{F_e}{\max(C_e)} \tag*{[P2] (2)} \]

docs.title: 7. The paper's case study without learning ([P1] §4–5)
docs.text:
The case study of [P1] trains nothing: its agents bid at random within the rules. That makes it the reference for a market without learning.

Item Value Agents 7, 24-hour daily cycle Grid Mesh topology, nominal capacity 1200 kW Clearing Bid-ask spread mechanism Price / quantity range 35–280 $/MWh; 0.1–200 kWh Generation Base capacity 60 kW per agent (random variation) Scenarios (1) no battery; (2) strategic battery: battery ratios 0.5–1.2, 95 % efficiency, profiles designed for time-shifting (morning generation with storage vs evening demand) Agents' policy Zero-intelligence: uniform random bids within valid bounds that respect physical constraints. No MARL training in [P1]. Reported P2P price distribution, net grid imbalance and P2P trading ratio over 24 h, coordination score, trading-network plots

docs.title: 8. Points the paper leaves unspecified
docs.text:
Needed to implement the market but not defined in [P1]:

  • The formula of \(F_{\text{trans}}\), and the meaning of \(f_{\text{threshold}}\) in (8d).
  • The fee factors \(f_{\ast}\).
  • Reputation weights and the decay factor.
  • The loss factor \(\kappa\), the edge-capacity allocation rule, whether edge flows reset each period, and the capacity-violation policy ("penalized or disallowed").
  • Battery charge and discharge rate limits.
  • The bid-ask spread mechanism used in the case study (§7), which §3.3.3 does not define.
Not in [P1]: the original code

What the original implementation uses for each point:
