Point In the code \(F_{\text{trans}}\) Always 0; the distance is computed but unused (dso.py) \(f_{\text{threshold}}\) (8d) A cap: \(F_{\text{thermal}} = \min(0.3,\ f_{\text{thermal}})\, q_{ij}\, p_{ij}\) Fee factors \(f_{\ast}\) \(f_{\text{cong}} = 0.5\), \(f_{\text{volt}} = 0.15\), \(f_{\text{zone}} = 0.15\), \(f_{\text{imb}} = 0.15\); a distance_factor = 0.35 is defined but never used (dso.py) Reputation weights \(w_{\text{rel}} = 0.3\), \(w_{\text{fair}} = 0.2\), \(w_{\text{grid}} = 0.5\) (reputation.py) Decay factor The time of day: \(r_i \leftarrow \tau_t\, r_i + (1 - \tau_t)\, r_i^{\text{new}}\), \(\tau_t = (t \bmod T)/T\) (reputation.py) Loss factor \(\kappa\) 0.03 per unit of graph distance, a default argument no caller changes (network.py) Edge capacity The grid capacity \(C\) shared in inverse proportion to edge length: \(C_e = C \cdot \dfrac{1/d_e}{\sum_{e'} 1/d_{e'}}\) (network.py) Edge flows per period Never reset. Each edge starts at a random \(U(0, 0.3) \cdot C_e\), every trade on its path adds its quantity, and the flow is capped at \(C_e\) (network.py, L325) Capacity-violation policy "Disallowed", in two different checks. Stage 1 (validate_grid_constraints) rejects a pair if \(\lvert B_{\text{DSO}} + q \rvert\) exceeds the grid capacity or the path congestion exceeds 0.8 (dso.py). Stage 2 skips a match while \(\lvert B \rvert > q_{\max} \cdot N\) (matching.py, L299). Trades with the DSO are never checked. Nothing is penalised Battery rate limits None. A charge or discharge is limited only by the room to \(SoC_{\max}\) or \(SoC_{\min}\) (battery.py) Bid-ask spread mechanism \(p_{ij} = p_{\text{sell}} + \phi\,(p_{\text{buy}} - p_{\text{sell}})\) with \(\phi\) clipped to [0, 1], default 0.5 (the midpoint) (mechanism.py). The matcher passes the market price as \(\phi\), so with prices above 1 it returns \(p_{\text{buy}}\)

Several of these are faults against [P1]; see the market validation.

docs.title: One training iteration, from observation to update
docs.text:
Every calculation in one training iteration, in the order it happens: the agents observe, act and collect a batch of steps; the batch is turned into targets; the losses are computed and the networks updated; the new weights go back to the agents. PPO is followed in full, with the shapes of what flows through each step and what the three paradigms (CTCE, CTDE, DTDE) change on the way. APPO and SAC follow as differences from it. Steps that repeat (every environment step, every minibatch) are written out once, with how often they happen. The training cycle is the shorter overview of the same material. Worked examples puts numbers on the parts our own code defines.

Sources. As in The training cycle: RLlib is Ray 2.51.1, read in its installed source and linked at tag ray-2.51.1; MARLEM's code at the original commit 15d6715; settings are the original's (train.py L215-L259), completed with RLlib's defaults. Where the original code computes something other than what is described, the step says so and links to RL layer: what is wrong.

docs.title: Notation
docs.text:
Symbol Meaning \(N\) number of agents, \(i = 1 \dots N\) \(d_o\), \(d_a\) size of one agent's observation and action (taken equal for all agents here) \(t\) environment step: all \(N\) agents act at once \(o_{i,t} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_o}\) agent \(i\)'s observation \(s_t = (o_{1,t}, \dots, o_{N,t}) \in \mathbb{R}^{N d_o}\) all observations, concatenated (CTCE and CTDE) \(u_{i,t} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_a}\) the action as the policy sampled it, before any rescaling \(a_{i,t}\) the action the environment receives \(r_{i,t}\), \(R_t = \sum_i r_{i,t}\) agent \(i\)'s reward; the group reward of CTCE and CTDE \(m\), \(\ell = \log\sigma\) the Gaussian's mean and log standard deviation, one per action dimension \(\pi_\theta\), \(\mu\) the policy being trained; the copy that collected the data \(V_\phi\) the critic (state value) \(T\) environment steps per iteration: 4000 for PPO \(K\) number of env runners (the original sets \(K\) = cpu_count() - 4)

Settings used below (PPO): \(\gamma = 0.99\), \(\lambda = 0.95\), clip \(\epsilon = 0.2\), value coefficient \(c_v = 1\), value-loss cap 10, entropy coefficient \(c_H = 0.01\), KL coefficient \(\beta = 0\), gradient-norm clip 0.5, learning rate \(10^{-5}\), 30 epochs, minibatches of 128.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    subgraph A["A. Collect (env runners), T = 4000 times"]
        A1["A1 observe o"] --> A2["A2 actor forward: m, log σ"]
        A2 --> A3["A3 sample u, log μ(u)"]
        A3 --> A4["A4 rescale u to the bounds: a"]
        A4 --> A5["A5 env step: r, next o, done"]
        A5 --> A1
    end
    subgraph B["B. Targets (learner), once"]
        B1["B1 episodes to batch"] --> B2["B2 add a bootstrap step"]
        B2 --> B3["B3 critic forward: V(o)"]
        B3 --> B4["B4 λ-returns G"]
        B4 --> B5["B5 advantages Â, standardised"]
    end
    subgraph C["C. Update (learner), ≈ 940 times"]
        C1["C1 forward: m', log σ', V"] --> C2["C2 ratio ρ"]
        C2 --> C3["C3-C7 losses"]
        C3 --> C4["C8 gradients"]
        C4 --> C5["C9 clip norm, C10 Adam step"]
    end
    subgraph D["D. After the update, once"]
        D1["D1 KL coefficient"] --> D2["D2 weights to env runners"]
    end
    A --> B --> C --> D --> A

What happens how often in one PPO iteration:

Step How often Done by A1-A5: observe, act, step the environment \(T = 4000\) environment steps, \(4000/K\) per env runner env runners, with \(\mu\) A2: actor forward pass 4000 per network: \(N \times 4000\) in DTDE and CTDE (one per agent's network), 4000 in CTCE env runners B1-B5: value predictions, returns, advantages once, over the whole batch learner, critic before the update C1-C10: one gradient step 30 epochs × ≈ 31 minibatches ≈ 940; every step used 30 times learner D1: KL coefficient once learner D2: weights to the env runners once learner → env runners

docs.title: A. Collect: from observation to environment step
docs.text: Each env runner holds a copy \(\mu\) of the policy, identical to \(\pi_\theta\) at the start of the iteration (D2 of the previous one). Per environment step it does A1 to A5. Nothing is learned here: no gradients, no critic.

docs.title: A1. Observe
docs.text:
The environment returns one observation per agent, \(o_{i,t} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_o}\).

CTCE CTDE DTDE What the module receives the tuple \((o_{1,t}, \dots, o_{N,t})\), one input for the group (GroupedLEM) the same tuple \(o_{i,t}\), each agent's module its own

RLlib passes the observation to the network as it comes: the default pipeline adds a batch dimension and converts to a tensor, but does not normalise (no MeanStdFilter). The scale of the market's observation features goes straight into the first layer.

docs.title: A2. Actor forward pass
docs.text:
The network turns the observation into the parameters of a Gaussian: a mean \(m\) and a log standard deviation \(\ell = \log\sigma\) per action dimension (forward_exploration, which all three modules route to their inference pass).

DTDE, RLlib's default PPO module per agent (fcnet_hiddens = [256, 256], tanh):

\[h = \tanh\big(W_2 \tanh(W_1 o_{i,t} + b_1) + b_2\big) \in \mathbb{R}^{256}, \qquad [m, \ell] = W_\pi h + b_\pi \in \mathbb{R}^{2 d_a}, \qquad \ell \leftarrow \text{clip}(\ell, -20, 20).\]

CTCE, the custom module (ctce.py L290-L322):

\[e = \text{ReLU}\big(W_2\, \text{ReLU}(W_1 s_t + b_1) + b_2\big) \in \mathbb{R}^{128}, \qquad [m_1, \ell_1, \dots, m_N, \ell_N] = W_\pi e + b_\pi \in \mathbb{R}^{2 N d_a}.\]

One network outputs every agent's mean and log-std, from all observations. There is no clip on \(\ell\) (R-01).

CTDE, the custom module's acting heads (ctde.py L51-L57, L86-L89): one small network \(g_i\) per agent, on its own observation only,

\[[m_i, \ell_i] = g_i(o_{i,t}), \qquad g_i:\ \mathbb{R}^{d_o} \xrightarrow{\text{Linear, ReLU}} \mathbb{R}^{128} \xrightarrow{\text{Linear, ReLU}} \mathbb{R}^{128} \xrightarrow{\text{Linear}} \mathbb{R}^{2 d_a},\]

concatenated over the agents. No clip on \(\ell\). These heads are what acts in CTDE, and they are never trained (I-48).

The value \(V_\phi\) is not computed while collecting; PPO needs it only in B3.

docs.title: A3. Sample the action and its log-probability
docs.text:
Per action dimension \(k\), with \(\sigma_k = e^{\ell_k}\) and fresh noise \(\varepsilon_k \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)\) (get_actions.py):

\[u_k = m_k + \sigma_k \varepsilon_k, \qquad \log\mu(u) = \sum_k \left[-\frac{(u_k - m_k)^2}{2\sigma_k^2} - \ell_k - \tfrac12 \log 2\pi\right].\]

In CTCE and CTDE the sum runs over all \(N d_a\) dimensions, so the group's log-probability is the sum of the agents': \(\log\mu(\mathbf{u}) = \sum_i \log\mu(u_i)\).

Stored for the learner, per step: the observation (\(o_{i,t}\) or \(s_t\)), the sampled \(u\), \(\log\mu(u)\), and the distribution's inputs \([m, \ell]\) (needed for the KL in C6).

docs.title: A4. Rescale to the action bounds
docs.text:
The policy's actions are meant to live in \([-1, 1]\); RLlib rescales them to the environment's bounds and clips (normalize_actions=True, space_utils.py L469-L481):

\[a_k = \text{clip}\left(\text{low}_k + (u_k + 1)\,\frac{\text{high}_k - \text{low}_k}{2},\ \text{low}_k,\ \text{high}_k\right).\]

The environment gets \(a\); the batch keeps the unclipped \(u\). So every \(u_k\) beyond \(\pm 1\) acts as the bound, while the learner still sees and trains on the exact \(u_k\). In CTCE and CTDE each agent's slice is rescaled with the grouped space's bounds, which may be another agent's (I-59).

docs.title: A5. Environment step
docs.text:
The environment applies all \(N\) actions at once and returns, per agent, the reward \(r_{i,t}\), the next observation \(o_{i,t+1}\) and whether the episode ended (terminated, or truncated by a time limit).

CTCE CTDE DTDE Reward stored \(R_t = \sum_i r_{i,t}\) (train.py L684) \(R_t\) \(r_{i,t}\) in agent \(i\)'s episode Done flag one, __all__ one per agent, and __all__

docs.title: A6. Until the batch is full
docs.text: A1-A5 repeat until the env runners together have 4000 environment steps (train_batch_size), each about \(4000/K\). An episode that is still running when a runner's share is full is cut there (batch_mode="truncate_episodes") and continues in the next iteration, with the next iteration's weights. A cut episode is bootstrapped with the critic in B2.

docs.title: B. Targets: what the loss will be compared with
docs.text: Once per iteration, on the learner, before any weight changes (ppo_learner.py L60-L80).

docs.title: B1. Episodes to a batch
docs.text:
The collected episode pieces are laid out as one table per RLlib module.

CTCE CTDE DTDE Modules 1 1 \(N\) Rows per module 4000 4000 ≈ 4000 (one per step the agent acted) One row holds \(s_t\), \(\mathbf{u}_t \in \mathbb{R}^{N d_a}\), \(R_t\), \(\log\mu(\mathbf{u}_t)\), \([m, \ell]\) the same \(o_{i,t}\), \(u_{i,t}\), \(r_{i,t}\), \(\log\mu(u_{i,t})\), \([m, \ell]\)

docs.title: B2. Add a bootstrap step
docs.text: Each episode piece gets one artificial step at its end: the last observation repeated, reward 0, and truncated set if the episode did not terminate (add_one_ts_to_episodes_and_truncate.py). It exists only so that B3 computes \(V_\phi\) of the last observation; a loss mask removes it from every loss in C.

docs.title: B3. Critic forward pass
docs.text:
The critic, with its weights from before this iteration's update, evaluates every row:

CTCE CTDE DTDE Value \(V_\phi(s_t) = w_V^\top e + b_V\), on the actor's encoder output \(e\) the same: central encoder and value head (ctde.py L46-L49) \(V_{\phi_i}(o_{i,t}) = w_V^\top h + b_V\), on the actor's encoder output \(h\)

In all three the critic is a linear head on the same encoder as the actor (RLlib's default is vf_share_layers=True), so in C both losses train the encoder.

docs.title: B4. λ-returns
docs.text:
Backwards in time over each episode piece, with \(\bar V_{t} = V_\phi(o_t)\), or 0 if \(o_t\) ends a terminated episode (value_predictions.py L7-L38):

\[G_t = r_t + \gamma \left[(1 - \lambda)\, \bar V_{t+1} + \lambda\, G_{t+1}\right], \qquad \text{starting from } G = \bar V \text{ at the bootstrap step.}\]

A cut episode therefore ends on the critic's estimate, a terminated one on 0. Written with the one-step error \(\delta_t = r_t + \gamma \bar V_{t+1} - V_\phi(o_t)\), this is the GAE sum: \(G_t = V_\phi(o_t) + \sum_{l \ge 0} (\gamma\lambda)^l \delta_{t+l}\). \(\lambda = 0.95\) sets how far real rewards are used before the critic's estimate takes over (about \(1/(1 - \gamma\lambda) \approx 17\) steps).

\(G_t\) is the value target. It is not rescaled, so it is on the scale of the summed rewards: in CTCE and CTDE about \(N\) times one agent's.

docs.title: B5. Advantages
docs.text:
\[\hat A_t = G_t - V_\phi(o_t), \qquad \hat A_t \leftarrow \frac{\hat A_t - \operatorname{mean}(\hat A)}{\max\big(10^{-4}, \operatorname{std}(\hat A)\big)},\]

the mean and standard deviation taken over the module's whole batch (general_advantage_estimation.py L144-L150). \(\hat A_t > 0\) means "the action taken at \(t\) did better than the critic expected". After standardising, about half of the actions in the batch are reinforced and half discouraged, whatever the reward scale.

In CTCE and CTDE there is one advantage per step for the whole group: every agent's action at \(t\) is pushed in the same direction by the summed outcome, however much that agent contributed to it.

docs.title: C. Update: one gradient step, repeated ≈ 940 times
docs.text: The 4000 rows are shuffled and cut into minibatches of 128; one pass over all of them is an epoch; there are 30 epochs, so ≈ 31 × 30 ≈ 940 gradient steps, and every row is used 30 times (ppo.py L389-L458). In DTDE each step updates all \(N\) modules, each on 128 rows of its own agent. One gradient step, on a minibatch \(b\):

docs.title: C1. Forward pass with the current weights
docs.text:
The same network as in A2 and B3, now with the weights as they are at this step: \([m', \ell'] = \pi_\theta(\cdot)\) and \(V_\phi(\cdot)\) for the 128 rows, the encoder computed once and shared by both heads.

In CTDE this pass goes through the central actor \([m', \ell'] = W_\pi\, \text{enc}(s_t) + b_\pi\), not through the heads \(g_i\) that sampled the actions in A2 (ctde.py L121-L128, I-48).

docs.title: C2. Probability ratio
docs.text:
\[\rho_t = \exp\big(\log\pi_\theta(u_t \mid o_t) - \log\mu(u_t \mid o_t)\big),\]

with \(\log\pi_\theta\) computed as in A3 but with \(m', \ell'\), and \(\log\mu\) the value stored in A3. \(\rho_t > 1\): the current policy makes the stored action more likely than the collecting policy did. On the very first minibatch \(\pi_\theta = \mu\), so \(\rho_t = 1\) exactly; that is a check that the stored and recomputed log-probabilities agree.

In CTCE and CTDE, \(\log\pi_\theta\) is a sum over agents, so \(\rho_t = \prod_i \rho_{i,t}\): one ratio for the joint action. In CTDE, \(\mu\) was the heads and \(\pi_\theta\) is the central actor, two different networks, so \(\rho\) starts far from 1 (I-48).

docs.title: C3. Clipped surrogate
docs.text:
\[S_t = \min\big(\rho_t \hat A_t,\ \text{clip}(\rho_t, 0.8, 1.2)\, \hat A_t\big).\]

Its gradient is \(\hat A_t \rho_t \nabla_\theta \log\pi_\theta(u_t \mid o_t)\) while the policy has not yet moved more than 20 % on this action in the direction \(\hat A_t\) asks for, and zero once it has: a good action (\(\hat A > 0\)) stops being pushed when \(\rho > 1.2\), a bad one when \(\rho < 0.8\). This is what keeps 30 epochs on the same data from running away.

docs.title: C4. Value loss
docs.text:
\[L_{V,t} = \min\big((V_\phi(o_t) - G_t)^2,\ 10\big).\]

Its gradient is \(2 (V_\phi(o_t) - G_t)\, \nabla_\phi V_\phi(o_t)\) while the error is below \(\sqrt{10} \approx 3.2\), and zero above (vf_clip_param = 10). Since \(G_t\) is on the reward scale (B4), rows whose return the critic misses by more than 3.2 units teach the critic nothing.

docs.title: C5. Entropy
docs.text:
\[\mathcal{H}_t = \sum_k \left(\ell'_k + \tfrac12 \log 2\pi e\right).\]

Its gradient with respect to each \(\ell'_k\) is exactly 1: with coefficient 0.01 it is a constant push to widen every action dimension. Where the reward does not depend on the action, nothing pushes back; with \(\ell\) unclipped (CTCE, CTDE) \(\ell\) then grows without limit (R-01).

docs.title: C6. KL between the collecting and the current policy
docs.text:
From the stored \([m, \ell]\) and the current \([m', \ell']\), per row (ppo_torch_learner.py L74-L80):

\[\mathrm{KL}_t(\mu \,\|\, \pi_\theta) = \sum_k \left[\ell'_k - \ell_k + \frac{e^{2\ell_k} + (m_k - m'_k)^2}{2\, e^{2\ell'_k}} - \frac12\right].\]

It is computed because use_kl_loss stays on, although \(\beta = 0\) (R-02).

docs.title: C7. Total loss
docs.text:
Averaged over the minibatch's real rows (the bootstrap rows of B2 masked out):

\[L = \frac{1}{|b|} \sum_{t \in b} \Big[-S_t + 1 \cdot L_{V,t} - 0.01\, \mathcal{H}_t\Big] + \beta\, \frac{1}{|b|} \sum_{t \in b} \mathrm{KL}_t, \qquad \beta = 0.\]

If \(\mathrm{KL}_t = \infty\), then \(\beta \cdot \infty\) is NaN and so is \(L\) (R-02).

docs.title: C8. Gradients: where each term goes
docs.text:
Backpropagation gives \(\partial L / \partial w\) for every weight \(w\) the loss depends on.

CTCE CTDE DTDE Surrogate and entropy actor head \(W_\pi\) and the encoder central actor \(W_\pi\) and the encoder; not the heads \(g_i\) agent \(i\)'s actor head and encoder, from agent \(i\)'s rows only Value loss value head and the encoder value head and the encoder agent \(i\)'s value head and encoder Networks with no gradient – the acting heads \(g_i\) (I-48) –

The encoder receives both the policy gradient and the value gradient, weighted 1 : 1 (\(c_v = 1\)); while value errors are large, the value loss dominates what the shared layers learn.

docs.title: C9. Clip the gradient norm
docs.text:
All gradients of a module are scaled together so that their global norm is at most 0.5 (grad_clip, grad_clip_by="global_norm"):

\[g \leftarrow g \cdot \min\left(1, \frac{0.5}{\lVert g \rVert_2}\right).\]

The direction is kept, the length capped. If \(g\) contains NaN (C7), RLlib replaces it with zeros, logs a warning and carries on (R-02).

docs.title: C10. Adam step
docs.text:
One optimiser per module (torch's Adam, \(\beta_1 = 0.9\), \(\beta_2 = 0.999\)), learning rate \(\eta = 10^{-5}\), for every weight \(w\):

\[m_w \leftarrow 0.9\, m_w + 0.1\, g_w, \qquad v_w \leftarrow 0.999\, v_w + 0.001\, g_w^2, \qquad w \leftarrow w - \eta\, \frac{\hat m_w}{\sqrt{\hat v_w} + 10^{-8}},\]

with \(\hat m_w, \hat v_w\) the bias-corrected averages. Adam divides by the gradient's running size, so each weight moves by about \(\eta\) per step whatever the loss scale: after 940 steps, at most about \(0.01\).

Then the next minibatch: C1 again, with the weights just updated.

docs.title: D1. KL coefficient
docs.text: Once, from the KL of the last minibatch: \(\beta \leftarrow 1.5\,\beta\) if \(\mathrm{KL} > 2 \times 0.01\), \(\beta \leftarrow 0.5\,\beta\) if \(\mathrm{KL} < 0.5 \times 0.01\) (ppo_torch_learner.py L141-L166). From \(\beta = 0\) it stays 0.

docs.title: D2. Weights to the env runners
docs.text: The updated weights are copied to every env runner: \(\mu \leftarrow \pi_\theta\). The next iteration starts at A1 with them. The batch is discarded: PPO never uses a step again after its iteration.

docs.title: D3. Between iterations
docs.text: The trainer reports the iteration's metrics. Every checkpoint_freq iterations, population-based training may replace a trial's weights with a better trial's and resample its learning rate, entropy coefficient and \(\lambda\) (I-49).

docs.title: APPO: the same cycle, what changes
docs.text:
Asynchronous PPO: the env runners do not wait for the learner, so the data is a little older than the policy, and V-trace corrects for it (appo_torch_learner.py L44-L214).

Stage What changes from PPO A. Collect A1-A5 are the same. The env runners never stop: they send pieces of 50 steps to the learner as they fill and keep acting, so \(\mu\) can be a few updates behind \(\pi_\theta\). B. Targets No GAE, no standardisation. The pieces are gathered into batches of 500 steps, kept in a circular buffer of 4 batches; each batch is trained on at most twice. Targets are computed inside the loss (C), with the current critic. C. Update One gradient step per 500-step batch. In it: (1) \(V_\phi\) for every step; (2) truncated weights \(\rho_t = c_t = \min(1, \bar\pi(u_t \mid o_t) / \mu(u_t \mid o_t))\) against a target policy \(\bar\pi\); (3) V-trace targets backwards in time, \(v_t = V_\phi(o_t) + \rho_t \delta_t + \gamma (1 - d_t) c_t (v_{t+1} - V_\phi(o_{t+1}))\); (4) advantage \(A_t = \rho_t (r_t + \gamma (1 - d_t) v_{t+1} - V_\phi(o_t))\); (5) the clipped surrogate on \(\pi_\theta / \bar\pi\) with clip 0.4, value loss \(0.5 \cdot \frac12 (V_\phi - v_t)^2\) (no cap), entropy 0.01, no KL term; (6) gradient-norm clip 0.5, Adam step, learning rate \(10^{-5}\). There is no λ: the original's lambda_ has no effect (R-06). D. After The target policy is overwritten with \(\pi_\theta\) every 8000 trained steps. New weights go to the env runners while they keep sampling. An iteration ends after at least 10 s, so the number of steps per iteration depends on the machine.

The paradigm differences of A2, B3 and C8 hold unchanged, I-48 included.

docs.title: SAC: the same cycle, what changes
docs.text:
Off-policy: steps go into a replay buffer and are trained on later, in random batches (sac_torch_learner.py L270-L350). SAC learns two critics \(Q_{\psi_1}, Q_{\psi_2}\) of state and action, their slowly following copies \(\bar Q_1, \bar Q_2\), the actor, and a temperature \(\alpha\).

Stage What changes from PPO A. Collect A1-A3 as in PPO, but in DTDE (RLlib's SAC module) the sample is squashed, \(\tanh(u) \in (-1, 1)\), before A4's rescaling. CTCE and CTDE use the plain Gaussian of A3, and A4 clips it (R-04). Whole episodes are collected (complete_episodes), about 256 environment steps per gradient step, and each step \((o, a, r, o', d)\) goes into a buffer of 1000 steps, the oldest dropped first. Training starts after 1500 steps. B. Targets A random batch of 256 steps from the buffer, old and new. For each: a next action \(a' \sim \pi_\theta(\cdot \mid o')\) and the target \(y = r + \gamma (1 - d)[\min_j \bar Q_j(o', a') - \alpha \log\pi_\theta(a' \mid o')]\). In the original's CTCE and CTDE, \(a'\) comes from a target copy of the actor instead. C. Update Three losses on the same batch, each with its own Adam optimiser: critics \(L_Q = \sum_j \text{Huber}(Q_{\psi_j}(o, a) - y)\), learning rate \(10^{-5}\); actor \(L_\pi = \alpha \log\pi_\theta(\tilde a \mid o) - \min_j Q_{\psi_j}(o, \tilde a)\) with a reparameterised \(\tilde a = m + \sigma\varepsilon\), so the actor's gradient runs through \(\partial Q / \partial \tilde a\), learning rate \(10^{-5}\); temperature \(L_\alpha = -\log\alpha\, (\log\pi_\theta(\tilde a \mid o) + \bar{\mathcal{H}})\) with target \(\bar{\mathcal{H}} = -\dim A\), learning rate \(3 \cdot 10^{-4}\). In the original's CTCE and CTDE, \(\tilde a\) is drawn with sample(), so the actor gets no gradient from the critic (R-05). D. After After every gradient step the critic copies follow: \(\bar\psi_j \leftarrow 0.005\, \psi_j + 0.995\, \bar\psi_j\). Weights go to the env runners; the buffer is kept, so a step is trained on about once while it stays in the 1000-step buffer. CTCE CTDE DTDE Critic \(Q_\psi(s, \mathbf{a})\) on all observations and actions the same \(Q_{\psi_i}(o_i, a_i)\) per agent Entropy target \(\bar{\mathcal{H}}\) \(-N d_a\) \(-N d_a\) \(-d_a\)

docs.title: Where the original code departs from this
docs.text: Step What the original does Recorded as A2, C1, C8 CTDE acts with heads \(g_i\) that receive no gradient; the loss trains a central actor I-48 A2, C5 CTCE and CTDE: \(\ell\) unclipped, so the entropy bonus can grow it until it overflows R-01 A4 CTCE and CTDE: an agent's slice can be rescaled with another agent's bounds I-59 C6, C7, C9 \(\beta = 0\) still computes the KL; an infinite KL makes the loss NaN, and the NaN gradient is zeroed silently R-02 D3 Population-based training raises the learning rate 10-1000× and the entropy coefficient up to 10 I-49 APPO, C lambda_ is set and tuned, but V-trace has no λ R-06 SAC, A CTCE and CTDE: unsquashed Gaussian, clipped R-04 SAC, C CTCE and CTDE: the actor's sample is not reparameterised, so no gradient through the critic R-05

docs.title: Worked examples: the parts we define
docs.text:
The training cycle with numbers, limited to what our own code decides: how the agents are grouped, how CTDE's per-agent actor is put together, the settings we choose, and how a trained policy is evaluated. Everything else (the networks' layers, sampling, GAE, the losses, Adam) is RLlib's and is described in One training iteration; it appears here only where our code feeds it or reads from it. Step labels (A4, C2, ...) are those of that page.

The code is the fixed implementation in core/rl/ in this repository. The links point to the local files. Every number below was computed with that code or with RLlib's own functions (unsquash_action), not by hand.

File What it defines Section here grouping.py GroupedEnv: all agents as one, for CTCE and CTDE 1, 2, 4 ctde_modules.py CTDE: RLlib's modules with one actor per agent 3, 5 config.py the settings of each of the nine combinations 6 policy.py acting with a trained policy, baselines, the team score 7 train.py the budget, the NaN stop, when evaluation runs 8

docs.title: The example
docs.text:
Three agents, listed by the environment in the order agent_2, agent_10, agent_1 (alphabetically agent_1, agent_10, agent_2, the case that broke the original, I-59). Each observes 2 numbers and sets 2 actions: a quantity (kWh, negative = sell) and a price (€/kWh). The quantity bound is each agent's own capacity.

Agent Observation \(o_i\) Quantity bounds Price bounds agent_2 (0.4, 0.8) [−5, 5] [0.05, 0.35] agent_10 (−0.2, 0.5) [−20, 20] [0.05, 0.35] agent_1 (0.9, 0.1) [−2, 2] [0.05, 0.35]

So \(N = 3\), \(d_o = 2\), \(d_a = 2\).

docs.title: 1. Grouping the observations (A1, CTCE and CTDE)
docs.text:
GroupedEnv turns the three agents into one agent, "group". Its observation is the agents' observations side by side, in the environment's order (join, grouping.py L55-L59):

\[s = (\underbrace{0.4,\ 0.8}_{\texttt{agent\_2}},\ \underbrace{-0.2,\ 0.5}_{\texttt{agent\_10}},\ \underbrace{0.9,\ 0.1}_{\texttt{agent\_1}}) \in \mathbb{R}^6.\]

The action space is joined the same way (join_spaces, L28-L34), each agent's bounds in its own slice:

Position 1 2 3 4 5 6 Belongs to agent_2 q agent_2 p agent_10 q agent_10 p agent_1 q agent_1 p low −5 0.05 −20 0.05 −2 0.05 high 5 0.35 20 0.35 2 0.35

To RLlib the group is an ordinary agent with a 6-dimensional Box observation and action. That is the whole point: RLlib's own module and algorithm then train CTCE without any custom network. In DTDE nothing is grouped: each agent's module gets its own \(o_i\) and its own bounds.

docs.title: 2. From the policy's output to the market (A3-A5)
docs.text:
What RLlib does (A3). Say the policy outputs, for the 6 dimensions, means and log-stds

\[m = (0.30,\ -0.10,\ -0.60,\ 0.20,\ 0.10,\ 0.50), \qquad \ell = (-0.50,\ -1.00,\ -0.70,\ -1.20,\ -0.40,\ -0.90),\]

so \(\sigma = e^\ell = (0.607, 0.368, 0.497, 0.301, 0.670, 0.407)\), and draws the noise \(\varepsilon = (1.0, -0.5, 0.2, 1.5, -2.0, 0.3)\):

\[u = m + \sigma\varepsilon = (0.907,\ -0.284,\ -0.501,\ 0.652,\ -1.241,\ 0.622).\]

What our bounds decide (A4). RLlib rescales each dimension from \([-1, 1]\) to the joint space's bounds and clips, \(a_k = \text{clip}(\text{low}_k + (u_k + 1)(\text{high}_k - \text{low}_k)/2)\):

Dimension \(u_k\) low, high \(a_k\) agent_2 q 0.907 −5, 5 −5 + 1.907 × 5 = 4.53 agent_2 p −0.284 0.05, 0.35 0.05 + 0.716 × 0.15 = 0.157 agent_10 q −0.501 −20, 20 −20 + 0.499 × 20 = −10.01 agent_10 p 0.652 0.05, 0.35 0.298 agent_1 q −1.241 −2, 2 −2 + (−0.241) × 2 = −2.48 → clipped to −2 agent_1 p 0.622 0.05, 0.35 0.293

The same \(u = -0.501\) would be −2.5 kWh for agent_2 and −1.0 kWh for agent_1: the bounds must belong to the right agent. The original put the bounds in sorted name order (agent_1, agent_10, agent_2) but the data in this order, so positions 1-2 carried agent_1's bounds and positions 5-6 agent_2's: agent_2 would have bid \(-2 + 1.907 \times 2 = 1.81\) kWh instead of 4.53, and agent_1 would have been clipped at −5 instead of −2, beyond its own capacity (I-59). agent_10 happens to sit in the middle of both orders and would have been right.

agent_1's quantity shows the clip: \(u = -1.241\) is outside \([-1, 1]\), so the market gets the bound −2, but the batch keeps \(u = -1.241\) and the learner trains on it.

Splitting back (A5). GroupedEnv.step cuts the joint action into the agents' parts (split, L46-L52) and passes them to the environment:

{"agent_2": [4.53, 0.157], "agent_10": [-10.01, 0.298], "agent_1": [-2.0, 0.293]}

docs.title: 3. CTDE: one actor per agent (A2)
docs.text:
In CTDE each agent's action may depend only on its own observation. Our module (ctde_modules.py L134-L140) is RLlib's PPO module for the group with the actor replaced by three separate ones, each the network RLlib would build for that agent alone (agent_actors, L99-L119). The critic is left as RLlib builds it, on all of \(s\).

Encoders (AgentEncoders, L48-L66). Agent \(i\)'s encoder reads only its slice of \(s\): agent_2's positions 1-2 = (0.4, 0.8), agent_10's 3-4 = (−0.2, 0.5), agent_1's 5-6 = (0.9, 0.1). Each turns its 2 numbers into a 256-number latent, \(h_i\); the three latents are put side by side (768 numbers).

Heads (AgentHeads, L69-L96). Head \(i\) reads only \(h_i\) and outputs \([m_{i}, \ell_{i}]\) for its 2 action dimensions. Say:

Agent Head output \([m_q, m_p, \ell_q, \ell_p]\) agent_2 (0.30, −0.10, −0.50, −1.00) agent_10 (−0.60, 0.20, −0.70, −1.20) agent_1 (0.10, 0.50, −0.40, −0.90)

RLlib's Gaussian for a 6-dimensional action reads a 12-number input as first the 6 means, then the 6 log-stds (loc, log_std = logits.chunk(2)). So the heads' outputs are rearranged before they leave the module:

\[(\underbrace{0.30, -0.10}_{m,\ \texttt{agent\_2}}, \underbrace{-0.60, 0.20}_{m,\ \texttt{agent\_10}}, \underbrace{0.10, 0.50}_{m,\ \texttt{agent\_1}}, \underbrace{-0.50, -1.00}_{\ell,\ \texttt{agent\_2}}, \underbrace{-0.70, -1.20}_{\ell,\ \texttt{agent\_10}}, \underbrace{-0.40, -0.90}_{\ell,\ \texttt{agent\_1}}).\]

These are exactly the \(m\) and \(\ell\) of section 2, so from here on CTDE is the same as CTCE: RLlib samples, rescales, stores and trains a 6-dimensional Gaussian. Had the outputs simply been concatenated, \((0.30, -0.10, -0.50, -1.00, -0.60, 0.20, \dots)\), RLlib would have read agent_2's log-stds as agent_10's means.

Sizes (RLlib's default network, 2 × 256 tanh, actor and critic separate):

Actor parameters Critic parameters DTDE, per agent 67 588 (input 2, output 4) 66 817 (input 2) CTCE 70 668 (input 6, output 12) 67 841 (input 6) CTDE 3 × 67 588 = 202 764 (three DTDE actors) 67 841 (CTCE's critic)

CTDE's actor is the three DTDE actors, and its critic is CTCE's.

docs.title: 4. The group's reward (A5, B4)
docs.text:
GroupedEnv.step returns one reward for the group, the sum of the agents' (L104-L123). With the market paying

\[r_{\texttt{agent\_2}} = 1.50, \qquad r_{\texttt{agent\_10}} = -0.50, \qquad r_{\texttt{agent\_1}} = 0.25,\]

the group gets \(R = 1.25\). The agents' own rewards travel along in the group's infos (for evaluation), but the learner sees only 1.25.

What follows from it, all computed by RLlib:

  • The critic \(V(s)\) learns the group's return. Its targets are about \(N = 3\) times the size of one agent's, which matters for RLlib's value-loss cap of 10 (cycle.md C4).
  • One advantage for the group. \(\hat A\) is computed from \(R\), so agent_1's bid is reinforced or discouraged by the same number as agent_2's, although here agent_10 lost money and agent_2 earned it. Telling the agents' contributions apart is left to the averaging over many steps (the credit-assignment cost, I-60).

In DTDE each agent's module learns from its own \(r_i\) and nothing is summed.

docs.title: 5. CTDE in the update: what the per-agent actor means for the loss (C2, C3, C8)
docs.text:
The loss is RLlib's; what our module decides is that the joint policy is a product of the agents' policies. Here is what that does in numbers.

Log-probability. For the stored \(u\) of section 2, per dimension \(\log\pi = -\frac{(u - m)^2}{2\sigma^2} - \ell - \frac12\log 2\pi\):

agent_2 agent_10 agent_1 Group \(\log\mu(u_i)\) when sampled −0.963 −1.083 −2.583 −4.629 (the sum)

Ratio (C2). Some minibatches later the heads have moved a little: agent_2's quantity mean 0.30 → 0.36, agent_10's price mean 0.20 → 0.235, agent_1's price mean 0.50 → 0.53. Recomputed:

agent_2 agent_10 agent_1 Group \(\log\pi_\theta(u_i)\) −0.869 −0.915 −2.563 −4.347 \(\rho_i = e^{\log\pi_\theta - \log\mu}\) 1.099 1.182 1.020 $\rho = 1.099 \times 1.182 \times 1.020 = $ 1.324

Clip (C3). RLlib clips the group's ratio, \(\rho = 1.324\), to \([0.8, 1.2]\). With \(\hat A = +0.8\):

\[S = \min(1.324 \times 0.8,\ 1.2 \times 0.8) = \min(1.060,\ 0.960) = 0.960,\]

the clipped branch: no gradient for any agent, although each agent alone (\(1.099\), \(1.182\), \(1.020\)) is still inside \([0.8, 1.2]\). Three agents that each moved a little count as one policy that moved too far. With \(\hat A = -0.8\) the unclipped branch is the smaller one (\(-1.060 < -0.960\)), so all three keep receiving gradient. The more agents, the sooner the product leaves the band. Clipping each agent's ratio separately instead, as MAPPO does, is the open choice recorded in training.md; the fixed code keeps RLlib's joint clip.

Where the gradient goes (C8). Agent \(i\)'s network appears only in its own term of \(\log\pi = \sum_i \log\pi_i(u_i \mid o_i)\), so it receives only that term's gradient. On the first minibatch (\(\rho = 1\), unclipped), with \(\hat A = +0.8\), the push on each mean is \(\hat A \cdot \partial\log\pi / \partial m_k = \hat A\,(u_k - m_k)/\sigma_k^2\):

agent_2 q agent_2 p agent_10 q agent_10 p agent_1 q agent_1 p \((u_k - m_k)/\sigma_k^2\) 1.649 −1.359 0.403 4.980 −2.984 0.738 × \(\hat A = 0.8\) 1.319 −1.087 0.322 3.984 −2.387 0.590

Each mean is pulled toward the action that was sampled, in proportion to how far the noise took it (\(\varepsilon_k / \sigma_k\)). agent_10's head gets only the two numbers in its columns, from the gradient of its own 2 outputs, and nothing from the other agents' actions; that is "decentralised execution" in the loss. In CTCE the same six numbers arrive, but all at one network that sees \(s\).

In the original, these gradients went to a central actor and the acting heads got none (I-48).

docs.title: 6. The settings we choose
docs.text:
SETTINGS and MODEL, and what each changes in the cycle:

Setting Value What it does in the cycle lr \(10^{-5}\) Adam moves each weight about \(10^{-5}\) per step (C10) gamma, lambda_ 0.99, 0.95 discount and GAE horizon, ≈ 17 steps (B4) num_epochs, minibatch_size 30, 128 with RLlib's 4000 steps per batch: 30 × ⌈4000/128⌉ ≈ 940 gradient steps per iteration clip_param 0.2 the band \([0.8, 1.2]\) of section 5 entropy_coeff 0.01 the constant push to widen \(\sigma\) (C5) grad_clip 0.5 gradient norm capped at 0.5 (C9) use_kl_loss False the KL term is not computed at all (C6 disappears; fixes R-02) vf_share_layers False actor and critic have separate encoders: the value loss no longer trains the actor's layers (C8) SAC target_entropy "auto" \(-\dim A\) of each module: −2 per agent in DTDE, −6 for the group in CTCE and CTDE

Steps per iteration. One PPO iteration samples 4000 environment steps. In CTCE and CTDE that is 4000 rows of the group; in DTDE 4000 rows for each of the three modules, 12 000 rows in total, but still 4000 environment steps. The budget counts environment steps, so all paradigms get the same amount of experience.

docs.title: 7. Evaluating a trained policy
docs.text:
Policy acts with the trained module outside RLlib, the same way RLlib does in training, but without noise.

The action (act, L96-L111). The most likely action is the mean, then RLlib's own rescaling with the joint bounds, then the split:

agent_2 agent_10 agent_1 PPO, APPO: \(a = \text{rescale}(m)\) (1.50, 0.185) (−12.0, 0.230) (0.20, 0.275) SAC: \(a = \text{rescale}(\tanh m)\) (1.46, 0.185) (−10.74, 0.230) (0.199, 0.269)

For example agent_10's quantity: \(-20 + (-0.60 + 1) \times 20 = -12.0\). SAC's actions are squashed by tanh, so its most likely action is \(\tanh m\); RLlib's own deterministic SAC action skips the tanh in Ray 2.51.1, so _deterministic (L39-L51) applies it. The original's inference used the mean without rescaling, so agent_10 would have bid −0.60 kWh (I-61).

Baselines (L137-L165). "Random" draws each action uniformly within its bounds. "Zero" sends 0 in the market's units, clipped to the bounds: quantity 0, price \(\max(0, 0.05) = 0.05\) for every agent. It is not the network's 0, which would be the middle of the bounds (price 0.20).

The team score (Episode, L172-L192). Every paradigm is scored in the original multi-agent environment, from the raw per-agent rewards. Over a 3-step episode:

Step agent_2 agent_10 agent_1 1 1.50 −0.50 0.25 2 0.80 0.30 −0.10 3 −0.20 1.10 0.40 Return 2.10 0.90 0.55

Team score \(= 2.10 + 0.90 + 0.55 = 3.55\), reported with the three returns. The same number for CTCE, CTDE and DTDE, computed the same way, so the nine combinations and the baselines can be ranked on one scale (I-73). Evaluation episodes use seeds from 1 000 000 on, which training never reaches (evaluation_seeds, L245-L249).

Policy.values gives the critic's estimate of a state; in CTCE and CTDE that is the group's value, comparable to the team score, not to one agent's return.

docs.title: 8. The run: budget, NaN stop, evaluation
docs.text:
train repeats RLlib's iteration until the budget of environment steps is used up.

Budget. budget = 100_000 with PPO's 4000 steps per iteration: 25 iterations, for every paradigm. With eval_every = 20_000, the policy and baselines are evaluated at 0 (untrained, together with random and zero), 20 000, 40 000, 60 000, 80 000 and at the end, 100 000 (L283-L302).

NaN stop (_nonfinite, L194-L209). After each iteration the learner's results are searched for losses, entropies and the SAC temperature that are NaN or infinite. For

{"group": {"policy_loss": nan, "vf_loss": 0.31, "entropy": inf,
           "num_env_steps_trained_throughput": nan}}

it finds group/policy_loss and group/entropy and stops the run with an error, which run.json records. The throughput is skipped on purpose: RLlib reports it as NaN in the first iteration. The original carried on with zeroed gradients (R-02).

docs.title: The training cycle: 3 algorithms × 3 paradigms
docs.text:
The math that has to happen in one training iteration of each of MARLEM's nine combinations: PPO, APPO and SAC, each trained as CTCE, CTDE and DTDE. First the common skeleton, then each algorithm worked through (PPO in full), then what each paradigm changes, then how many steps each algorithm takes, so runs can be compared. Where the original code computes something else, the section says so and points to RL layer: what is wrong. The same iteration, step by step from the observation, is in One training iteration.

Sources. RLlib is Ray 2.51.1, the version in the marlem conda env; every statement about it was read in its installed source, linked at tag ray-2.51.1. MARLEM's code is linked at the original commit 15d6715, as in the validation document. Settings are the original's (train.py L215-L259), completed with RLlib's defaults. [P2] is the implicit-cooperation preprint.

docs.title: Notation
docs.text:
Symbol Meaning \(N\) number of agents, \(i = 1 \dots N\) \(t\) environment step: all \(N\) agents act at once \(o_{i,t}\), \(a_{i,t}\), \(r_{i,t}\) agent \(i\)'s observation, action and reward at step \(t\) \(s_t = (o_{1,t}, \dots, o_{N,t})\) all observations, concatenated (the grouped paradigms' input) \(\mathbf{a}_t = (a_{1,t}, \dots, a_{N,t})\) the joint action \(R_t = \sum_i r_{i,t}\) the group reward of CTCE and CTDE (train.py L684) \(d_t\) 1 if the episode terminates at \(t\), else 0 \(\pi_\theta\), \(\mu\) the policy being trained (parameters \(\theta\)); the policy that collected the data \(V_\phi\), \(Q_\psi\) state-value critic (PPO, APPO); action-value critic (SAC) \(\gamma\), \(\lambda\) discount 0.99; GAE parameter 0.95

Every policy is a diagonal Gaussian over the action dimensions (SAC-DTDE then squashes it with tanh, section 4): the network outputs a mean \(m\) and \(\log\sigma\) per dimension, and

\[\log \pi(a) = \sum_k \left[-\frac{(a_k - m_k)^2}{2\sigma_k^2} - \log\sigma_k - \tfrac12\log 2\pi\right], \qquad \mathcal{H}(\pi) = \sum_k \left(\log\sigma_k + \tfrac12 \log 2\pi e\right).\]

A sum over dimensions is also a sum over agents when one policy outputs all agents' actions. That is the key to the paradigms (section 5).

docs.title: 1. One iteration: the common skeleton
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A["1 Sample<br/>env runners act with μ"] --> B["2 Group<br/>(CTCE, CTDE only)"]
    B --> C["3 Targets<br/>returns, advantages<br/>or replay sample"]
    C --> D["4 Loss and<br/>gradient steps"]
    D --> E["5 After the update<br/>target nets, KL coefficient"]
    E --> F["6 Sync weights<br/>to the env runners"]
    F --> A
  1. Sample. Each env runner holds a copy \(\mu\) of the policy. Per step it computes the distribution from \(o\), samples \(a \sim \mu(\cdot \mid o)\), rescales it from \([-1, 1]\) to the action's bounds (normalize_actions=True), and records \(o, a, r, d\), \(\log\mu(a \mid o)\) and the distribution's inputs.
  2. Group (CTCE, CTDE). GroupedLEM turns the \(N\) agents into one: observation \(s_t\), action \(\mathbf{a}_t\), reward \(R_t\), one done flag (train.py L676-L687).
  3. Targets. What the loss regresses on: λ-returns and advantages (PPO), V-trace targets (APPO, computed inside the loss), or a batch drawn from the replay buffer (SAC).
  4. Loss and gradient steps. One Adam step per (mini)batch, after clipping the gradient's global norm to 0.5 (grad_clip).
  5. After the update. Target networks are copied (APPO, SAC); PPO's KL coefficient is adapted.
  6. Sync. The new weights go to the env runners: the next iteration samples with the updated \(\mu\).

What changes between the nine combinations is only steps 2 to 5.

docs.title: 2. PPO, worked through
docs.text:
On-policy: every iteration collects fresh data with the current policy, trains on it, and throws it away (ppo.py L389-L458).

Sample. 4000 environment steps (train_batch_size), split over the env runners. Episodes are cut where the batch is full (truncate_episodes).

Targets (value_predictions.py L7-L38). With the critic as it is before the update, compute backwards in time the λ-return

\[G^\lambda_t = r_t + \gamma (1 - d_t)\left[(1 - \lambda)\, V_\phi(o_{t+1}) + \lambda\, G^\lambda_{t+1}\right],\]

which equals the usual GAE sum: with \(\delta_t = r_t + \gamma(1-d_t) V_\phi(o_{t+1}) - V_\phi(o_t)\), \(\hat A_t = \sum_{l \ge 0} (\gamma\lambda)^l \delta_{t+l}\) and \(G^\lambda_t = \hat A_t + V_\phi(o_t)\). A truncated episode is bootstrapped with \(V_\phi\) of its last observation; a terminated one with 0. The advantages are then standardised over the batch, \(\hat A_t \leftarrow (\hat A_t - \text{mean}) / \text{std}\) (general_advantage_estimation.py L148). \(G^\lambda_t\) is the value target.

Loss (ppo_torch_learner.py L74-L120), averaged over the minibatch:

\[\rho_t(\theta) = \exp\big(\log\pi_\theta(a_t \mid o_t) - \log\mu(a_t \mid o_t)\big)\] \[L = -\min\big(\rho_t \hat A_t,\; \text{clip}(\rho_t, 1 - \epsilon, 1 + \epsilon)\, \hat A_t\big) + c_v \min\big((V_\phi(o_t) - G^\lambda_t)^2,\; 10\big) - c_H\, \mathcal{H}\big(\pi_\theta(\cdot \mid o_t)\big) + \beta\, \mathrm{KL}(\mu \,\|\, \pi_\theta)\] Term Setting What it does clipped surrogate \(\epsilon = 0.2\) raise the probability of actions with \(\hat A > 0\), but stop once \(\rho\) leaves \([0.8, 1.2]\) value loss \(c_v = 1\), cap 10 (vf_clip_param) fit \(V_\phi\) to \(G^\lambda\); the squared error is capped, so an error above \(\sqrt{10} \approx 3.2\) gives no gradient entropy bonus \(c_H = 0.01\) keep exploring KL penalty \(\beta = 0\) (kl_coeff) switched off, but still computed: \(0 \cdot \infty\) = NaN (R-02)

Gradient steps. 30 epochs over the 4000 steps in shuffled minibatches of 128: \(30 \times 4000 / 128 \approx 940\) Adam steps, learning rate \(10^{-5}\). In the first minibatch \(\pi_\theta = \mu\), so \(\rho = 1\) exactly; later minibatches move away and the clip takes over.

After the update. The KL coefficient would be multiplied by 1.5 or 0.5 depending on the measured KL; from 0 it stays 0.

What to check. \(\rho = 1\) on the first minibatch; advantages with mean 0 and standard deviation 1; the value loss mostly below the cap; explained variance of \(V_\phi\) rising toward 1; entropy falling slowly, never NaN.

docs.title: 3. APPO
docs.text:
Asynchronous PPO: env runners keep sampling while the learner trains, so the data is always a little older than the policy. V-trace corrects for that (appo_torch_learner.py L44-L214). APPO keeps a target policy \(\bar\pi\), a copy of \(\pi_\theta\) refreshed now and then, as the "old" policy that the update is anchored to.

Sample. Env runners send fragments of 50 steps; the learner trains on batches of 500. A circular buffer holds 4 batches, and each batch is trained on at most twice.

Targets: V-trace (vtrace_torch_v2.py L72-L168). With truncated importance weights between the target policy and the collecting one,

\[\rho_t = \min\!\left(1, \frac{\bar\pi(a_t \mid o_t)}{\mu(a_t \mid o_t)}\right), \qquad c_t = \min\!\left(1, \frac{\bar\pi(a_t \mid o_t)}{\mu(a_t \mid o_t)}\right),\]

the value target is computed backwards in time,

\[v_t = V_\phi(o_t) + \rho_t \delta_t + \gamma (1 - d_t)\, c_t\, \big(v_{t+1} - V_\phi(o_{t+1})\big), \qquad \delta_t = r_t + \gamma (1 - d_t) V_\phi(o_{t+1}) - V_\phi(o_t),\]

and the policy-gradient advantage is \(A_t = \rho_t \big(r_t + \gamma (1 - d_t) v_{t+1} - V_\phi(o_t)\big)\). With \(\bar\pi = \mu\) this is the \(n\)-step return; the weights only cut off what the older data can no longer vouch for. There is no λ in it: RLlib's V-trace takes none, so the original's lambda_=0.95, and its population-based training of lambda_ for APPO, change nothing. Advantages are not standardised.

Loss.

\[\rho^{\text{PPO}}_t = \text{clip}\!\left(\frac{\mu(a_t \mid o_t)}{\bar\pi(a_t \mid o_t)}, 0, 2\right) \cdot \frac{\pi_\theta(a_t \mid o_t)}{\mu(a_t \mid o_t)} \approx \frac{\pi_\theta}{\bar\pi}\] \[L = -\min\big(\rho^{\text{PPO}}_t A_t,\; \text{clip}(\rho^{\text{PPO}}_t, 0.6, 1.4)\, A_t\big) + 0.5 \cdot \tfrac12 \big(V_\phi(o_t) - v_t\big)^2 - 0.01\, \mathcal{H}\big(\pi_\theta(\cdot \mid o_t)\big)\]

The clip is 0.4 (RLlib's APPO default), the value coefficient 0.5, and the KL term is off (use_kl_loss=False). One Adam step per 500-step batch, learning rate \(10^{-5}\).

After the update. The target policy is overwritten with \(\pi_\theta\) (\(\tau = 1\)) every \(2 \times 4 \times 2 \times 500 = 8000\) trained environment steps, reuse counted (appo_learner.py L85-L117).

What to check. \(\bar\pi/\mu\) near 1 (data not too stale); the same health signals as PPO.

docs.title: 4. SAC
docs.text:
Off-policy: transitions go into a replay buffer, and the learner trains on random batches from it, old and new (dqn.py L647-L755, which SAC inherits). It learns two critics \(Q_{\psi_1}, Q_{\psi_2}\), their slowly following copies \(\bar Q_1, \bar Q_2\), the actor, and the temperature \(\alpha\).

Sample. About 256 environment steps per training step, in whole episodes (complete_episodes), added to a buffer of 1000 transitions (uniform, the original's setting; RLlib's default is prioritised with \(10^6\)). Training starts after 1500 sampled steps.

Targets. A batch of 256 transitions \((o, a, r, o', d)\) from the buffer. For each, a next action \(a' \sim \pi_\theta(\cdot \mid o')\) and

\[y = r + \gamma (1 - d)\left[\min_{j=1,2} \bar Q_j(o', a') - \alpha \log \pi_\theta(a' \mid o')\right].\]

Loss (sac_torch_learner.py L270-L350), three losses, each with its own Adam optimiser:

\[L_Q = \sum_{j=1,2} \text{Huber}\big(Q_{\psi_j}(o, a) - y\big), \qquad \text{learning rate } 10^{-5}\] \[L_\pi = \alpha \log \pi_\theta(\tilde a \mid o) - \min_j Q_{\psi_j}(o, \tilde a), \qquad \tilde a = m_\theta(o) + \sigma_\theta(o)\,\varepsilon,\; \varepsilon \sim \mathcal N(0, I), \qquad \text{lr } 10^{-5}\] \[L_\alpha = -\log\alpha \,\big(\log \pi_\theta(\tilde a \mid o) + \bar{\mathcal H}\big), \qquad \text{lr } 3 \cdot 10^{-4}\]
  • The actor learns through the critic. \(\tilde a\) is a reparameterised sample (rsample, default_sac_torch_rl_module.py L155), so \(\partial L_\pi / \partial\theta\) runs through \(\partial Q / \partial \tilde a\): the actor moves its actions uphill on the critic. Without it the actor only maximises entropy.
  • The temperature \(\alpha\) (starting at 1) rises when the entropy is below the target \(\bar{\mathcal H} = -\dim A\) and falls when above.
  • The actions are squashed: in RLlib's own module \(\tilde a = \tanh(\cdot)\), and \(\log\pi\) includes the \(-\sum_k \log(1 - \tanh^2)\) correction.

After the update. Polyak averaging after every gradient step: \(\bar\psi_j \leftarrow 0.005\, \psi_j + 0.995\, \bar\psi_j\).

What to check. \(Q\) near the true discounted return (on a probe it is known); \(\alpha\) settling; the entropy near its target.

docs.title: 5. What each paradigm changes
docs.text:
The algorithm's math stays the same; the paradigm decides what counts as one agent for RLlib: what the actor and the critic see, which reward they learn from, and how many networks there are.

CTCE CTDE (as [P2] eq. 18 intends) DTDE RLlib agents 1 (the group) 1 (the group) \(N\), one module each Actor \(\pi_\theta(\mathbf{a} \mid s)\) \(\pi_{\theta_i}(a_i \mid o_i)\) per agent \(\pi_{\theta_i}(a_i \mid o_i)\) Critic (PPO, APPO) \(V_\phi(s)\) \(V_\phi(s)\) \(V_{\phi_i}(o_i)\) Critic (SAC) \(Q_\psi(s, \mathbf{a})\) \(Q_\psi(s, \mathbf{a})\) \(Q_{\psi_i}(o_i, a_i)\) Reward \(R = \sum_i r_i\) \(R = \sum_i r_i\) own \(r_i\) SAC entropy target \(-\sum_i \dim A_i\) \(-\sum_i \dim A_i\) \(-\dim A_i\) Networks in the code custom, 2 × 128 ReLU custom; acting heads 3 layers per agent RLlib default, 2 × 256 tanh Actor and critic share the encoder central actor and critic share the encoder share the encoder (vf_share_layers=True, RLlib's default)

docs.title: CTCE
docs.text:
One policy outputs every agent's action from all observations. Because it is a diagonal Gaussian over all action dimensions,

\[\log \pi_\theta(\mathbf{a} \mid s) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} \log \pi_{\theta}(a_i \mid s), \qquad \rho_t = \prod_{i=1}^{N} \rho_{i,t}, \qquad \mathcal{H} = \sum_i \mathcal{H}_i.\]

So PPO clips the product of the agents' ratios, one advantage from the summed reward weights every agent's action, and the entropy bonus is \(N\) times larger than one agent's. The learning signal for \(a_i\) carries every other agent's reward noise: the credit-assignment cost that makes CTCE learn more slowly (I-60).

docs.title: CTDE
docs.text:
CTDE is CTCE's loss with the actor restricted: each agent's part of the policy may only look at its own observation,

\[\pi_\theta(\mathbf{a} \mid s) = \prod_{i=1}^{N} \pi_{\theta_i}(a_i \mid o_i), \qquad \log \pi_\theta(\mathbf{a} \mid s) = \sum_i \log \pi_{\theta_i}(a_i \mid o_i).\]

The critic stays central (\(V_\phi(s)\) or \(Q_\psi(s, \mathbf{a})\)), because it is only needed during training. With this actor:

  • PPO, APPO. Two choices, to be decided and recorded: the joint ratio \(\prod_i \rho_i\) clipped once (exactly CTCE's loss), or a clipped term per agent, \(\sum_i \min(\rho_i \hat A, \text{clip}(\rho_i)\hat A)\), as in MAPPO (Yu et al., 2022). Both use one advantage from \(V_\phi(s)\) and \(R\).
  • SAC. \(L_\pi = \alpha \sum_i \log \pi_{\theta_i}(\tilde a_i \mid o_i) - \min_j Q_{\psi_j}(s, \tilde{\mathbf{a}})\) with every \(\tilde a_i\) reparameterised: each \(\theta_i\) gets the gradient of the joint critic through its own action.

The gradient for \(\theta_i\) goes into the network that acts. In the original code it does not: the loss trains a central actor \(\pi(\mathbf{a} \mid s)\) and the agents act with per-agent heads that never change (I-48).

docs.title: DTDE
docs.text: \(N\) independent copies of sections 2-4, each with index \(i\): agent \(i\)'s advantage comes from its own reward and its own critic, its ratio from its own policy. The other agents are part of agent \(i\)'s environment, and that environment changes as they learn.

docs.title: 6. The 3 × 3 matrix
docs.text:
What the policy gradient of each combination is built from. "→" marks where the original code computes something else.

CTCE CTDE DTDE PPO \(\prod_i \rho_i\), GAE on \(R\) with \(V_\phi(s)\) \(\rho_i\) of \(\pi_{\theta_i}(a_i \mid o_i)\), GAE on \(R\) with \(V_\phi(s)\) → central actor trained, heads act (I-48) per agent: \(\rho_i\), GAE on \(r_i\) with \(V_{\phi_i}(o_i)\) APPO V-trace on \(R\), joint ratio as PPO-CTDE with V-trace → I-48 per agent: V-trace on \(r_i\) SAC \(Q_\psi(s, \mathbf{a})\), gradient through \(\tilde{\mathbf{a}}\) → no gradient through \(\tilde{\mathbf{a}}\) (R-05), unsquashed Gaussian (R-04) \(Q_\psi(s, \mathbf{a})\), gradient through each \(\tilde a_i\) → I-48, R-05, R-04 per agent: \(Q_{\psi_i}(o_i, a_i)\), squashed Gaussian

docs.title: 7. Steps per iteration, and comparing runs
docs.text:
An iteration is one call of RLlib's training step, repeated until the iteration's minimum time and step counts are met. It means something different for each algorithm:

Per iteration PPO APPO SAC Ends when after one training step (4000 sampled steps) at least 10 s have passed (min_time_s_per_iteration) at least 1 s and 100 sampled steps Environment steps sampled 4000, fixed whatever the env runners deliver in 10 s about 256 per training step, 1 training step or more Batch per gradient step 128 500 256 Gradient steps ≈ 940 1 per batch, each batch at most twice 1 per training step Gradient steps per 1000 env steps ≈ 234 ≤ 4 ≈ 4 Times each sample is used 30 ≤ 2 ≈ 1 while in the buffer (1000 transitions) Data fresh, then discarded slightly stale, V-trace corrects replayed, off-policy

Across paradigms. Batches are counted in environment steps (count_steps_by="env_steps"). One environment step is one transition for the group in CTCE and CTDE, and \(N\) transitions in DTDE, one per agent's module. So in a PPO iteration each of DTDE's \(N\) networks trains on 4000 transitions of its own agent, and CTCE's single network on 4000 joint transitions: the same number of samples per network, for a problem \(N\) times larger.

What makes runs comparable.

  • A budget in environment steps, the same for all nine combinations, not iterations (I-50): APPO's and SAC's iterations depend on wall-clock time and differ between machines.
  • Report the gradient steps alongside: at the same budget PPO takes about 60 times more gradient steps than APPO or SAC, by design.
  • Evaluate at the same environment-step counts, with the same seeds, on the same team score (I-73).

docs.title: 8. Where the original code differs
docs.text: What Section Where it is recorded CTDE's loss trains a central actor; the acting heads never change 5, 6 I-48 CTCE and CTDE: \(\log\sigma\) unbounded, entropy can overflow 2 R-01 kl_coeff = 0 still computes the KL; NaN loss is skipped silently 2 R-02 SAC in CTCE and CTDE uses an unsquashed Gaussian 4 R-04 SAC in CTCE and CTDE: the actor's sample \(\tilde{\mathbf{a}}\) is drawn with sample(), not rsample(), so \(L_\pi\) has no gradient through the critic and the actor only maximises entropy (ctce.py L136, ctde.py L147) 4 R-05 SAC in CTCE and CTDE: \(a'\) comes from a target copy of the actor, not the current one; the critic is not frozen while \(L_\pi\) is computed, as RLlib's module does 4 not recorded: deviations from RLlib's SAC whose effect is not established APPO: lambda_ is set and tuned but V-trace has no λ 3 R-06

docs.title: SimBench: the networks behind the Studio
docs.text:
What SimBench is, how its codes and element names read, which grids and scenarios it has, and the study cases it defines. Every network on the Studio's Inspect page comes from here. The networks one by one: network catalogue · The time series of their loads and generators: profiles.

Source of everything not measured in the Studio: the SimBench documentation, version 1.1.0 (Meinecke et al., University of Kassel, Fraunhofer IEE, RWTH Aachen, TU Dortmund), and the paper Meinecke et al. (2020), "SimBench—A Benchmark Dataset of Electric Power Systems to Compare Innovative Solutions Based on Power Flow Analysis", Energies 13(12), 3290. Section numbers like §4.2.3 refer to the documentation. Downloads: simbench.de.

docs.title: 1. What SimBench is
docs.text:
A benchmark dataset of German electricity grids from low to extra-high voltage, made so that methods can be compared on the same grids. It has:

  • Grids for four voltage levels (LV 0.4 kV, MV 20 kV, HV 110 kV, EHV 220/380 kV), each in several types, and combinations of two levels (§4.1).
  • Time series for one whole year, 2016, every 15 minutes, for every load, generator and storage unit (§3.5, §4.1.5). See profiles.
  • Three scenarios per grid: today and two future years with more PV, heat pumps, electric vehicles and storage (§3.6, §4.1.6).
  • Two switch variants per grid (§4.2.3).
  • Study cases: fixed scaling factors for the classic planning cases (§5.1).

The grids are not real networks. They are built so that the use cases of grid planning and operation are covered, and checked against real grid data. The LV grids, for example, were generated from OpenStreetMap data for six representative German municipalities and compared with 180 real LV grids (§3.4, §4.1.4).

The Studio reads SimBench through the Python package simbench, which gives each grid as a pandapower network.

docs.title: 2. The SimBench code
docs.text:
Every grid or grid combination has a code of six parts separated by - (§4.2.3, Table 4.9). Example: 1-MVLV-rural-2.107-0-sw.

Part Meaning Values Example 1 SimBench version 1 1 2 Voltage level(s) LV, MV, HV, EHV, or two levels: MVLV, HVMV, EHVHV MVLV 3 Grid type (of the higher level) LV: rural1, rural2, rural3, semiurb4, semiurb5, urban6; MV: rural, semiurb, urban, comm; HV: mixed, urban; EHV: mixed rural 4 Which lower-level grid is modelled in detail (combinations only): one subnet number, or all empty for one level 2.107 5 Scenario 0 today, 1 2024, 2 2034 ("heute", "morgen", "übermorgen") 0 6 Switches sw all switches modelled, no_sw only open line and transformer switches sw

So 1-LV-semiurb4--0-sw is the semi-urban LV grid 4 alone (part 4 empty), today, with switches.

Switches. In sw every switch is a bus-to-bus switch, with extra auxiliary buses between the bus bar and each line or transformer. In no_sw buses joined by closed switches are merged: the same grid with fewer buses, often a faster power flow. The loads and generators are the same in both.

Combinations. A grid of two levels models the higher grid in detail and either one chosen lower grid or all of them. For the MV-LV combinations SimBench preselected three LV grids at different places in the MV grid (e.g. 1.108, 2.107, 4.101), which keeps the number of codes manageable (§4.2.3).

The Inspect page's filters follow the code: Voltage level is part 2, Type part 3, Scenario part 5, Switches part 6. The Studio's catalogue has 240 SimBench codes: the full "complete data" set and the four-level combination are left out because they are far larger than a local market needs.

flowchart LR
  code["1-MVLV-rural-2.107-0-sw"]
  code --> v["1 · version"]
  code --> l["MVLV · levels"]
  code --> t["rural · grid type"]
  code --> s["2.107 · LV grid in detail"]
  code --> sc["0 · scenario"]
  code --> sw["sw · switches"]

docs.title: 3. Element names: the subnet
docs.text:
Every element has a subnet that says which grid it belongs to (§4.2.2, Table 4.8). That is why the Inspect page shows names like LV4.101 Load 1.

Subnet Reads as HV2 HV grid of type 2 (HV and EHV subnets have two parts) MV3.201 MV grid of type 3, the first one (01) connected to an HV grid of type 2 (2xx) LV4.101 LV grid of type 4 (semi-urban 4), the first one connected to an MV grid of type 1

The third part counts from 1 + 100 · (type of the higher grid). Buses on the border between two grids carry both subnets, joined by _. Equivalent elements, which stand in for a grid that is not modelled in detail, end in _eq.

docs.text:
How many codes the Studio offers per level (all types × 3 scenarios × 2 switch variants, combinations × their lower grids):

docs.text:
The grids a local energy market lives on (§4.1.4, Table 4.5). Each is radial and fed from the 20 kV grid through one MV/LV transformer.

Values are scenario 0. At LV all generation is PV (no wind at this level). The consumers' rated power comes from the building floor area in OpenStreetMap (2 kW per average dwelling, varied by grid), and some values were raised by hand to load the grids more. Load types (household, commercial, farm) were assigned to the consumers by hand and at random. "LV rural 1" holds many farms, which is why its loads are larger than in real grids of its class.

docs.title: 5. Scenarios
docs.text:
Scenario Year What changes 0 today (2016 data) the grids as built 1 2024 more PV, plus heat pumps, electric vehicles and PV batteries 2 2034 more of the same; some grids get new lines and buses to priority areas for wind and PV (MV, HV)

How the future grids were made (§3.6): new generators and consumers were added following German forecasts (the grid development plan) until the grid shows problems, i.e. until about 15 % of its lines or nodes are overloaded or out of voltage limits in at least some of the grids. The scenarios are meant to be challenging, not to predict any one place.

At LV, averaged over all six grids (§4.1.6):

Scenario 1 (2024) Scenario 2 (2034) New PV, as a share of all PV plants 55 % 70 % Houses with an electric vehicle 4.5 % 19 % Houses with a heat pump 6 % 23 %

In LV rural 3, scenario 1 mostly brings overvoltage (PV at noon), scenario 2 mostly undervoltage and overloaded lines and transformer (heat pumps and EVs). Scenario 0 has no heat pumps, EV charging or storage in any LV grid. The network catalogue shows the effect on every grid.

docs.title: 6. Study cases
docs.text:
Fixed snapshots for planning studies, as scaling factors of the rated load and generation (§5.1, Tables 5.1 and 5.2). The Studio works with the time series instead, but the cases are useful to judge a power flow: a network should pass hL and lPV.

Case Situation Load Wind PV Other DER hL high load, low DER 1.00 0 0 0 n1 as hL, with one element out (contingency) 1.00 0 0 0 hW high load, very high wind 1.00 1.00 0.80 1.00 hPV high load, very high PV 1.00 0.85 0.95 1.00 lW low load, very high wind 0.10 (MV/LV), 0.25 (HV) 1.00 0.80 1.00 lPV low load, very high PV 0.10 (MV/LV), 0.25 (HV) 0.85 0.95 1.00

Slack and transformer voltage set points: in hL, n1, hW and hPV 1.025 pu (HV), 1.035 pu (MV), 0.965 pu (LV); in lW and lPV 1.015 pu (HV), 1.055 pu (MV). Load power factor cos φ = 0.93 (high-load cases) or 0.9 (low-load cases), underexcited. The cases ship with every network (StudyCases.csv, in pandapower net.loadcases).

docs.title: 7. Data format
docs.text: SimBench's own format is a set of CSV tables, one per element type plus type tables (e.g. cable types) and profile tables (§4.3.1). Voltages and currents are three-phase and symmetrical, powers three-phase, 50 Hz. The pandapower networks the Studio uses are converted from these tables by the simbench package; their profiles are in net.profiles (tables load, renewables, powerplants, storage), linked to the elements by their profile column.

docs.title: Network catalogue: what each grid offers
docs.text: Every network the Studio's Inspect page offers, with the facts that matter when choosing one for a study: size, load, generation, PV penetration, how many buses could become agents, and which load and generation types it contains. Use it to find networks of interest before opening them in the Studio. What SimBench is and how its codes read: SimBench overview · The time series behind the loads and generators: profiles · Raw data: networks.json.

docs.title: 1. How to read the tables
docs.text:
All values come from the networks themselves, as the Studio loads them (generated by python docs/networks.py --collect; the tables are rewritten from the stored data by python docs/networks.py).

246 networks (128 SimBench grid × scenario rows after merging the switch variants, 6 pandapower built-ins), from docs/simbench/networks.json.

Column Meaning Network SimBench code without the switch suffix: 1-LV-rural1--0 stands for 1-LV-rural1--0-sw and 1-LV-rural1--0-no_sw, which have the same elements (the variants differ only in whether bus-bar switches are modelled). The number after -- is the scenario: 0 today, 1 and 2 future scenarios with more PV, heat pumps, EV charging and storage Load, Generation Sum of the rated power of all loads and static generators (SimBench's reference values; the profiles scale these over the year, factor ≤ 1) Gen / load, PV / load Rated generation (all, or PV only) as a share of rated load: a simple measure of penetration. Above 100 % the network can export at times Load buses Buses with at least one load: the most agents a one-agent-per-bus placement can have Prosumer buses Buses with a load and a generator: candidates for prosumer agents, together with the buses that have storage Ratings, Geodata Whether lines have real current ratings (loading checks) and real coordinates (map layout) Loads by type Number of loads per SimBench class (households, commercial, farms, heat pumps, EV charging, aggregated grids; see Inspect → Profiles)

Rated values are not energy: a 3 kW household with the H0 profile uses far less than 3 kW on average. The Studio's Inspect page shows the profiles over time.

docs.title: 2. Highlights
docs.text:
What the tables below show, for choosing a network for a local-market study:

  • The Studio's default network has almost no local generation. 1-LV-semiurb4--0 (the network Inspect opens first) has one PV generator, 6.5 kW against 243 kW of load (3 %), on 1 of its 39 load buses. A peer-to-peer market there has little to trade unless the agents get catalogue generation profiles. Scenario 2 of the same grid raises PV to 51 % on 6 buses.
  • 1-LV-rural1 is the small, generation-rich grid: 15 buses, 13 load buses (mostly farms), PV at 200–572 % of the load. Good for quick tests with real prosumers, but it has at most 13 agents (8 prosumers).
  • 1-LV-rural3 has the most real prosumers at LV: 17 (scenario 0) to 27 (scenario 2) buses with load and PV out of 118, and in scenario 2 also 35 heat-pump and EV-charging loads and 16 storage units: the richest LV grid for heterogeneous agents.
  • Scenarios matter more than the grid choice suggests. Scenario 0 has no heat pumps, EV charging or storage in any LV grid; scenarios 1 and 2 add them. PV/load can fall from scenario 1 to 2 because the load grows (heat pumps, EVs) faster than the PV.
  • At LV, storage never shares a bus with PV. Every LV storage unit (scenarios 1 and 2) sits on a bus with only a load, so the LV bus kinds are load, load+pv and load+storage; no LV bus has load, PV and storage together. Each unit holds 2 h of its power. MV networks do have load+gen+storage buses. Participants are placed by these kinds (placement.place_all, placement.kind_counts).
  • MV networks are not prosumer markets. Their loads are mostly whole LV grids aggregated into one element (lv_… profiles), and their generation is wind, biomass, hydro and aggregated LV generation; PV of their own is 0–5 % of the load. Every bus there is a "prosumer bus", but each is a neighbourhood.
  • The combined networks (MVLV, HVMV, EHVHV, the "all" variants) are large: up to 10,458 buses and 14,589 loads. They are listed for completeness; they are far beyond what multi-agent RL can train on.
