docs.title: SimBench profiles: the time series of loads and generators
docs.text:
What a SimBench profile is, how the Studio turns it into power, and where each class of profiles comes from: households, businesses, farms, heat pumps, electric vehicles, PV, wind, biomass, hydro, storage and whole grids. SimBench in general: overview · Which networks use which profiles: network catalogue.

Section numbers like §3.5.2 refer to the SimBench documentation, version 1.1.0 (see the overview for the full reference). Counts, means and peaks in the tables are measured from the data set the Studio reads (scenario 0 unless stated).

docs.title: 1. What a profile is
docs.text:
A profile is a normalised time series: for every quarter hour of 2016 it gives a factor of an element's rated power. The element (a load, static generator or storage unit) names its profile in its profile column; many elements share one profile.

\[ P_e(t) = p_{e} \cdot f_{\text{profile}(e)}(t), \qquad Q_e(t) = q_{e} \cdot f^{q}_{\text{profile}(e)}(t) \]

with \(p_e\) the element's rated active power (p_mw) and \(q_e\) its rated reactive power (q_mvar).

Property Value Year 2016, a leap year: 366 days Resolution 15 minutes: 96 values per day, 35,136 per year Scale factor of rated power; 1.0 = rated power Reactive power loads have a P and a Q profile (H0-A_pload, H0-A_qload); generators and storage have P only Tables load, renewables (PV, wind, biomass, hydro, grids), powerplants (EHV plants, imports), storage

Things to know when reading the numbers:

  • Peaks are not always 1. Load profiles reach 1.0; PV profiles peak at most at 0.63 of rated power, because panels rarely deliver their rating.
  • Q factors can be negative: some measured loads feed reactive power back at times.
  • Rated power is not energy. A household of 3 kW with H0-A draws on average 0.19 × 3 kW ≈ 0.6 kW. The mean factors below show how far each class stays below its rating.
  • Time stamps. Measurements from other years (feed-in 2011/2012, hydro 2017, households 2010) were moved onto the 2016 calendar, with daylight saving time taken into account; the leap day was filled with the mean of the neighbouring same weekdays (§3.5.4).

docs.title: In the Studio
docs.text:
The Inspect page shows profiles in two ways:

  • Factor (the Profiles section of a network, and the Profiles tab with SimBench's whole catalogue): the normalised values above.
  • kW ("Sum per profile" / "Per element"): factor × rated power of the elements that use the profile, as in the formula above.

Resolutions: 15 min is the raw data; hourly is the mean of the four quarter hours of each hour (the market's default step, 24 per day); daily is the mean of all 96 values of a day.

docs.title: 2. The classes at a glance
docs.text:
Grouped as in SimBench's own overview (Meinecke et al., 2020, Figures 1 and 8); the Studio classifies every profile by its name (studio/adapters/profile_classes.py).

Group Class Names Profiles P / Q Mean factor Section Load, accumulated Households H0-A … H0-L 6 P, Q 0.19 §3 Commercial G0-A … G6-A 15 P, Q 0.35 §3 Agricultural L0-A, L1-A, L2-A, L2-M 4 P, Q 0.31 §3 Other standard profiles BL-H, WB-H 2 P, Q 0.52 §3 Load, individual Heat pumps Air_…, Soil_… 8 P, Q 0.10 §4 Electric vehicles HLS_…, APLS_… 15 P, Q 0.01 §4 Generation PV PV1 … PV8 8 P 0.07 §5 Wind WP1 … WP12 12 P 0.36 §5 Biomass BM1 … BM5 5 P 0.33 §5 Hydro Hydro1 … Hydro3 3 P 0.29 §5 Conventional plants pp_1 … 318 P 0.22 §5 Storage Storage Storage_PV…_… 0 (scenario 0), 60 (scenarios 1, 2) P 0.10 §6 Aggregated grids SimBench grids, load lv_…, mv_…, hv_… 16 P, Q 0.18 §7 SimBench grids, generation lv_…, mv_…, hv_… 14 P 0.15 §7 Omitted HV grids HS0 … HS27, HSexp0/1 30 P, Q 0.53 §7 Import imp0, imp1 2 P 0.39 §5

The whole catalogue has 458 profiles in scenario 0 and 518 in scenarios 1 and 2: the difference is the 60 storage profiles.

docs.title: 3. Accumulated consumers: households, businesses, farms
docs.text:
Accumulated consumers are many similar customers that are planned with a standard load profile (SLP), the German utilities' typical-day curves: H0 households, G0–G6 businesses, L0–L2 farms, B0 band load (§3.5.1). SimBench replaces each SLP by a real measured time series that matches it, so the profiles keep the randomness of real customers.

How the series were chosen:

  1. Data. Businesses and farms: 2,539 anonymised 15-minute measurements of 2016 (customers with a power meter, mostly under 100,000 kWh a year), after removing faulty files (~10 %) and series with cos φ < 0.8 (~14 %). Households: the IZES data set (HTW Berlin, 2010), resampled to 15 minutes by taking every 15th value instead of averaging, so the short-term peaks stay.
  2. Average week. Each series is averaged to one week (each weekday over the year, seasons ignored) and normalised to the week's mean.
  3. Matching. The distance to every SLP is the cumulative Euclidean distance (load and time) between the points of the two curves. A series is assigned to the SLP it is closest to, if it is not as close to another one.
  4. Size classes. By mean consumption per 15 minutes: 0–4 kWh for LV, 10–20 kWh for MV (318 series, 12.5 %), above 100 kWh for HV (17 series, 0.7 %).

The suffix after the dash is the consumption level and size class: -A, -B, -C … are different low-consumption series of the same class (LV), -M medium (MV), -H high (HV).

docs.title: Households (H0)
docs.text: H0-A, H0-B, H0-C: the three household series closest to H0 (§4.1.5, Figure 4.15). H0-G and H0-L: households that match the business profile G6 and the farm profile L1 better than H0. They were kept on purpose, so the set covers the spread of real households: many real households use much more at weekends than H0 assumes. H0-H: an HV-size industrial customer whose shape resembles H0 (high base load, even rise over the week).

docs.title: Commercial (G0–G6)
docs.text:
G for Gewerbe. SLP meaning: G0 business in general, G1 weekdays 8–18 h, G2 mainly evening, G3 continuous, G4 shops and hairdressers, G5 bakeries, G6 weekend business. Series: G0-A, G0-M, G1-A, G1-B, G1-C, G2-A, G3-A, G3-M, G3-H, G4-A, G4-B, G4-M, G4-H, G5-A, G6-A.

G0 is itself a mix of the other G profiles, so no real customer is "G0"; a measured series is supplied anyway because grid operators often use G0 for all businesses. Most measured business series matched G1 (over 20 % of the data).

docs.title: Agricultural (L0–L2)
docs.text: L for Landwirtschaft: L0 farms in general, L1 farms with dairy, L2 other farms. Series: L0-A, L1-A, L2-A, L2-M. Farm profiles have an even demand over the week with high morning and evening peaks, which is also why many measured households matched them.

docs.title: Other (BL-H, WB-H)
docs.text: Two HV-size series with an almost constant demand ("band load"). They matched B0 and L2 only loosely and are listed as "other".

docs.title: 4. Individual consumers: heat pumps and electric vehicles
docs.text: One device each, simulated bottom-up rather than measured (§3.5.2). Both use a fixed lagging power factor cos φ = 0.93, since the models give no reactive power.

docs.title: Heat pumps
docs.text:
The electrical demand of a heat pump that heats a three-person single-family house in Hanover or Lübeck (heat demand of 2016 with 2011 weather, so it correlates with the PV and wind series).

Name Heat source and operation Air_Parallel_1/2 Air source. Below −2 °C the pump and a backup heater run together Air_Alternative_1/2 Air source. Below −2 °C the pump stops and the heater covers everything Air_Semi-Parallel_1/2 Air source. Both run between −2 °C and −5 °C; below −5 °C only the heater Soil_Alternative_1/2 Ground source (probe), soil at a constant 7 °C. The documentation describes only parallel operation for ground-source pumps; the data names it "Alternative"

_1 and _2 are the two cities. How the series behave:

  • Lockout periods. The utility blocks heat pumps every day 07:45–09:30, 11:30–12:30 and 16:45–19:00: the profile is 0 then, and catches up afterwards.
  • Storage. A hot-water tank (8.7 kWh) and a space-heating tank (11–14 kWh) are charged when either falls below 50 % and filled to 100 %; hot water first.
  • Efficiency. COP = 0.36 · Carnot COP, flow temperature 55 °C.
  • Size. Pumps of 3.8–4.9 kW with heaters of 0.5–10.7 kW; in the grids, heat pumps of 2–30 kW use these profiles (larger ones at MV).

docs.title: Electric vehicles
docs.text:
Charging power at one charging point, from a bottom-up simulation of drivers (§3.5.2, §4.1.5): car model, battery (20–100 kWh) and consumption (15 or 25 kWh/100 km) drawn from the German fleet, measured charging curves of ten EV models, and trips from the survey Mobilität in Deutschland (number of trips, arrival times, purpose, distance, speed). A car charges with 80 % probability if it parks over three hours (20 % otherwise), always below 20 % state of charge.

Name Charging point Power HLS_A_3.7, HLS_B_3.7, HLS_C_3.7 at home (Heimladestation) 3.7 kW HLS_A_11.0, HLS_B_11.0 at home 11 kW HLS_A_22.0 at home 22 kW APLS_A_3.7, APLS_B_3.7 at work (Arbeitsplatzladestation) 3.7 kW APLS_A_11.0, APLS_B_11.0 at work 11 kW APLS_A_22.0 at work 22 kW APLS_A_50.0 at work 50 kW APLS_0.1014, APLS_0.5202, APLS_0.033 aggregated workplace charging for MV grids (name: nominal power in MW) e.g. 101.4 kW, the sum of the LV workplace series; ×5 for large companies

The single-point series are normalised to a maximum of 1. The aggregated ones are not, because all chargers never run at once. With a mean factor of 0.01, an EV charger draws its full power only for short times: these are the most "peaky" profiles in SimBench.

docs.title: PV, wind, biomass, hydro
docs.text:
PV, wind and biomass series were simulated with SIMONA, an agent-based grid simulation of the TU Dortmund, from weather data of the German Weather Service for 2011 and 2012 (§3.5.4). Plant sites follow the HV grids, so a wind farm in an HV grid gets the weather of its region. Hydro series are real, anonymised plant data of 2017. All are normalised to the plant's rating and have no reactive power: reactive power depends on how a plant is controlled, which SimBench leaves to the user (the study cases assume cos φ = 1).

Name Site PV orientation PV1 Hanover (site 3) east PV2 Lübeck (site 1) east PV3 Hanover (site 1) south PV4 Hanover (site 2) south PV5 Lübeck (site 2) south PV6 Lübeck (site 3) south PV7 Hanover (site 2) west PV8 Lübeck (site 2) west WP1, WP2 Baltic Sea, North Sea (offshore) WP3, WP9, WP6 Baltic coast, North Sea coast, East Germany WP4, WP7, WP10 east, north and south of HV grid 1 WP5, WP8, WP11 east, north and south of HV grid 2 WP12 (not listed in the documentation's table) BM1 … BM5 biomass plants: almost constant output (mean factor 0.33) Hydro1 … Hydro3 run-of-river plants

For a local market at LV, PV is the generation that matters: it is the only generation SimBench connects at LV. Its mean factor of 0.07 means a 10 kW system yields on average 0.7 kW, concentrated around noon and in summer.

docs.title: Power plants and imports
docs.text: Only in the EHV grids: pp_1 … pp_318, one profile per conventional power plant (many are constant), and imp0, imp1, generators at the border that stand for power from neighbouring countries.

docs.title: 6. Storage
docs.text:
SimBench models two kinds of batteries (§3.5.5, §4.1.5):

  • PV batteries that maximise self-consumption: the PV series is coupled to a household or business series; surplus PV charges the battery, a deficit discharges it. PV size = household energy × 0.00071 /h; the battery is large enough to store any surplus; charge and discharge efficiency 0.95; self-discharge 4 % per month.
  • Grid-beneficial batteries next to wind and PV plants that store the top 3 % of the plant's energy (a fixed power limit above which the feed-in is stored).

The profile is the battery's power at its bus as if only the PV system and the battery were connected; the household's own load is a separate element. Only the batteries actually installed in a grid have a profile, named after the series they combine: Storage_PV3_H0-A is a battery with PV3 next to an H0-A household.

Scenario 0 ships no storage profiles: batteries only appear in the future scenarios, which have 60 of them.

docs.title: 7. Aggregated grids
docs.text:
Where a network connects a whole grid of the level below as one element, that element follows the summed time series of the grid it stands for (§3.5.3, §4.1.5):

  • lv_…, mv_…, hv_… (bottom-up). A year-long power flow of each SimBench grid, recorded at its slack: lv_rural1 is the total load (or generation) of LV rural 1, used by an MV network's loads. Load versions have P and Q; generation versions P only. mv_add1, mv_add2 are further MV grids.
  • HS0 … HS27, HSexp0, HSexp1 (top-down). The EHV grid covers all of Germany, but only some HV grids are modelled. The rest come from Germany's total demand (ENTSO-E), split into households (by population, H0), farms (2 % of demand, by farmland, L0), businesses (by employees and area, G0) and industry and transport (the remainder), assigned to EHV/HV nodes by Voronoi areas and reduced to 28 representative series by k-means. exp marks the two series for nodes outside Germany. cos φ = 0.93.

For a local market these matter only as the background of MV and higher networks: an MV load called lv_semiurb4 is a whole neighbourhood, not a prosumer.

docs.title: 8. Where the data differs from the documentation
docs.text:
Found while writing this page, by comparing the documentation (v1.1.0) with the profiles the simbench package ships. The data is what the Studio uses.

Topic Documentation says Data has Ground-source heat pumps only parallel operation (§3.5.2) profiles named Soil_Alternative_1/2 Wind profiles table of sites lists WP1 … WP11 (Table 4.7) 12 profiles, WP1 … WP12 Feed-in scale "normalised to one" (§4.1.5) factors of rated power: PV peaks at 0.63, not 1 Aggregated grid profiles "normalised to one" (§4.1.5) peaks of 0.95 (load) and 0.92 (generation) Storage profiles active and reactive power series (§4.1.5) active power only Storage profiles per scenario — none in scenario 0; 60 in scenarios 1 and 2

The documentation's wording "normalised to one" most likely means "relative to the rated power", which the data follows; the other rows are open.

docs.title: Market layer: what was wrong and what changed
docs.text: Every problem found in the market layer of MARLEM: in the original code, in the paper [P1], or in the method itself. For each one, what was wrong, where it came from, and what marlem-clean does about it. The reinforcement-learning layer (actions, observations, reward, KPIs, training) is validated separately, starting with the training layer in rl.md, and is left out here.

docs.title: Scope and sources
docs.text:
Market layer means everything that turns orders into trades, money and energy:

  • order validation and the three clearing stages;
  • pricing mechanisms;
  • the DSO (stage 3, balance, fees);
  • transmission losses;
  • settlement, the battery and each participant's balance and profit;
  • reputation and the trade ledger;
  • the grid model as the market uses it.

Sources.

  • IDs I-xx are from the validation issue register (docs_thesis/thesis/validation/issues.md on the refactor branch).
  • The original code is the authors' MARLEM repository, salazarna/marlem, at its current main (commit 15d6715, March 2026). Every code link and snippet points there, pinned to that commit, so the line numbers stay valid.
  • IDs N-xx are new findings made while rebuilding the market in marlem-clean. They are not in the register.
  • [P1] is the MARLEM paper (Salazar-Peña et al., Applied Energy 412, 2026); its method is summarised in methodology.md.

Origin (as in the register):

Origin Meaning Paper The paper itself is wrong, contradictory or silent where the method needs an answer Fidelity The original code does not do what the paper says Code A programming defect that the paper has nothing to say about

Status in marlem-clean:

Status Meaning Fixed Rebuilt to match the paper; the wrong behaviour is gone Replaced The part was replaced by the SimBench network and its AC power flow, so the problem no longer exists Decided The paper is silent or contradictory; a rule was chosen and recorded (see structure.md, Choices) Open Known, not resolved yet Flagged Kept as in the original on purpose, but worth questioning

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Part of the market Issues Fixed Replaced Decided Open Flagged 1. The market step 4 3 1 0 0 0 2. Orders and feasibility 4 4 0 0 0 0 3. Clearing stages 3 1 0 2 0 0 4. Pricing mechanisms 3 2 0 1 0 0 5. Settlement, battery and balances 8 7 0 1 0 0 6. DSO: balance and grid fees 11 5 0 3 0 3 7. Grid model used by the market 7 1 5 1 0 0 8. Reputation 4 2 0 2 0 0 9. Trade ledger 1 0 0 0 0 1 Total 45 25 6 10 0 4

The most consequential ones for any result produced with the original:

  • Batteries ran backwards. Selling energy charged the battery (I-18), and the discharge efficiency was applied the wrong way round (I-20).
  • Two pricing mechanisms returned the buyer's bid. One was SELLER (I-13). The other was BID_ASK_SPREAD (I-17), which the paper's own case study uses.
  • The money and the DSO balance never moved. Profit was never updated (I-27), fees were never charged (I-28), and the DSO balance stayed at 0 (I-24).
  • Reputation only ever measured one thing. Reliability was always 1 and the grid part was always neutral, so only price fairness moved. The decay was weighted by the time of day (I-38).
  • The grid's edge flows started random and piled up over the day (I-33). Only stage-1 trades fed them (I-32).

docs.title: How to read an issue
docs.text:
Each issue below has the same parts:

  • Header: ID, title, origin and status in marlem-clean.
  • Original code: the lines at fault, copied from the original repository (salazarna/marlem, commit 15d6715). The caption links to them on GitHub with their line numbers. # ... stands for lines cut for length, and a few long calls are shortened with ....
  • Why it is wrong: what the lines do, which other code calls them or reads their result, and how that differs from [P1]. Where a definition looks harmless on its own, this part shows the call site that makes it wrong.
  • In marlem-clean: what the rebuild does, with a link, and the new code when it is short enough to compare.

Fixed green: fixed, and you're fine with what was done Review yellow: the AI fixed it, but you want to look again Open red: still open

docs.title: I-01: only 23 of 24 periods run
docs.text:
Fidelity · Fixed

src/environment/lem.py L433-L445

# STEP 4. Update environment state
self.current_step += 1
# ...
# STEP 5. Check if episode is done
if self.current_step >= self.max_steps - 1:
    terminateds = {agent_id: True for agent_id in self.agents_id}

Why it is wrong. The counter is raised before the check, and the check is against \(\text{max_steps} - 1\). With \(\text{max_steps} = 24\), the step that played period 22 raises the counter to 23, and \(23 \ge 23\) ends the episode. Periods 0-22 run, and period 23 (the last hour of the day) never does (T1). Every episode loses its last hour of demand and generation.

In marlem-clean. A day is \(24 / \text{step_hours}\) steps, and done is true only after all of them are recorded (lem.py).

docs.title: I-78: an invalid order stops the simulation
docs.text:
Fidelity · Fixed

Review This raises a bigger topic, how to deal with invalid actions across all the features

src/environment/lem.py L336-L343

for id in self.agents_id:
    action = action_dict[id]
    action_dict[id] = self._agents[id].adjust_action_for_battery(...)

    if not self.action_handler.is_valid_action(id, action_dict[id]):
        raise ValueError(f"Invalid action for {id}: {action_dict[id]}")

Why it is wrong. [P1] Algorithm 1 keeps an order only if ValidateOrder(o_i, S_t): an invalid order is dropped, and the market goes on. Here one bad action raises an exception, which ends the whole episode.

In marlem-clean. _validate clips the price to the market bounds and the quantity to eq. 15, drops what is left at or below \(q_{\min}\), and records each change as a note (lem.py).

docs.title: I-56: units and time step are mixed
docs.text:
Paper · Fixed

src/market/matching.py L33-L36, src/agent/der.py L35, src/agent/battery.py L99, L117, L135, L162

# MarketConfig
min_price: float = 0.0  # Minimum allowed price ($/Wh)
max_price: float = 1000.0  #  Maximum allowed price($/Wh)
min_quantity: float = 0.0  # Minimum allowed quantity (Wh)
max_quantity: float = 1000.0  # Maximum allowed quantity (Wh)

# DERAgent docstring
capacity: Maximum capacity of the DER (W)

# Battery docstrings
energy: Charging energy in kWh        # _can_charge
energy: Discharge energy in kWh       # _can_discharge
energy: Charging energy in Wh         # charge
energy: Discharging energy in Wh      # discharge

Why it is wrong. The market's own configuration says prices are in $/Wh and quantities in Wh. The battery's methods say kWh for the checks and Wh for the actual charging, and the DER capacity is in W. [P1]'s case study prices in $/MWh (35-280), and [P2] plots prices in "$/kWh". There is no step length anywhere, so "quantity" means energy per 1-hour step only by convention. Between the comments, the code and the two papers, a price differs by up to a factor of a million ($/Wh vs $/MWh), and any number that mixes energy, power and price is ambiguous.

In marlem-clean. Energy is kWh per step, power is kW, prices are per kWh, and the step length is explicit: GridSetup.step_hours, 1 h or 15 min (scenario.py). Power becomes energy with \(\text{kW} \cdot \text{step_hours}\) (der.py).

docs.title: I-05, I-06: a reset cannot be told which profiles to use
docs.text:
Code / Fidelity · Replaced

src/environment/lem.py L281-L293

for agent in self._agents.values():
    reputation = self.reputation_handler.reset(seed)
    generation, demand = self.der_profile_handler.reset(agent.capacity,
                                                        self.max_steps)
    agent.reset(reputation, generation, demand, seed)

src/profile/base.py L40-L43, src/profile/der.py L119-L129

df = pd.read_csv(path)
selected_col = np.random.choice(df.columns)       # a random column
return df[selected_col].tolist()

base_profile = self._load_profile(self.generation_file_path)
scale_factor = np.random.uniform(1.0, 1.3)        # and a random scale
# ...
    varied_value = value * scale_factor * (1 + noise)

src/profile/der.py L187-L198

base_value = effective_max_value * np.exp(-normalized_hour**2)
cloud_noise = np.random.uniform(-0.2 * cloudiness, 0.2 * cloudiness)
noise = np.random.uniform(-noise_magnitude, noise_magnitude)
value = max(0.0, (base_value + noise + cloud_noise) * capacity)

Why it is wrong. The reset has no way to say which profiles an episode should use, so the market cannot be put back into a defined starting state at all:

  • Profiles given to an agent are thrown away (I-05). DERAgent(...) takes generation and demand profiles, but reset() always replaces them with the profile handler's (T11). reset() itself takes no day or profile argument. There is no supported way to run the market on a chosen day, or to run the same day again.
  • What the handler produces is not a choice of day (I-06). A CSV profile is a random column of the file at a random 1.0-1.3 scale. Depending on what the columns hold, that is either a different household for the same agent, or a different day with an invented scale; the code does not say which.
  • With a seed, nothing varies; without one, nothing is reproducible. The reset reseeds the global random generator with the configured seed whenever no seed is passed (I-03). With a seed set, as in [P2] (seed 42), every episode draws the same profiles. Without one, no two runs can be compared. Neither is a defined rule.
  • The procedural profile is not eq. 17. [P1] eq. 17 is multiplicative, \(G = C \cdot I \cdot (1 + \varepsilon_{\text{noise}} + \varepsilon_{\text{cloud}})\). The code adds the noise to the irradiance shape instead, \((I + \varepsilon_{\text{noise}} + \varepsilon_{\text{cloud}}) \cdot C\), so the noise does not scale with the sun and appears at full size at dawn and dusk.

The market needs a reset with a clear rule: the same scenario and day give the same profiles, and an agent stays the same agent (same elements, same load type) whatever day is played. The original offers no such reset.

Outside the market layer. Whether profiles should differ between episodes is a reinforcement-learning question, not a market one. For training, playing a different day each episode (e.g. sampled from a year of data, with held-out days for evaluation) is desirable, so that agents generalise instead of memorising one day. That needs exactly the controllable reset the original lacks: the RL layer chooses the day, the market builds it. Under [P2]'s fixed seed, the original instead trains on the same profiles in every episode.

In marlem-clean. Generation and demand come from the SimBench profiles of the network elements a participant owns, for the scenario's day (GridSetup.day), and reset() rebuilds exactly that day every time (der.py). Eq. 17 is not used. Choosing a different day per episode is not built yet: the grid contract already provides for it (GridModel.reset(episode_seed, day), contract.py), but LocalEnergyMarket.reset() does not take a day yet. That is for the RL layer to call.

docs.title: I-08: feasibility clipping is not eq. 15
docs.text:
Fidelity · Fixed

src/agent/der.py L184-L228

price, quantity, is_buy, preferred_partner = action
# ...
if is_buy:
    # Calculate how much energy we need to buy after using our own generation
    energy_deficit = quantity - current_generation
    # ...
    quantity = max(0.0, energy_deficit)
else:
    # Calculate how much energy we can export after using our own generation
    energy_surplus = quantity - current_demand
    # ...
    quantity = max(0.0, energy_surplus)

Why it is wrong. [P1] eq. 15 bounds an order by the agent's physical position:

  • \(q_{\text{sell,max}} = \max(0, G - D) + E_{\text{dischargeable}}\)
  • \(q_{\text{buy,max}} = \max(0, D - G) + E_{\text{chargeable}}\)

The code instead treats the requested quantity as if it were the agent's demand (buying) or generation (selling) and subtracts the other side from it. A buyer with \(G = 0,\ D = 5\) that asks for 2 kWh is not limited to 5 + its battery room: its "deficit" is \(2 - 0\), and its battery may then cover that, so the order shrinks to 0. A seller with \(G = 10,\ D = 1\) asking to sell 3 kWh gets \(3 - 1 = 2\). The limit has nothing to do with what the agent can actually deliver or take.

In marlem-clean. Eq. 15a-b, with the battery's room from eq. 15c-d (der.py):

def max_sell_kwh(self, step: int) -> float:
    """Eq. 15a: q_sell,max = max(0, G_t − D_t) + E_dischargeable."""
    return max(0.0, self.net_kwh(step)) + self.battery_room()[1]

docs.title: I-09: an order can be sized as a buy and submitted as a sell
docs.text:
Fidelity · Fixed by design

src/agent/der.py L196, src/environment/lem.py L358

# DERAgent.adjust_action_for_battery: sizing the order
if is_buy:
    energy_deficit = quantity - current_generation
    # ...

# LocalEnergyMarket.step: submitting it
is_buy = bool(is_buy > 0.5)

Why it is wrong. The action's direction is a continuous number. The sizing code reads it as truthy (any non-zero value is a buy); the submitting code reads it as > 0.5. A raw value of 0.3 is sized with the buy logic, then submitted as a sell order (T8): the quantity was computed for the wrong side of the market.

In marlem-clean. The side is a boolean in OrderIntent, set once. Turning a continuous action into a side is RL-layer work.

docs.title: I-11: no way to submit nothing
docs.text:
Paper · Fixed at the market layer

src/agent/der.py L231-L232

price = max(market_config.min_price, min(market_config.max_price, price))
quantity = max(market_config.min_quantity, min(market_config.max_quantity, quantity))

Why it is wrong. After clipping for the battery the quantity can be 0, but it is then raised to min_quantity. With \(q_{\min} > 0\), an agent that has nothing to trade still submits an order of \(q_{\min}\). [P1] eq. 2 has no "no order" action either.

In marlem-clean. A participant with nothing to trade places no order, and _validate drops orders at or below \(q_{\min}\). Whether an RL action can express "nothing" is left to the RL layer.

docs.title: I-12: clearing overwrites the submitted orders
docs.text:
Code · Fixed

src/market/matching.py L347-L348, src/market/dso.py L232, L253

# Stage 2
buy_order.quantity -= (proposed_quantity - transmission_loss)
sell_order.quantity -= proposed_quantity

# Stage 3 (DSO), for every remaining order
sell_order.quantity = 0
buy_order.quantity = 0

src/environment/lem.py L424-L425, src/environment/reward.py L406

rewards = {id: self.reward_handler.calculate_reward(agent, orders[id], ...)
# ...
execution_ratio = executed_quantity / order.quantity if order.quantity > 0 else 0

Why it is wrong. The clearing stages subtract matched quantities from the order objects themselves, and the DSO sets every remaining one to 0. After clearing, every order in orders has quantity 0. Everything that reads the orders afterwards (the reward, the KPIs, the info dictionary) sees 0 instead of what was submitted (T3). The reward's order.quantity > 0 guard then makes every execution ratio 0. This is the root cause of the RL layer's I-43.

In marlem-clean. Every stage works on copies, work = [replace(o) for o in orders], and returns the remaining orders separately; the submitted orders are never changed (clearing.py).

docs.title: I-15: DSO-preferred orders are cleared before the peer market
docs.text:
Paper · Decided

src/market/matching.py L608-L623

# STAGE 1: Handle DSO preferences first
dso_preferred_orders = [o for o in orders if o.partner_id == self.dso.id]
# ...
if dso_preferred_orders:
    dso_trades, _ = self.dso.clear_unmatched_orders(current_step,
                                                    dso_preferred_buys,
                                                    dso_preferred_sells)
    preference_trades.extend(dso_trades)

Why it is wrong. [P1] §3.3.2 has three stages: mutual preferences, the double auction, then the DSO for the residual. The code adds a sub-stage the paper does not have: an order naming the DSO is cleared with the DSO first, before any peer matching. The paper gives no reason for naming the DSO at all, since its prices are the worst in the market.

In marlem-clean. Orders that prefer the DSO skip stages 1 and 2 and are cleared in stage 3 with the rest (clearing.py, L144).

docs.title: I-77: partner choice is a sort and a random pick, not a weighted score
docs.text:
Fidelity · Fixed

Review How to weight the formula, 50/50 ok?

src/agent/der.py L154-L159, src/environment/lem.py L362-L365

candidates = [agent for agent in candidates if agent.id != self.id]
candidates.sort(key=lambda x: (-x.reputation, self.location.distance_to(x.location, graph)))
return np.random.choice(candidates[:max(1, len(candidates) // 2 + 1)]).id if randomize else candidates[0].id

# called from step() with:
preferred_partner = self._agents[id].select_preferred_partner([...], graph, randomize=True)

Why it is wrong. [P1] §3.4: the rule-based strategy "prioritizes partners based on a weighted score of high reputation and short grid distance". The code does three other things:

  • it sorts by reputation first and uses distance only to break exact ties;
  • it picks at random from the top half;
  • its candidates include agents on the same side of the market, so a seller can name another seller, a preference stage 1 can never match.

In marlem-clean. A weighted score of reputation and closeness, over participants on the other side of the market only. Both are rescaled over the candidates, 1 for the best and 0 for the worst, so the weight \(w\) (partner_reputation_weight, 0.5) gives each the same say:

\[ \text{score}_j = w\, \frac{r_j - r_{\min}}{r_{\max} - r_{\min}} + (1 - w)\, \frac{d_{\max} - d_j}{d_{\max} - d_{\min}} \]

Without the rescaling, reputations that all start at 0.5 and drift by a few hundredths would lose to distance every time. Ties go to the nearer candidate (der.py, lem.py).

docs.title: I-55: the stage-2 capacity check can never trigger
docs.text:
Code · Decided

src/market/matching.py L158, L299-L307

self.grid_capacity: float = config.max_quantity * self.num_agents
# ...
if abs(grid_balance) > self.grid_capacity:
    # Grid is already at capacity, skip this match
    if grid_balance > 0:
        sell_idx += 1
    else:
        buy_idx += 1
    continue

Why it is wrong. "Grid capacity" here is \(\text{max_quantity} \cdot N\) (1000 kWh per agent by default), not anything about the grid. It is compared with the current balance, not with the balance after the trade, and that balance is the DSO balance, which stays 0 (I-24). The check never fires, so stage 2 has no grid constraint at all.

In marlem-clean. The check is gone. [P1] says violating trades "can be penalized or disallowed by the DSO" without choosing. Decided: penalized. The congestion and thermal fees (eq. 8a, 8d) price the loading of the lines on a trade's path in the previous power flow, trades with the DSO included (I-54). The power flow reports voltage and loading violations but blocks no trade. Disallowing would need a grid check per trade, for example with sensitivity factors as in Guerrero, Chapman and Verbič (2019), and a rollback: future work. The episode runs show whether violations occur at all.

docs.title: I-13: SELLER pricing returns the buyer's price
docs.text:
Fidelity · Fixed

src/market/mechanism.py L72-L84, src/market/matching.py L310-L312

class SellerPricing(BasePricing):
    def calculate_price(self,
                        sell_order: Order,
                        *args,
                        **kwargs) -> float:
        return sell_order.price

# the only caller, for every mechanism
trade_price = self.config.price_mechanism.get_instance().calculate_price(buy_order,
                                                                         sell_order,
                                                                         market_price)

Why it is wrong. The definition looks right on its own: it returns sell_order.price. But the caller passes the arguments by position, buy order first. The parameter named sell_order receives the buy order, and the real sell order disappears into *args. SELLER therefore returns the buyer's bid: buy 200, sell 50 gives 200 (T6). It behaves exactly like BUYER.

In marlem-clean. Every mechanism has one fixed signature, (buy_order, sell_order, reference_price), so an argument can no longer land in the wrong parameter (clearing_price.py).

docs.title: I-17: BID_ASK_SPREAD returns the buyer's price too
docs.text:
Fidelity · Fixed

src/market/mechanism.py L90-L111

def calculate_price(self,
                    buy_order: Order,
                    sell_order: Order,
                    factor: float = 0.5,
                    *args,
                    **kwargs) -> float:
    bid_ask_spread = buy_order.price - sell_order.price
    return sell_order.price + bid_ask_spread * max(0.0, min(factor, 1.0))

Why it is wrong. The same positional call as above passes market_price as the third argument, which here is factor. The factor is meant to be 0-1 (0.5 = midpoint), but it receives a price. With prices in $/MWh, as in [P1]'s case study (35-280), any market price above 1 is clipped to 1, and the trade price is the buyer's bid: buy 200, sell 50, market 100 gives 200 (T12). With prices below 1 the trade price lands at a meaningless point of the spread. This is the mechanism [P1]'s Case 5 uses, and §3.3.3 does not define it.

In marlem-clean. factor is a constructor argument (default 0.5), not a call argument (clearing_price.py):

def __init__(self, factor: float = 0.5) -> None:
    self.factor = max(0.0, min(factor, 1.0))

docs.title: I-16: the clearing price includes the DSO's trades
docs.text:
Paper · Decided

src/market/matching.py L368-L371, L385

# Update totals with DSO trades
for trade in dso_trades:
    total_volume += trade.quantity
    total_value += trade.quantity * trade.price
# ...
clearing_price = total_value / total_volume if total_volume > 0 else self.dso.get_market_price(current_step)

Why it is wrong. The step's "clearing price" is a volume-weighted average over all trades, including the DSO's at its feed-in tariff and utility price. When most energy goes to the DSO, the clearing price is mostly the DSO's tariffs. It is then used as the market signal everywhere: observations, the reputation's fairness (I-38), and the reference price of the proportional mechanism (eq. 11). [P1] does not define the clearing price.

In marlem-clean. Volume-weighted price of the peer trades only, and the previous price when there were none (lem.py).

docs.title: I-18: selling charges the battery
docs.text:
Fidelity · Fixed

src/agent/der.py L294-L305

current_generation = self.generation_profile[step]
current_demand = self.demand_profile[step]
net_trade_energy = energy_sold - energy_bought

energy_balance = current_generation - current_demand + net_trade_energy

if energy_balance > 0:
    # Surplus energy - charge battery
    self.battery.charge(energy_balance)
elif energy_balance < 0:
    # Energy deficit - discharge battery
    self.battery.discharge(abs(energy_balance))

Why it is wrong. Energy sold leaves the household, so it must reduce what is left for the battery; energy bought adds to it. [P1] eq. 13 is \(B = (G - D) + (E_{\text{bought}} - E_{\text{sold}})\). The code has the trade term the other way round, \((G - D) + (\text{sold} - \text{bought})\).

This is not the paper's logic with every sign reversed, which would still give the right battery behaviour. The one expression mixes two conventions: \(G - D\) counts a surplus as positive, while \(\text{sold} - \text{bought}\) counts exports as positive. A consistently mirrored version would need \(D - G\) as well, and would charge the battery when the result is negative; the code charges it when the result is positive. The inputs are what their names say: energy_sold is the energy the agent sold (lem.py), so no other sign makes up for it.

The original code itself, run on five households (battery at 50 kWh, efficiencies 1):

Household Left for the battery, eq. 13 The code's balance Battery after \(G = D\), sells 10 kWh −10 +10 60, charged Surplus 5, sells its surplus 0 +10 60, charged Deficit 5, buys its deficit 0 −10 40, drained Surplus 5, no trade +5 +5 55 Deficit 5, no trade −5 −5 45

The code agrees with the paper only when the agent does not trade. As soon as it trades, the trade term doubles the surplus or deficit instead of cancelling it: a household that sells its 5 kWh surplus still charges 10 kWh into its battery, and one that buys its deficit still drains 10 kWh from it (T7). Every result involving batteries is affected.

In marlem-clean. Eq. 13, then the battery (der.py):

balance = (g - d) + (bought - sold)  # [P1] eq. 13
charge = b.charge(balance) if b and balance > 0 else 0.0
discharge = b.discharge(-balance) if b and balance < 0 else 0.0

docs.title: I-19: a charge that would fill the battery is refused entirely
docs.text:
Fidelity · Fixed

src/agent/battery.py L104-L111, L140-L156

def _can_charge(self, energy: float) -> bool:
    if energy <= 0:
        return False
    # Check if battery is already full
    if self.energy_level + energy >= self.max_soc * self.nominal_capacity:
        return False
    return True

def charge(self, energy: float) -> float:
    if self._can_charge(energy):
        max_energy = min(energy, self.max_soc * self.nominal_capacity - self.energy_level)
        # ...
    else:
        self.state = BatteryState.IDLE
        return 0.0

Why it is wrong. charge already caps the energy at what fits (min(energy, room)), but _can_charge refuses any charge that would reach \(SoC_{\max}\), so that cap is never used. A battery with 1 kWh of room offered 1.5 kWh takes nothing. [P1] eq. 16 is \(\min(E + E_{\text{in}} \cdot \eta,\ SoC_{\max} \cdot C)\): it fills to the limit. _can_discharge has the same problem at \(SoC_{\min}\).

In marlem-clean. The battery takes what it can and returns how much (battery.py).

docs.title: I-20: discharge efficiency is applied the wrong way
docs.text:
Fidelity · Fixed

src/agent/battery.py L167-L179

if self._can_discharge(energy):
    max_energy = min(energy, self.energy_level - self.min_soc * self.nominal_capacity)
    energy_discharged = max_energy * self.discharge_efficiency

    self.energy_level -= energy_discharged
    # ...
    return energy_discharged

Why it is wrong. [P1] eq. 16: delivering \(E_{\text{out}}\) drains \(E_{\text{out}} / \eta_{\text{discharge}}\) from storage, more than is delivered. The code drains \(E_{\text{out}} \cdot \eta\), less than is delivered: at \(\eta = 0.95\), delivering 10 kWh removes only 9.5 kWh from the battery. The battery creates energy on every discharge.

In marlem-clean. \(E \leftarrow E - E_{\text{out}} / \eta_{\text{discharge}}\) (battery.py):

given = min(max(0.0, kwh), self.dischargeable_kwh)
self.energy_kwh = max(self.min_kwh, self.energy_kwh - given / self.discharge_efficiency)

docs.title: I-71: no power limit, and eq. 15 ignores efficiency
docs.text:
Paper · Decided

src/agent/battery.py L205-L214

def estimate_available_energy(self) -> Tuple[float, float]:
    available_charge = self.max_soc * self.nominal_capacity - self.energy_level
    available_discharge = self.energy_level - self.min_soc * self.nominal_capacity
    return (available_charge, available_discharge)

Why it is wrong. This is [P1] eq. 15c-d as printed, and the paper is the problem. It counts room in stored energy, but orders are in energy at the bus: with \(\eta_{\text{charge}} = 0.95\) the battery can take \(\text{room} / 0.95\) from the bus, and give only \(\text{room} \cdot 0.95\) to it. [P1] §3.4 also says operations are bound by "maximum charge/discharge rates", but eq. 16 has no rate, and neither does the code.

In marlem-clean. The room is seen from the bus, \((E_{\max} - E) / \eta_{\text{charge}}\) and \((E - E_{\min}) \cdot \eta_{\text{discharge}}\), and an optional max_power_kw caps both (battery.py).

The power limit comes from SimBench. A participant that takes over a SimBench storage unit gets it as its battery, with its energy capacity and power rating. Storage exists only in SimBench's future scenarios (--1-, --2-); scenario 0 has none. A battery added anywhere else gets SimBench's ratio, capacity ÷ 2 h, which holds for all 84 storage units of the twelve LV future-scenario networks. BATTERY_PRESETS offers their 10th, 50th and 90th percentile sizes: 6.8, 13.7 and 66.4 kWh (placement.py). A BatterySetup written by hand has no limit unless max_power_kw is given.

Review Can simbench provide the battery power value also or we should provide it ourselves?

docs.title: I-22: no household energy balance
docs.text:
Paper · Fixed

src/environment/lem.py L392-L411

for id in self.agents_id:
    # ... energy_bought, energy_sold from the trades
    self._agents[id].update_energy_tracking(self.current_step, energy_bought, energy_sold)
    self._agents[id].update_battery_from_trades(self.current_step, energy_bought, energy_sold)

Why it is wrong. After the trades, each household's energy is never closed: \(G - D + \text{bought} - \text{sold}\) goes to the battery (with the wrong sign, I-18), and whatever the battery refuses (I-19) or cannot hold simply disappears. Nothing says where it went, and nothing checks that the energy adds up. [P1] gives eq. 13 but no conservation rule.

In marlem-clean. Eq. 13 → battery → the rest is exchanged with the upstream grid untraded and recorded as external_kwh. The power flow uses this physical outcome, never the trades (der.py). The notebook checks it every step ("nothing left untraded").

docs.title: I-26: the agent's "balance" is its net trade, in the other sign convention
docs.text:
Fidelity, inconsistency · Fixed

src/environment/lem.py L440, src/market/matching.py L435-L445

agent.balance = self.market.get_agent_position(id)

def get_agent_position(self, agent_id: str) -> float:
    position = 0.0
    # ...
        if trade.seller_id == agent_id:
            position += trade.quantity  # Positive when selling
        if trade.buyer_id == agent_id:
            position -= trade.quantity  # Negative when buying
    return position

What is going on. [P1] eq. 13 defines the balance as \(B = (G - D) + (E_{\text{bought}} - E_{\text{sold}})\): positive means surplus. The code's agent.balance is a different quantity under the same name: only the agent's trades, \(\text{sold} - \text{bought}\), with no \(G - D\), and positive when the agent is a net seller. An agent that bought exactly its deficit has \(B = 0\) in the paper but a negative "balance" here.

The sign on its own is not a fault. Its only reader in the original code is the reward's impact term, prev_balance = self.dso.balance - agent.balance (reward.py), where the DSO balance counts excess supply as positive. Selling adds supply, so subtracting the agent's net selling correctly gives the market without this agent. The convention is used consistently there.

It is an inconsistency, not a fault:

  • The name says eq. 13, the content is something else. The paper's balance is a household's energy left after trading; this is its net trade only.
  • The sign convention differs from the rest of the market code. Everywhere else a positive balance means surplus (eq. 13, eq. 20, the DSO balance, the reputation, the fees); here positive means "sold more than bought".
  • Its one reader sees it a step late. agent.balance is set after the rewards are computed (lem.py), so the reward uses the previous step's value. In the first step it is the random start \(U(-C, C)\) that reset() puts there (der.py).

In marlem-clean. balance_kwh is eq. 13 (der.py).

docs.title: I-27: profit is never updated
docs.text:
Fidelity · Fixed

src/agent/der.py L61, L109, src/environment/observation.py L342

# DERAgent.__init__ and DERAgent.reset: the only two assignments
self.profit: float = 0.0
self.profit = 0.0

# ObservationHandler: read every step
agent.profit,

Why it is wrong. [P1] eq. 14 is \(\text{profit}_{t+1} = \text{profit}_t + \sum (p_{\text{sell}} q_{\text{sell}} - p_{\text{buy}} q_{\text{buy}})\). In the whole original code base, the agent's profit is assigned only twice, both times 0. Nothing adds the trades to it. The observation reports it every step, and it is always 0 (T5). (The DSO's profit, by contrast, is updated.)

In marlem-clean. settle adds each step's revenue minus cost minus grid fees (der.py). The participants' and the DSO's money adds up to 0 every step (notebook check "money adds up").

docs.title: I-21: demand satisfied ignores battery discharge
docs.text:
Code · Fixed

Review does salazar say anything about this in their paper? If the trades could always be settled with the DSO then Im not sure why he even included it?

src/agent/der.py L254-L259

# Demand can be satisfied by: own generation + market purchases + battery discharge
energy_available_for_demand = current_generation + energy_bought

demand_satisfied_this_step = min(current_demand, energy_available_for_demand)
demand_deferred_this_step = max(0.0, current_demand - demand_satisfied_this_step)

Why it is wrong. The comment lists battery discharge, the code leaves it out. An agent that covers its night demand from its battery is counted as having deferred that demand. Also, update_energy_tracking runs before update_battery_from_trades (lem.py L416-L423), so the discharge is not even known yet when this runs.

In marlem-clean. [P1] §3.4.1 tracks "the total demand satisfied versus the demand deferred, providing a measure of the agent's energy security", and [P1] and [P2] list the cumulative values among the observations. Every participant's outcome now has its demand and supply satisfied and deferred (der.py). Generation, purchases and battery discharge all count, and the battery has settled before they are read.

Since the DSO clears every order, no demand goes physically unmet. Deferred is what the participant's own orders and battery left uncovered, exchanged with the upstream grid untraded (external_kwh). It is a signal of how well an agent ordered, not a market rule: the reward's unmet-demand penalty \(\gamma_{UD}\) is about the same quantity. With the rule-based bidding it is always 0 (notebook checks "nothing left untraded" and "satisfied + deferred = demand").

docs.title: I-24: the DSO balance stays at 0
docs.text:
Fidelity · Fixed

src/market/matching.py L259-L266, L338-L344, L374

# after stage 1
for trade in preference_trades:
    if trade.buyer_id == self.dso.id:
        grid_balance -= trade.quantity
    elif trade.seller_id == self.dso.id:
        grid_balance += trade.quantity

# inside the stage-2 loop
if buy_order.agent_id == self.dso.id:
    grid_balance -= proposed_quantity
elif sell_order.agent_id == self.dso.id:
    grid_balance += proposed_quantity

# after stage 3
self.dso.balance = grid_balance

Why it is wrong. [P1] eq. 7: \(B_{\text{DSO}} = \sum (E_{\text{sold}} - E_{\text{bought}})\) over the DSO's trades. The balance here changes only for DSO trades made in stage 1 or stage 2. But stage 2 never contains a DSO order (the DSO places none), and stage 1 has one only when an agent names the DSO as partner, which the rule-based partner choice never does. Stage 3, where all DSO trades normally happen, does not touch grid_balance. So dso.balance stays at its start value, 0, for the whole episode (T4). It also carries over from step to step (it is passed back in as the next step's start), so it is not a per-period quantity either.

In marlem-clean. Dso.settle computes eq. 7 from every DSO trade, per step and over the day, with the DSO's revenue and fees (dso.py).

docs.title: I-25: two opposite sign conventions for the DSO balance
docs.text:
Code · Fixed

src/market/matching.py L261-L266 vs L630-L633

# match_orders: by the DSO's trade
if trade.buyer_id == self.dso.id:
    grid_balance -= trade.quantity      # DSO buys  -> balance down
elif trade.seller_id == self.dso.id:
    grid_balance += trade.quantity      # DSO sells -> balance up

# _match_preferred_partners: by the agent's order
if order.is_buy:
    grid_balance -= order.quantity      # agent buys = DSO sells -> balance down
else:
    grid_balance += order.quantity      # agent sells = DSO buys -> balance up

Why it is wrong. The same DSO-preferred trade is counted with opposite signs in the two functions: when the DSO sells, match_orders raises the balance and _match_preferred_partners lowers it. Which one a trade passes through decides the sign.

In marlem-clean. One convention everywhere: sold − bought, so + means the market imported from the DSO.

docs.title: I-23: the market balance \(B_{\text{grid}}\) is never computed
docs.text:
Fidelity · Fixed

src/environment/lem.py L472, src/environment/observation.py L285

"grid_balance": self.dso.balance,     # info
matching.grid_balance,                # observation (= dso.balance)

Why it is wrong. [P1] eq. 20 defines the grid balance as \(B_{\text{grid}} = \sum_i (G_i - D_i + E_{\text{bought},i} - E_{\text{sold},i})\) over the agents. The code never computes it. Every "grid balance" in the info, the observation, the reputation and the reward is the DSO balance, which is itself always 0 (I-24).

In marlem-clean. grid_balance_kwh is the energy offered minus the energy asked in the step's orders (lem.py). It is taken before stage 3 on purpose: after the DSO clears every order, eq. 20 is 0 by construction.

docs.title: I-28: grid fees are computed but never charged
docs.text:
Fidelity · Fixed

src/market/dso.py L342-L345, src/market/matching.py L319-L332

# DSOAgent.calculate_fees
total_fee = congestion_fee + transmission_fee + imbalance_fee + voltage_fee + thermal_fee + zone_bonus
self.fees += total_fee
return total_fee

# stage 2: the fee is stored on the trade
grid_fees = self.dso.calculate_fees(buy_order, sell_order, trade_price, proposed_quantity)
trades.append(Trade(..., distance, transmission_loss, grid_fees))

Why it is wrong. The fee (eq. 8) is computed, added to the DSO's own counter and stored on the trade, and then nothing reads it. Settlement (lem.py L404-L423) uses only the trade quantities, and the agents' profit is never updated anyway (I-27). No agent ever pays a fee, so the fees cannot shape any incentive, which is their purpose in [P1].

In marlem-clean. The DSO puts the fee on every trade and says who pays it, split 50/50 between peers or paid in full by the participant on a DSO trade. Settlement takes it off profit, and the DSO collects it (dso.py):

fees = sum(t.buyer_fee for t in trades if t.buyer_id == self.id)
fees += sum(t.seller_fee for t in trades if t.seller_id == self.id)
# ...
profit -= fees

docs.title: I-29: \(F_{\text{trans}}\) has no formula, and the code uses 0
docs.text:
Paper · Decided

Review How to calculate transmission fee? what examples are used in other literature?

src/market/dso.py L293, L314

transmission_fee = 0.0
# ...
# Calculate transmission distance and fee
distance = buy_order.location.distance_to(sell_order.location, self.grid_network.graph) if ...

Why it is wrong. [P1] eq. 8 lists \(F_{\text{trans}}\) among the fee parts but gives no formula. The code computes the trade's distance under the comment "calculate transmission distance and fee", then never uses it for a fee: transmission_fee stays 0. (The distance does feed the voltage fee.)

In marlem-clean. The form is set; its values are open. [P1] gives two hints. The text of eq. 8 calls \(F_{\text{trans}}\) a charge for "usage per unit of distance of the transmission lines (predefined by the DSO)", and §3.5.2 says the losses "are incorporated into trading fees". Both give a fee of quantity × distance × a price factor. Here it is the lost energy (eq. 18) at the trade price (dso.py):

\[ F_{\text{trans}} = l_{ij}\, p_{ij} = \kappa\, d_{ij}\, q_{ij}\, p_{ij} \]

Still to choose: the price factor (\(\kappa\, p_{ij}\), or a fixed tariff per kWh and km as in the MW-mile method) and the distance (line length now; an impedance-based electrical distance is an option). The same fee applies to trades with the DSO, along the path to the transformer (I-54).

docs.title: I-30: \(F_{\text{volt}}\) is gated by its threshold and capped at 0.2
docs.text:
Fidelity · Decided

src/market/dso.py L326-L333

voltage_drop = distance * self.voltage_factor
if voltage_drop > self.voltage_threshold:
    voltage_fee = min(0.2, voltage_drop) * quantity * trade_price

if congestion_level > self.instability_threshold:
    thermal_factor = (congestion_level - self.instability_threshold) / (1.0 - self.instability_threshold)
    thermal_fee = min(0.3, thermal_factor) * quantity * trade_price

Why it is wrong. [P1] eq. 8c is \(F_{\text{volt}} = \min(V_{\text{drop}}, V_{\text{threshold}}) \cdot q \cdot p\): the threshold is the cap, and the fee is charged from the first metre. The code uses the threshold as a gate (no fee at all below 0.05) and a different cap (0.2). On a low-voltage feeder, where trades are a few hundred metres apart, \(V_{\text{drop}} = 0.15 \cdot 0.2\ \text{km} = 0.03\) is below the gate, so the voltage fee is always 0. The thermal cap 0.3 is \(f_{\text{threshold}}\) of eq. 8d, which [P1] leaves undefined.

In marlem-clean. \(F_{\text{volt}}\) exactly as eq. 8c; the thermal cap kept at the original's 0.3 as thermal_cap (dso.py).

docs.title: I-31: the imbalance fee can never apply
docs.text:
Fidelity / Paper · Decided

src/market/dso.py L336-L339, L421-L425, L227-L229

# calculate_fees, called only for peer trades
balance_impact = self._calculate_balance_impact(buy_order.agent_id, sell_order.agent_id, quantity)
if balance_impact < 0:
    imbalance_fee = abs(balance_impact) * quantity * trade_price * self.imbalance_factor

# _calculate_balance_impact
if self.balance > 0:
    if buyer_id != self.id and seller_id != self.id:
        # P2P trade doesn't directly affect grid balance
        return 0.0

# clear_unmatched_orders: every DSO trade
dso_trades.append(Trade(self.id, sell_order.agent_id, ..., 0.0, 0.0, 0.0))  # No grid fees for DSO trades

Why it is wrong. Three pieces that cannot meet. calculate_fees runs only for peer trades, and for a peer trade the balance impact is 0 by definition. Eq. 8h defines a non-zero impact only for trades with the DSO, but every DSO trade is created with a fee of 0. On top, the impact is measured on self.balance, which is always 0 (I-24), so even that branch is never reached. \(F_{\text{imb}}\) is 0 in every possible run (N-04).

In marlem-clean. The imbalance fee is charged on DSO trades that worsen the market's balance \(B_{\text{grid}}\) (the DSO buying in excess demand, or selling in excess supply); a trade that helps pays nothing (dso.py).

Review What trade could exactly help at the same time while bringing in more of the quantity that already exists in the P2P market? I dont see a situation

docs.title: I-54: DSO trades skip the grid, and the grid check ignores direction
docs.text:
Code · Fixed

Review What options do we have here? It would make sense to atleast use the feeder distance from the bus as the closest point to the DSO but im not sure if that is good enough, in any case some dynamics instead of nothing!?

src/market/dso.py L224-L226, L371

# every DSO trade
0.0,  # DSO is assumed to be at zero distance
0.0,  # No transmission loss with DSO
0.0)) # No grid fees for DSO trades

# validate_grid_constraints
if self.grid_network and abs(self.balance + proposed_quantity) > self.grid_network.capacity:
    return False

Why it is wrong. Energy bought from or sold to the DSO travels through the same lines as peer energy, but DSO trades have no distance, no loss and no fee, and are never checked against the grid. The check that does exist adds the quantity to the balance whatever the trade's direction, so a trade that would reduce an imbalance is treated as increasing it.

In marlem-clean. The DSO's energy enters where the upstream grid feeds the network, the transformer's low-voltage busbar. A trade with the DSO runs along the participant's path to that busbar (powerflow.py, dso.py). It has a distance, a loss (eq. 18) and the fees of that path: congestion and thermal on its lines, voltage and transmission by its length. It gets no zone bonus, since the DSO is in no participant's zone. A neighbour is closer than the transformer, so a peer trade pays less in fees than a trade with the DSO: the local incentive of [P1] §3.5.2. In the notebook's example day the DSO trades pay about 1.4 in fees, the peer trades about −1.1 (notebook check "DSO trade runs to the transformer").

No trade is blocked for grid reasons (I-55): the fees penalize, and the power flow shows the physical result of all energy.

docs.title: I-74: the thermal fee starts far below the congestion fee
docs.text:
Paper · Flagged

Review How is this usually handeled in real life? Who is to say that the thermal fee cant start much earlier, I understand congestion might be more important but they are different effects.

src/market/dso.py L65-L67

self.congestion_threshold: float = 0.8  # Threshold for congestion intervention
self.voltage_threshold: float = 0.05  # Threshold for voltage drop
self.instability_threshold: float = 0.2  # Threshold for grid stability

Why it is wrong. The thermal fee (eq. 8d, 8g) starts at 20 % line loading, the congestion fee (eq. 8a) at 80 %. A line at 50 % already pays a thermal fee for "thermal instability" while it is far from congested. [P1] gives no values; these are the original's.

In marlem-clean. Kept as defaults (thermal_threshold, congestion_threshold), each its own setting.

Real distribution grids have no fee that starts at 20 % loading. "Congestion" means loading beyond a line's thermal rating, and operators act near that limit, for example through flexibility markets such as the Dutch GOPACS. The thermal costs underneath grow smoothly: losses with the square of the current, transformer ageing steeply above rated load.

In the model the two fees are not separate effects anyway: eq. 8a and 8g read the same loading \(C_t\). Together they form one fee that rises with loading in two steps, gently from \(T_{\text{threshold}}\) and steeply from \(C_{\text{threshold}}\) (with \(x^+ = \max(x, 0)\)):

\[ \frac{F_{\text{thermal}} + F_{\text{cong}}}{q_{ij}\, p_{ij}} = \min\!\left(\frac{(C_t - T_{\text{threshold}})^+}{1 - T_{\text{threshold}}},\ f_{\text{threshold}}\right) + f_{\text{cong}}\, (C_t - C_{\text{threshold}})^+ \]

The values are set once the episode runs show how loaded the lines of SimBench's LV networks get. Below about 30 % loading both parts are close to 0, and the choice does not matter.

docs.title: N-05: the same-zone bonus outweighs every fee
docs.text:
Paper · Flagged

src/market/dso.py L317-L319, L72

self.zone_factor: float = 0.15  # Factor for cross-zone fees
# ...
if buy_order.location and sell_order.location and buy_order.location.zone == sell_order.location.zone:
    zone_bonus = -quantity * trade_price * self.zone_factor

Why it is wrong. A same-zone trade gets 15 % of its value back. On a low-voltage feeder the other fees are small: the voltage fee is about 3 % of the value (once charged as eq. 8c), the loss fee less than 1 %, and congestion and thermal fees are 0 at normal loading. Total fees are therefore negative: the DSO pays peers to trade locally. In the notebook's example day the peer trades' fees add up to about −1.1: a zone bonus of −1.6 against 0.5 of other fees. [P1] gives no factor values; whether a subsidy is intended is not said.

In marlem-clean. Kept at the original's 0.15 for now. zone_factor is one setting, and its value is open: it should be of the size of the other fees, a few percent of a trade's value.

docs.title: N-06: zones exist only for the paper's graphs
docs.text:
Paper · Flagged

Review I need suggestions here on options to see if they make sense, Im not sure how zones make sense on these small scale experiments but then again simbench has large networks also, how big were the zones for salazar or did he even use them?

src/market/dso.py L317

buy_order.location.zone == sell_order.location.zone

Why it is wrong. [P1] §3.5.4 defines zones as connected parts of its graph topologies (mesh, ring, line, IEEE feeders). A real distribution network has no such labels, so the zone bonus needs a definition that fits it.

In marlem-clean. A zone is a feeder: the branch a bus hangs on, named by the first bus after the transformer's low-voltage busbar (powerflow.py).

[P2] did use zones: its case study divides IEEE-34 into six named zones (substation, transformer, feeder 1 and 2, lateral 1 and 2) for 8 agents. Its zones are branches of the feeder, as here. On SimBench's networks they hold a few to a few dozen loads:

Network Zones with loads Loads per zone 1-LV-rural1--0-sw 4 1, 3, 4, 5 1-LV-semiurb4--0-sw 3 5, 8, 26 1-LV-urban6--0-sw 7 1 to 16 1-MV-rural--0-sw 9 1 to 18

A zone's only effect is the bonus of eq. 8e: a trade within one zone pays \(f_{\text{zone}}\) of its value less. Regulators do something similar: Austria's Renewable Expansion Act (EAG, 2021) cuts grid charges more for local energy communities (low-voltage level) than for regional ones. How large the bonus should be is the open question of N-05.

docs.title: 7. Grid model used by the market
I-33: edge flows start random and pile up all episode
docs.text:
Fidelity · Replaced

src/grid/network.py L85, L322-L325

# at construction
self.edge_flows[(u, v)] = np.random.uniform(0, 0.3) * edge_capacity

# update_flow_from_trade, for every trade on the path
self.edge_flows[key] += power_at_edge
self.edge_flows[key] = float(min(self.edge_flows[key], self.edge_capacities[key]))

Why it is wrong. Each line starts at a random 0-30 % of its capacity, and every trade adds its energy to the lines on its path. Nothing ever resets or reduces the flows, so congestion only grows within an episode (T10) until lines sit at the capacity cap. [P1] §3.5.3 describes a per-period update; congestion here measures the episode's history, not the current period.

In marlem-clean. One AC power flow per step on a fresh state of the network (powerflow.py).

docs.title: I-32: only stage-1 trades reach the grid
docs.text:
Fidelity · Replaced

src/market/matching.py L575, L346-L353

# _create_trade (used by stage 1 only)
self.grid_network.update_flow_from_trade(buyer_node, seller_node, proposed_quantity)

# stage 2 builds its trades directly, without it
trades.append(Trade(buy_order.agent_id, sell_order.agent_id, trade_price, ...))

Why it is wrong. The flow update lives in _create_trade, which only stage 1 calls. Stage 2, where most peer trades happen, appends Trade(...) objects itself and never updates the flows. So the congestion the fees and the grid check rely on ignores almost all peer energy.

In marlem-clean. The flow comes from each participant's physical injection at its bus, whichever stage its trades came from.

docs.title: I-57: the IEEE-34 graph is disconnected
docs.text:
Fidelity · Replaced

src/grid/config.py L29-L39

"edges": [("800", "802", 0.486), ("802", "806", 0.527), ("806", "808", 0.932),
          # ...
          ("852", "832", 0.21), ("854", "856", 0.157), ("854", "852", 0.621),
          ("858", "864", 0.496), ("858", "834", 1.774), ("860", "836", 0.268),
          ("862", "838", 0.223), ("888", "890", 1.584)],

Why it is wrong. In the IEEE 34-node feeder, node 888 hangs off node 832 through the in-line transformer. The edge 832-888 is missing, so 888 and 890 form an island (T13): agents there have no path to anyone, and distances to them fall back to Euclidean (I-53). The impedance table defined next to the edges is never used.

In marlem-clean. SimBench networks.

docs.title: I-70: the grid physics is linear and unbounded
docs.text:
Paper · Replaced

src/grid/network.py L348, src/market/dso.py L326

return distance * quantity * np.clip(loss_factor, 0.0, 1.0)   # loss
voltage_drop = distance * self.voltage_factor                  # voltage drop

Why it is wrong. Losses grow linearly with \(d \cdot q\) instead of with the square of the current, and once \(d \cdot \kappa > 1\) a trade loses more than it carries. The voltage drop is a distance times a constant, independent of the load. Flows are quantities moved along graph edges, not power flow. [P1] nevertheless calls its grid "high-fidelity". This is the paper's model, not a coding slip.

In marlem-clean. The physics is a pandapower AC power flow. The paper's linear forms remain only inside the market's fee formulas (eq. 8f, eq. 18), where [P1] defines them.

docs.title: I-53: defensive code hides bad state
docs.text:
Code · Replaced

src/grid/network.py L38, L95, src/grid/base.py L51-L57

self.capacity = max(0.0, capacity)
# ... in _check_init, which can now never fail:
if self.capacity < 0:
    raise ValueError(...)

try:
    return nx.shortest_path_length(graph, source=self.node_id, target=other.node_id, weight='weight')
except:
    return self._euclidean_distance(other.x, other.y)

Why it is wrong. A negative capacity is silently turned into 0 before the check that should reject it. Any failure of the shortest path (a disconnected graph, I-57, or a wrong node ID) silently becomes a straight-line distance in made-up coordinates, so the fee and loss calculations go on with a number that has nothing to do with the grid.

In marlem-clean. The grid code is new. Elements reject impossible settings instead of correcting them (Battery._check, Scenario.problems()), and a missing bus raises an error (powerflow.py).

docs.title: I-14: losses are topped up from the DSO
docs.text:
Fidelity · Decided

src/market/matching.py L347, src/environment/lem.py L397-L401

# stage 2
buy_order.quantity -= (proposed_quantity - transmission_loss)  # Buyer receives less due to losses

# settlement
for trade in matching_result.trades:
    if trade.buyer_id == id:
        energy_bought += trade.quantity

Why it is wrong. The buyer's order is reduced by less than the trade, so the lost part stays open on the buyer's order and is then bought from the DSO in stage 3. The buyer pays the DSO for the peer trade's losses, while settlement counts the full trade quantity as delivered. The household receives \(q\) from the peer and the loss from the DSO, so energy bought exceeds what the agent needed. [P1] says only that the loss "derates the delivered quantity".

In marlem-clean. The market is lossless. Each trade records its loss (eq. 18) and pays for it in the fee (I-29); the physical losses are the power flow's.

docs.title: I-34: the loss factor is hard-coded
docs.text:
Code · Fixed

src/grid/network.py L331-L334, src/market/matching.py L316

def transmission_loss(self, distance: float, quantity: float,
                      loss_factor: float = 0.03) -> float:

# the caller never passes it
transmission_loss = self.grid_network.transmission_loss(distance, proposed_quantity)

Why it is wrong. \(\kappa\) of eq. 18 is a default argument that no caller sets and no configuration reaches, in "distance units" of whatever graph is used. [P1] gives no value.

In marlem-clean. loss_factor is a DSO setting, per km of line (scenario.py). Every trade also records its distance \(d_{ij}\), along the network's lines.

docs.title: I-38a: reliability is always 1
docs.text:
Fidelity · Fixed

src/market/reputation.py L125-L129, src/market/matching.py L382

# ReputationHandler._calculate_reputation, STEP 1
agent_trades = [t for t in matching_result.trades if t.buyer_id == agent.id or t.seller_id == agent.id]
agent_unmatched = [o for o in matching_result.unmatched_orders if o.agent_id == agent.id]
reliability = len(agent_trades) / (len(agent_trades) + len(agent_unmatched)) if ... else self._neutral

# OrderMatcher.match_orders, what it passes in
# DSO is always active, so all orders should be matched
unmatched_orders = []

Why it is wrong. The definition reads sensibly: trades over trades plus unmatched orders. But the matcher always passes an empty list of unmatched orders, because the DSO clears everything. So for any agent with a trade, reliability is \(n / (n + 0) = 1\). [P1] eq. 12 calls it "the ratio of matched to total order volume", and it never varies.

In marlem-clean. Order volume matched by peers ÷ order volume (reputation.py).

docs.title: I-38b: the decay follows the time of day
docs.text:
Fidelity · Decided (marlem-v1)

Review If and what formula to use? Just reverse salazars to the proper form?

src/market/reputation.py L86-L87, src/environment/lem.py L436, L441

new_reputation = self._calculate_reputation(agent, matching_result, dso_id)
return (time_of_day * agent.reputation) + ((1.0 - time_of_day) * new_reputation)

# the caller
self.time_of_day = (self.current_step % self.max_steps) / self.max_steps
agent.reputation = self.reputation_handler.update_reputation(agent, matching_result, self.time_of_day)

Why it is wrong. [P1] §3.3.4 updates the reputation "incorporating a decay factor to weigh recent behavior more heavily". Here the weight of the old reputation is the time of day. In the first hour the old reputation counts 1/24 and the new score almost everything; in the last hour the old reputation counts 23/24 and that hour's behaviour almost nothing. Recent behaviour weighs less as the day goes on, the opposite of the paper.

In marlem-clean. A constant decay, \(r \leftarrow 0.8\, r + 0.2\, \text{score}\), in update_reputation (reputation.py).

Decided (marlem-v1). A constant decay per hour, applied per step as \(\delta = 0.8^{\Delta t}\) with \(\Delta t\) the step length in hours (lem.py). Reversing the original's weights would still tie the memory to the hour of the day; a per-hour decay keeps the memory the same when the step length changes (I-56). With 0.8 the old reputation halves in about 3.1 hours (\(\ln 0.5 / \ln 0.8\)), whether the step is an hour or a quarter of an hour. Hourly scenarios behave exactly as before.

docs.title: I-38c: the grid part is always neutral, and fairness mixes in the DSO
docs.text:
Fidelity / Code · Fixed

src/market/reputation.py L133, L146, L185-L191

# STEP 2, fairness: every trade of the agent, DSO trades included
price_deviations = [abs(t.price - matching_result.clearing_price) / matching_result.clearing_price
                    for t in agent_trades if matching_result.clearing_price > 0]

# STEP 3, grid: measured on matching_result.grid_balance (= dso.balance)
impact = self._calculate_grid_impact(agent.id, trade, matching_result.grid_balance, dso_id)

# _calculate_grid_impact
if abs(grid_balance) < 0.1:
    return 0.0
if (trade.buyer_id == dso_id) or (trade.seller_id == dso_id):
    # DSO trades are always stabilizing by definition
    return self._neutral

Why it is wrong.

  • The grid part never moves. It is measured on grid_balance, which is the DSO balance and always 0 (I-24). abs(0) < 0.1 returns 0 for every trade, which maps to the neutral 0.5. The grid part has the largest weight (0.5), so half of the reputation is a constant.
  • A DSO trade counts as helping (N-03). The function returns values from −1 to 1, and 0 is neutral. For DSO trades it returns self._neutral, which is 0.5: "neutral" on the 0-1 scale, but a positive, helping impact on this one. (This branch is reached only once the balance is fixed.)
  • Fairness compares with the DSO's tariffs (N-02). The fairness part compares every trade of the agent, DSO trades included, with a clearing price that includes the DSO's tariffs (I-16). An agent forced to the DSO at night looks "unfair" for a price it did not choose.

In marlem-clean. The grid part uses the step's \(B_{\text{grid}}\), and DSO trades count 0. Fairness uses the agent's peer trades against the peer clearing price (reputation.py).

docs.title: I-07: every agent gets the same "random" initial reputation
docs.text:
Code · Decided

Review I started pondering about the reputation mechanism, it is a good feature and so on and makes sense to keep it and i want to but in the span of a single day especially if its dynamic, not sure how to handle this and like maybe the day is too short to make it meaningful, because very dependent on initial conditions.

src/market/reputation.py L65-L68, src/environment/lem.py L281-L283

def reset(self, seed: int = None) -> float:
    if seed is not None:
        np.random.seed(seed)
    return np.random.uniform(0.0, 1.0)

# the caller, once per agent with the same seed
for agent in self._agents.values():
    reputation = self.reputation_handler.reset(seed)

Why it is wrong. The global random generator is reseeded with the same seed before every agent's draw, so every agent draws the same number. The start looks random but is identical for all, and it also resets the global random state everything else uses. [P1] does not say how reputation starts.

In marlem-clean. Everyone starts at 0.5. reset is kept with its own random generator (np.random.default_rng(seed)), but is not used.

docs.title: I-66: the block hash leaves out losses and fees
docs.text:
Code · Flagged

src/market/validation.py L25-L34, src/market/matching.py L395-L396

block_content = {"timestamp": self.timestamp,
                 "previous_hash": self.previous_hash,
                 "trades": [{"buyer_id": trade.buyer_id,
                             "seller_id": trade.seller_id,
                             "price": float(trade.price),
                             "quantity": float(trade.quantity),
                             "timestamp": float(trade.timestamp)} for trade in self.trades],
                 "nonce": self.nonce}

# match_orders: a block is forced at the end of every step
if self.validator.pending_trades:
    self.validator._create_new_block()

Why it is wrong. The hash covers who traded what at which price, but not the trade's distance, loss or fee. Those could be changed after the fact without breaking the chain. The matcher also calls the validator's private _create_new_block to force one block per step, and the "proof of work" is a loop in one process, not a consensus between parties. [P1] §3.3.4 presents it as an emulation, which is fair, but the hash should cover everything that moves money.

In marlem-clean. Out of scope for now: the ledger changes no market result. The validator is kept as in the original; once the ledger matters, its hash should cover each trade's distance, loss and fee.

In marlem-clean. Original code, with a public seal_block in place of the private call; off by default (ledger_difficulty = 0). Now that fees are charged, the hash should cover them.

docs.title: Problems in the paper's market method
docs.text:
What the paper itself leaves wrong or open, whatever the code does. Each row needs a recorded decision, because the paper cannot settle it.

Topic The problem in [P1] Issues Battery (eq. 15–16) Eq. 15c-d ignores the efficiencies; the text claims rate limits that eq. 16 does not have I-71 Grid fees (eq. 8) \(F_{\text{trans}}\) has no formula. No fee factor has a value. The thermal threshold sits below the congestion threshold. Eq. 8c uses the "threshold" as a cap I-29, I-30, I-74, N-05 Imbalance fee (eq. 8b, 8h) Defined only for trades with the DSO; whether those pay fees is not said I-31 \(B_{\text{grid}}\) (eq. 20) Its timing is not given. After the DSO clears every order it is 0 by construction, so it only means something before stage 3 I-23 Clearing price Not defined. The original mixed peer prices with the DSO's tariffs I-16 Stage 1 The DSO-preferred sub-stage the original added is not in the paper I-15 Pricing The case study's bid-ask spread mechanism is not among the mechanisms of §3.3.3 I-17 Reputation (eq. 12) Weights and decay factor have no values; "fairness" and "grid contribution" have no formulas I-38 Grid physics Linear, unbounded losses and voltage drop, called "high-fidelity". Capacity violations "can be penalized or disallowed", with no choice made (penalized here) I-70, I-55 Zones Defined for graph topologies only N-06 Units $/MWh in the case study, kWh per implicit 1-hour step I-56

docs.title: What this means for the published results
docs.text:
[P1]'s Case 5 (batteries with zero-intelligence agents) ran on this market. If the paper's figures were produced with the original code, which cannot be confirmed independently:

  • The P2P prices in Fig. 5 are the buyers' bids. The case uses BID_ASK_SPREAD, which returned the buyer's price (I-17).
  • The batteries did not behave as described. Selling charged them (I-18), discharge drained less than it delivered (I-20), and a charge reaching \(SoC_{\max}\) was refused entirely (I-19).
  • No money moved: no profit (I-27), no fees (I-28), no DSO balance (I-24).

So the paper's conclusion that batteries stabilise prices is not supported by the original market. A thesis built on marlem-clean is a corrected reimplementation of the paper's market, not a reproduction of its results.
