docs.title: The two papers side by side
docs.text: Do the two MARLEM papers describe the same method? This page compares every equation and design statement that appears in both, says where they agree and where they differ, and which of the two the rebuild follows. It is a first pass on the method only; the second paper's results are not reviewed here.

docs.title: The papers and how they divide the work
docs.text:
[P1] [P2] Title MARLEM: a multi-agent reinforcement learning simulation framework for implicit cooperation in decentralized local energy markets (Applied Energy 412, 2026, 127546) Harnessing implicit cooperation: a multi-agent reinforcement learning approach towards decentralized local energy markets (SSRN preprint, not peer reviewed) Authors Salazar-Peña, Tabares, González-Mancera the same Role The framework: market, DSO, agents, batteries, grid, KPIs, reward, paradigms (overview only) The MARL study: implicit cooperation, the three paradigms and three algorithms in detail, the 3 × 3 experiment Equations (1)-(27) (1)-(20) Case study Batteries, zero-intelligence agents (§4) 8 agents on IEEE 34, 3 × 3 MARL matrix (§4)

Each paper hands part of the method to the other:

  • [P2] defers the environment to [P1]. "While the complete mathematical derivation of the environment is detailed in [9], we focus here on the specific augmentations that drive cooperative behavior" ([P2] §3.1; [9] is [P1]). [P2] restates no market, DSO, agent, battery or loss equation.
  • [P1] defers the MARL method to [P2]. "A detailed treatment of the MARL framework, including its full mathematical and implementation specifics, is reserved for a forthcoming paper" ([P1] §3.7).

So the two papers overlap in only five places, and only those can disagree:

  1. the Dec-POMDP and the observation;
  2. the grid balance and grid congestion;
  3. the reward;
  4. the KPIs;
  5. the training paradigms and algorithms.

For the market layer this means [P1] is the only specification. Everything in the market validation is checked against [P1] alone; [P2] neither confirms nor contradicts it.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Topic [P1] [P2] Verdict Dec-POMDP tuple, partial observability §3.2 §3.1 Agree Observation vector (16 + 16 + 10) Table 2 Table 5 Agree, word for word Grid balance \(B_{\text{grid}}\) eq. 20 eq. 1 Same formula. [P2] calls it "normalized"; it is not Grid congestion eq. 19 (per line) eq. 2 (mean over lines) Agree; [P2] writes out the mean [P1] describes in words Reward, overall form eq. 3-4 eq. 3 Differ, and the code is a third form; [P1] eq. 4 mistranscribes it Contribution factor \(f_{\text{contrib}}\) eq. 6 §3.1 text Differ; [P1] matches the code DSO penalty \(\gamma_{\text{DSO}}\) fixed, \(p_{\text{dso}} = 15\) scaled by grid imbalance Differ; [P2] matches the code Trading reward, P2P vs DSO weight 0.3 / 0.3 "a higher weight for P2P" Differ; the code meant [P2]'s, ran [P1]'s Base reward \(R_{\text{base}}\), components five, with weights and ranges the same five, no weights Agree; only [P1] has numbers Cooperation factor \(f_{\text{coop}}\) eq. 5, weights given text only Agree in words; only [P1] has the formula KPIs eq. 21-27 eq. 4-10 Agree, the same formulas Paradigms CTCE, CTDE, DTDE §3.7.1, words §3.4, eq. 16-20 Agree; [P2] adds the formulas Algorithms PPO, APPO, SAC §3.7.2, words §3.3, eq. 11-15 Agree; [P2] adds the formulas Grid Balance Index \(B_{\text{index}}\) — §4.3 Only in [P2], and undefined Market, DSO, fees, agents, battery, losses eq. 2, 7-18 — Only in [P1]

Four real disagreements, all in the reward, where the original code is a third version (§3 shows it next to both papers). Everything else either agrees or is written in only one of the papers.

docs.title: 1. Dec-POMDP and observation
docs.text:
Agree. Both formulate the market as a Dec-POMDP ⟨I, S, A, T, R, Ω, O⟩ in which each agent sees a local observation of three parts: market signals (public), agent-specific signals (private) and implicit-cooperation KPIs (shared). The paragraphs describing the three parts are the same text in both papers, and [P1] Table 2 and [P2] Table 5 list the same 42 signals in the same order:

Market signals (16) Agent signals (16) KPIs (10) step, time of day, clearing price and volume, grid balance, DSO buy/sell/total volume, P2P volume, DSO trade ratio, net grid import, DSO buy/sell price, mean local price, price spread, local price advantage generation, demand, cumulative demand satisfied/deferred, remaining demand, cumulative supply satisfied/deferred, remaining supply, mean profit, reputation, battery energy, SoC, available charge/discharge, cumulative charge/discharge social welfare, liquidity, mean bid-ask spread, price volatility, supply-demand imbalance, grid congestion, coordination score, coordination convergence, DER self-consumption, flexibility utilization

Small differences in wording only:

  • [P1] adds the state factorisation, eq. 1, \(s_t = \langle s^{\text{time}}, s^{\text{market}}, s^{\text{agents}}, s^{\text{DSO}}, s^{\text{grid}}, s^{\text{history}} \rangle\); [P2] does not repeat it.
  • [P2] §3.1 says agents "observe the P2P trade ratio". The table has the DSO trade ratio, which is its complement, so the information is the same.
  • [P2] Table 7 gives the forecast error (30 %) that [P1] mentions only as "forecasts".

The action \(a_i = \langle p_{\text{bid}}, q_{\text{bid}}, \alpha, \beta \rangle\) ([P1] eq. 2) is not restated in [P2].

docs.title: 2. Grid balance and grid congestion
docs.text:
Grid balance: same formula, different description.

\[ \text{[P1] (20), [P2] (1):}\qquad B_{\text{grid}} = \sum_{i \in \mathcal{I}} \left( G_i - D_i + E_{\text{bought},i} - E_{\text{sold},i} \right) \]
  • [P1] describes it as "the sum of all agents' net energy positions": close to 0 means a self-sufficient market, large values mean heavy reliance on the external grid.
  • [P2] calls it "a normalized indicator of the net energy position", with positive meaning surplus. Eq. 1 has no normalisation, and neither paper says what it would be normalised by.

Both papers also list "grid balance" as a KPI, described as "the difference between total generation and consumption". That is \(\sum (G - D)\) only, without the trade terms of the equation they cite.

Grid congestion: agree. [P1] eq. 19 defines it per line, \(\zeta_e = F_e / \max(C_e)\), and the KPI as "the average congestion level across all power lines as defined in (19)". [P2] eq. 2 writes that average out:

\[ \bar{\zeta} = \frac{1}{\lvert \xi \rvert} \sum_{e \in \xi} \frac{F_e}{\max(C_e)} \]

docs.title: 3. Reward
docs.text: This is where the papers disagree, and the original code is a third version. Each part below shows [P1], [P2] and the code. The code is copied from src/environment/reward.py in the original repository, salazarna/marlem (commit 15d6715).

docs.title: Overall form: three versions
docs.text:
\[ \text{[P1] (3):}\qquad R_i = \operatorname{sign}(r_{\text{raw}}) \cdot \ln\!\left(1 + \frac{\lvert r_{\text{raw}} \rvert}{20}\right) \cdot 20 \] \[ \text{[P1] (4):}\qquad r_{\text{raw}} = R_{\text{base},i} \cdot \left(1 + \ln\!\left(1 + \frac{\max(0,\ f_{\text{coop}} \cdot f_{\text{contrib},i} - 1)}{5}\right)\right) - \gamma_{\text{DSO},i} - \gamma_{\text{UD},i} \] \[ \text{[P2] (3):}\qquad R_i = R_{\text{base},i} \cdot \left(1 + f_{\text{coop}} \cdot f_{\text{contrib},i}\right) - \gamma_{\text{DSO},i} - \gamma_{\text{UD},i} \]

The code (reward.py L228-L242):

cooperation_boost = (1.0 + cooperation_factor * contribution_factor)

boosted_base_reward = base_reward * (1.0 + np.log1p(max(0.0, cooperation_boost - 1.0)) / 5.0)

penalty_scale = max(max(abs(boosted_base_reward), 1.0), 1.0) * 0.3
normalized_dso_penalty = dso_penalty * penalty_scale
normalized_demand_penalty = demand_response_penalty * penalty_scale / self.p_dso

raw_reward = boosted_base_reward - normalized_dso_penalty - normalized_demand_penalty

return np.sign(raw_reward) * np.log1p(np.abs(raw_reward) / 20.0) * 20.0

Written as an equation, the code is:

\[ \text{code:}\qquad r_{\text{raw}} = R_{\text{base},i} \cdot \left(1 + \frac{\ln\!\left(1 + f_{\text{coop}} \cdot f_{\text{contrib},i}\right)}{5}\right) - s \cdot \gamma_{\text{DSO},i} - s \cdot \frac{\gamma_{\text{UD},i}}{p_{\text{dso}}}, \qquad s = 0.3 \cdot \max(\lvert R_{\text{base},i} \cdot (\ldots) \rvert, 1) \] [P1] eq. 3-4 [P2] eq. 3 Code Final log compression Yes, scale 20 None Yes, scale 20 (as [P1] eq. 3) Cooperation bonus on \(R_{\text{base}}\) \(\ln\left(1 + \max(0,\ f_{\text{coop}} \cdot f_{\text{contrib}} - 1) / 5\right)\) \(f_{\text{coop}} \cdot f_{\text{contrib}}\) \(\ln(1 + f_{\text{coop}} \cdot f_{\text{contrib}}) / 5\) Bonus at \(f_{\text{coop}} \cdot f_{\text{contrib}} = 1\) (its maximum) 0 1 (doubles \(R_{\text{base}}\)) \(\ln 2 / 5 \approx 0.14\) Penalties scaled by the reward's size Said in the text ("implicitly scaled relative to the reward magnitude"), not in the equation No Yes, by \(s\)

What this shows.

  • [P1] eq. 4 is the code, mistranscribed. In the code, max(0, cooperation_boost − 1) subtracts the 1 that cooperation_boost itself added, so it is just \(f_{\text{coop}} \cdot f_{\text{contrib}}\). [P1] printed \(\max(0,\ f_{\text{coop}} \cdot f_{\text{contrib}} - 1)\), dropping the \(1 +\), and moved the \(/\,5\) inside the logarithm.
  • The printed version is inert. Both papers say \(f_{\text{coop}}\) and \(f_{\text{contrib}}\) lie in [0, 1], so their product is at most 1. Under [P1] eq. 4 the bonus is then always 0, and the reward is just \(R_{\text{base}}\) minus the penalties.
  • The code's bonus is small on paper but large in practice. With both factors in [0, 1] it reaches at most 14 % of \(R_{\text{base}}\). But the code's \(f_{\text{coop}}\) is not in [0, 1]: it is about 1811 in a traced episode (register I-41, below). With \(f_{\text{contrib}} = 0.5\) the bonus is then \(\ln(1 + 906) / 5 \approx 1.36\), which more than doubles \(R_{\text{base}}\).
  • [P2] states a far stronger bonus, up to 100 % of \(R_{\text{base}}\), and calls it "the core contribution of this work regarding implicit cooperation". [P2]'s experiments ran on the code (register I-42), so the bonus the trained agents saw was the code's, not [P2]'s.

docs.title: Contribution factor \(f_{\text{contrib}}\): [P1] matches the code, [P2] does not
docs.text:
[P1] eq. 6 [P2] §3.1 Formula \(0.5\, r_{\text{grid}} + 0.3\, r_{\text{share}} + 0.2\, r_{\text{dev}}\) "a weighted sum of the agent's marginal contribution to reducing grid imbalance (\(-\partial \lvert B_{\text{grid}} \rvert / \partial a_i\)), its contribution to price efficiency, and its contribution to local trading volume" (no weights) Grid part \(r_{\text{grid}}\): a score, 0.5 for neutral actions, toward 1 if the agent's trade reduces the imbalance, toward 0 if it worsens it The marginal effect of the agent's action on \(\lvert B_{\text{grid}} \rvert\)

The code (reward.py L487-L514):

grid_contribution = NEUTRAL                    # 0.5

if matching.grid_balance != 0:
    net_contribution = sum(t.quantity if t.seller_id == agent.id else -t.quantity for t in agent_trades)
    if (matching.grid_balance > 0 and net_contribution < 0) or (matching.grid_balance < 0 and net_contribution > 0):
        impact_ratio = min(1.0, abs(net_contribution) / abs(matching.grid_balance))
        grid_contribution = 0.5 + (0.5 * impact_ratio)   # [0.5-1.0] range for helpful actions
    else:
        impact_ratio = min(1.0, abs(net_contribution) / abs(matching.grid_balance))
        grid_contribution = 0.5 - (0.5 * impact_ratio)   # [0.0-0.5] range for unhelpful actions

# ...
    price_contribution = max(0.0, min(1.0, 1.0 - avg_price_deviation * 2))

local_contribution = len(agent_local_trades) / len(agent_trades) if agent_trades else 0

return (self._w_grid * grid_contribution) + (self._w_price * price_contribution) + (self._w_local * local_contribution)

with _w_grid = 0.5, _w_price = 0.2, _w_local = 0.3 (L92-L95).

What this shows.

  • [P1] eq. 6 describes this code exactly: the weights 0.5 / 0.3 / 0.2, the 0.5 neutral point, the share of P2P trades, the price deviation.
  • [P2]'s marginal contribution \(-\partial \lvert B_{\text{grid}} \rvert / \partial a_i\) exists nowhere. The code scores only whether the agent's net trade has the right sign and how large it is against the balance (register I-79). Neither paper shows how a derivative with respect to an action could be taken in an auction-cleared market.
  • The grid part is constant in practice. It reads matching.grid_balance, which is the DSO balance and always 0 (register I-24). The if never runs, so the grid part is always 0.5 (register I-44).

docs.title: DSO penalty \(\gamma_{\text{DSO}}\): [P2] matches the code, [P1] does not
docs.text:
• [P1]: "penalties for reliance on the DSO (\(p_{\text{dso}} = 15.0\)) and unmet demand (\(p_{\text{no_trades}} = 5.0\))". The penalties are fixed.
  • [P2]: \(\gamma_{\text{DSO}}\) "is applied for trading with the DSO, scaled by the current grid imbalance … amplified during critical imbalance periods".

The code (reward.py L207-L223, L138-L139):

# γ_DSO
dso_ratio = dso_quantity / total_quantity if total_quantity > 0 else 0.0
dso_penalty = dso_ratio * self.p_dso * abs(self.dso.balance) / max(self.grid_network.capacity, 1.0)

# γ_UD
if is_terminal:
    unmet_demand = max(0.0, agent.total_demand_required - agent.cumulative_demand_satisfied)
    if agent.total_demand_required > 0:
        unmet_demand_ratio = unmet_demand / agent.total_demand_required
        demand_response_penalty = self.p_dso * (unmet_demand_ratio ** 2)

# where p_no_trades is actually used: an agent without trades gets a fixed reward
if not agent_trades:
    return np.sign(-self.p_no_trades) * np.log1p(np.abs(-self.p_no_trades) / 20.0) * 20.0

What this shows.

  • \(\gamma_{\text{DSO}}\): [P2]'s description is the code's. The penalty is the agent's DSO share \(\times\ p_{\text{dso}} \times \lvert \text{imbalance} \rvert / \text{capacity}\). [P1]'s "\(p_{\text{dso}} = 15.0\)" is only the factor inside it.
  • In practice there is no DSO penalty. The imbalance used is dso.balance, always 0 (register I-24), so the penalty is always 0.
  • \(\gamma_{\text{UD}}\) uses \(p_{\text{dso}}\), not [P1]'s \(p_{\text{no_trades}} = 5\) (register I-46). It runs only when is_terminal is true, which never happens (register I-02).
  • \(p_{\text{no_trades}}\) does something else: it is the fixed reward −4.46 returned to an agent that made no trade at all, before any other term (register I-47).

docs.title: Trading reward: [P1] matches the code's accident, [P2] its intent
docs.text:
• [P1]: "Trading success (\(w_{\text{trade}} = 5.0\)): … defined as \(0.3\,\rho_{\text{local}} + 0.3\,\rho_{\text{dso}}\)". Local and DSO fills weigh the same.
  • [P2]: "a trading component which incentivizes successful transactions with a higher weight for P2P transactions to create a preference for local coordination".

The code (reward.py L80-L95, L262):

# Trade weights
self._w_local: float = 0.7  # Higher weight for local trades
self._w_dso: float = 0.3  # Lower weight for DSO trades
# ...
# Contribution weights
self._w_grid: float = 0.5  # Grid contribution
self._w_price: float = 0.2  # Price contribution
self._w_local: float = 0.3  # Local trading contribution

# _calculate_trading_reward
return (self._w_local * local_quantity_ratio) + (self._w_dso * dso_quantity_ratio)

What this shows. One attribute name, _w_local, is used for two different weights. The trading reward's local weight (0.7, "higher weight for local trades") is overwritten fifteen lines later by \(f_{\text{contrib}}\)'s local weight (0.3). The trading reward therefore runs as 0.3 / 0.3 (register I-45).

  • [P1] printed the result of the accident, 0.3 / 0.3.
  • [P2] describes the intent, a higher P2P weight, which is what the code's first assignment and its comment say.
  • The weights in the code are right for \(f_{\text{contrib}}\), which matches [P1] eq. 6 (above).

docs.title: \(R_{\text{base}}\) and \(f_{\text{coop}}\): agree, numbers only in [P1]
docs.text:
Both list the same five base components: economic efficiency, grid balance, resource allocation, trading and stability. Only [P1] gives weights (10, 1.5, 5, 2, 3) and ranges, and its weights match the code's.

Both describe \(f_{\text{coop}}\) as a weighted sum of normalised system KPIs. Only [P1] gives the formula and weights (eq. 5, total weight 56). The code (L176-L198) computes it as [P1] eq. 5 but feeds it raw, unnormalised KPIs, so \(f_{\text{coop}}\) is nowhere near [0, 1]: about 1811 in a traced episode (register I-41, I-75). Neither paper gives the normalisation ranges.

docs.title: 4. KPIs
docs.text:
Agree. [P2] §3.2 repeats [P1] §3.6.2 nearly word for word, with the same equations under new numbers:

KPI [P1] [P2] Formula Social welfare (21) (4) \(\sum_{\text{trades}} p \cdot q\) Market liquidity (22) (5) \(\sum_{\text{trades}} q\) Mean bid-ask spread (23) (6) \(\mathbb{E}[p_{\text{ask}}] - \mathbb{E}[p_{\text{bid}}]\) Price volatility text text std of the clearing price over a window Supply-demand imbalance (24) (7) \(\lvert \sum q_{\text{buy}} - \sum q_{\text{sell}} \rvert / C_{\text{grid}}\) Grid congestion (19) (2) mean line loading Grid balance (20) (1) as §2 DER self-consumption (25) (8) \(\sum q_{\text{P2P}} / \sum (q_{\text{P2P}} + q_{\text{DSO}})\) Flexibility utilization (26) (9) \(\sum q_{\text{P2P}} / \sum q_{\text{available}}\) Coordination score (27) (10) \(1 - \text{Imbalance}\) Coordination convergence text text "calculated similarly to the price volatility"

They agree, but they share the same problems, so [P2] does not resolve them:

  • Social welfare is described as "the sum of consumer and producer surplus" but written as \(\sum p \cdot q\), which is turnover. In true welfare, payments between agents cancel (register I-36).
  • Imbalance over trades is always 0, because every trade has one buyer and one seller. It means something only over orders or physical positions, and neither paper says which (register I-68). The coordination score, [P2]'s headline metric, is \(1 - \text{Imbalance}\).
  • Spread is \(\mathbb{E}[p_{\text{ask}}] - \mathbb{E}[p_{\text{bid}}]\), which is negative whenever bids exceed asks, that is, whenever there is anything to trade.
  • "DER self-consumption" measures the P2P share of traded energy, not self-consumption (register I-69).

docs.title: 5. Training paradigms and algorithms
docs.text:
Agree. [P1] describes CTCE, CTDE and DTDE in words; [P2] gives each a formula and says the same things:

Paradigm [P1] §3.7.1 [P2] §3.4 CTCE One policy, full global state, joint action; "a theoretical upper bound" The same, eq. 16 (joint policy) and eq. 17 (objective summed over all agents); "the theoretical upper bound for coordination quality" CTDE Centralized critic in training, local observation in execution The same, eq. 18 (actor gradient with a centralized critic Q(s, a)) DTDE Independent learners; non-stationarity mitigated by the shared KPIs The same, eq. 19-20 (each agent's transition absorbs the others' policies)

The same holds for the algorithms. [P1] §3.7.2 names PPO, APPO and SAC with one sentence each, and [P2] §3.3 gives their objectives (eq. 11-15). Both name Population-Based Training.

One addition in [P2] matters for comparing the paradigms: eq. 17 sums the reward over all agents for CTCE, while CTDE and DTDE optimise each agent's own return (eq. 19). Returns of the three paradigms are therefore on different scales (register I-73). [P1] does not say how CTCE's reward is formed.

docs.title: 6. Only in one paper
docs.text: Only in [P1] Only in [P2] The market: orders and validation (eq. 2, 15), three-stage clearing, pricing mechanisms (eq. 9-11) Algorithm objectives (eq. 11-15) and paradigm formulas (eq. 16-20) The DSO: balance (eq. 7), fees (eq. 8a-8h) The Grid Balance Index \(B_{\text{index}}\) (§4.3): "incorporates transmission losses and external grid reliance". Used as an evaluation metric, never defined, and absent from [P1] and from the code (register I-80) Reputation (eq. 12) and the ledger Agent responsiveness (§4.3): correlation between system signals and actions Agent balance and profit (eq. 13-14), battery (eq. 16), profiles (eq. 17) Losses (eq. 18), zones, the grid update Reward log-compression (eq. 3), all reward weights and penalty values

docs.title: Case setups (not a method difference)
docs.text:
The two case studies differ, as expected for different experiments. The table is here only so that numbers from one are not read as the other's:

[P1] §4 [P2] §4, Tables 6-7 Agents 7, base capacity 60 kW 8, 75-180 kW Grid Mesh, 1200 kW IEEE 34-node, 1800 kW Agents' policy Zero intelligence (random bids) Trained (3 paradigms × 3 algorithms) Clearing mechanism Bid-ask spread Not stated Price range 35-280 $/MWh 20-600; DSO prices plotted in "$/kWh" (Fig. 3) Quantity range 0.1-200 kWh 0-180 kWh Batteries Ratio 0.5-1.2, \(\eta\) 95 % Ratio 0.5-1.0, \(\eta\) 95 %, SoC 5-95 %

The price units differ by a factor of 1000 between the papers ($/MWh vs "$/kWh"), on top of the unit problems inside the code (register I-56).

docs.title: What the rebuild follows
docs.text:
• Market layer (marlem-clean): [P1] alone, since [P2] restates none of it. Its gaps are listed in the market validation.
  • RL layer: the reward must be chosen, because the papers give two. The choices to record:
  • the overall form: [P1] eq. 4 (bonus inert as printed), the code's (what [P1] meant, \(\ln(1 + f_{\text{coop}} \cdot f_{\text{contrib}}) / 5\)) or [P2] eq. 3;
  • whether to keep [P1]'s log compression, eq. 3;
  • \(f_{\text{contrib}}\)'s grid part, a scored direction ([P1]) or a marginal effect ([P2]);
  • \(\gamma_{\text{DSO}}\), fixed or scaled by the imbalance;
  • the trading weights.

The KPIs, observation and paradigms can follow either paper, since they agree.

docs.title: RL layer: what is wrong and how it was tested
docs.text: Every problem found so far in the reinforcement-learning layer of MARLEM: in the original code, in the papers [P1] and [P2], or in the method itself. For each one, what is wrong, where it comes from, how it was found and, where a test exists, what the test showed. Nothing is fixed yet: this document records the state of the original. How the market and the RL layer connect (actions, observations, reward, KPIs) is left to a separate document.

docs.title: Scope and sources
docs.text:
RL layer means everything that turns an environment into trained policies, independent of what the environment is:

  • the three training paradigms (CTCE, CTDE, DTDE) and their RL modules;
  • the grouping that turns all agents into one for CTCE and CTDE;
  • the algorithm settings (PPO, APPO, SAC) and the trainer around them (Ray Tune, population-based training, evaluation, checkpoints);
  • standalone inference of a trained policy.

The market environment itself (lem.py), and what it gives the agents (observations, actions, reward, KPIs), is not in scope. To keep the two apart, the RL code was copied out of the original repository onto its own branch (RL, worktree marlem-rl) and tested on small environments with known answers instead of the market (see The test bench). The original is kept in RL/ on the clean branch; the fixed layer is core/rl/ here, still independent of the market.

Sources.

  • IDs I-xx are from the validation issue register (docs_thesis/thesis/validation/issues.md on the refactor branch).
  • IDs R-xx are new findings made on the RL branch. They are not in the register.
  • The RL folder (RL/ on branch clean) holds the copied RL code, test environments, test bench and notebooks. Links below to the original code and its notebooks point into it on GitHub. The former RL branch retains the history of the separate validation work.
  • The original code is the authors' MARLEM repository, salazarna/marlem, at commit 15d6715 (March 2026). Every code link and snippet points there, pinned to that commit. The RL files were copied unchanged into core/rl/ (commit bf58193), so the line numbers are the same in both.
  • [P1] is the MARLEM paper (Salazar-Peña et al., Applied Energy 412, 2026, 127546). It describes the paradigms in words (§3.7) and leaves MARL training to future work.
  • [P2] is the companion preprint (Harnessing implicit cooperation: a multi-agent reinforcement learning approach towards decentralized local energy markets, SSRN 6685504, not peer reviewed). It gives the paradigms' formulas (§3.4, eq. 16-20), the algorithms' objectives (§3.3, eq. 11-15) and trains the 3 × 3 matrix of paradigms and algorithms (§4-5).
  • RLlib is Ray 2.51.1, the version in the marlem conda env. Statements about RLlib's behaviour were checked in its installed source.

Origin (as in the register):

Origin Meaning Paper The paper itself is wrong, contradictory or silent where the method needs an answer Fidelity The original code does not do what the paper says Code A programming defect that the paper has nothing to say about

Evidence:

Evidence Meaning Tested A test on the RL branch reproduces it; the result is given under the issue Read Found by reading the code; not tested yet. The issue says how it would be tested Judgment A question about the method that no test can settle; it needs a decision

Status. This register describes the original implementation in RL/core/rl/ (on the clean branch). The separate fixed implementation (core/rl/ in this branch) documents its fixes in its module docstrings; copying both into RL/ does not change the original results. The only changes to the copied code isolate it from the market (the trainer takes the environment class as an argument); each is marked DEVIATION: in the code, and none changes how training works.

In the code. In RL/core/rl/ (on the clean branch) every issue below is marked above the lines at fault in core/rl/: FAULT <ID>: for a defect, DECIDE <ID>: for a Judgment issue, so the document and the code can be read side by side. The comments are the only change; the line numbers in the links below are those of the original. I-52 is not marked: the original's test file is not copied to the RL branch.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Part of the RL layer Issues Tested Read Judgment 1. Training paradigms 4 2 1 1 2. Grouping the agents 1 0 1 0 3. Policy networks and loss 4 2 2 0 4. Trainer and hyperparameters 4 0 3 1 5. Inference, evaluation and tests 4 0 3 1 Total 17 4 10 3

The most consequential ones:

  • CTDE never trains the policies that act (I-48). The loss trains a central actor; the agents act with per-agent networks that stay at their random initial weights for any algorithm and any training length. Confirmed by test: the acting networks change by exactly 0.
  • CTCE and CTDE policies can diverge to NaN and keep "training" (R-01, R-02). Their action spread has no upper limit, so where the reward does not depend on the action the entropy bonus drives it to overflow. The KL term then becomes infinite, kl_coeff = 0 turns that into a NaN loss, and RLlib silently zeroes the NaN gradients and carries on. Confirmed by test.
  • SAC's actor in CTCE and CTDE never learns from the critic (R-05). It samples its action without the reparameterisation gradient, so it is trained only to raise its entropy.
  • The paradigms are not compared like for like (R-03, I-60, I-73). DTDE uses RLlib's standard network, CTCE and CTDE a smaller custom one without its safeguards; CTCE is trained on the sum of all rewards and learns more slowly.
  • Inference does not act like training (I-61). It skips RLlib's rescaling of actions to the action bounds and reads the market metrics from the wrong place.
  • Nothing in the original checks that anything learns (I-52, I-64). The trainer's test runs 5 iterations and asserts nothing, so I-48 passes it.

docs.title: How to read an issue
docs.text:
Each issue below has the same parts:

  • Header: ID, title, origin, evidence.
  • Original code: the lines at fault, copied from the original repository (salazarna/marlem, commit 15d6715). The caption links to them on GitHub with their line numbers. # ... stands for lines cut for length.
  • Why it is wrong: what the lines do, which other code or RLlib behaviour makes it a problem, and how that differs from [P1] or [P2].
  • Test (evidence Tested): the hypothesis, the test that would show it, the result, and what it tells us.
  • How to test it (evidence Read): the test that would confirm or refute it.

docs.title: The test bench
docs.text:
Validating RL code is harder than validating the market: a market rule can be checked by computing one step by hand, but a learning defect usually shows only as "the agents learn badly", which could also be the reward, the hyperparameters or too little training. The bench is built so that a failure has only one possible cause.

Isolation. The RL code runs on small test environments instead of the market (core/rl/envs/). They have the same interface as the market environment (one Box observation and action per agent, per-agent rewards, episodes that end), so the code under test is exactly the original's.

What is trusted. RLlib's algorithms themselves (the PPO, APPO and SAC losses, advantage estimation, the optimiser) are widely used and not re-validated. What is tested is MARLEM's own code around them: the grouping, the custom CTCE and CTDE modules, and the trainer's settings.

Probe environments (probes.py), after Andy Jones, Debugging RL, Without the Agonizing Pain. Each probe has an exact correct answer and adds one piece of the learning problem to the previous one, so the first probe a paradigm fails names the broken piece. All have 3 agents, one-dimensional observations and actions in [-1, 1], and a reward per agent. For CTCE and CTDE the correct value is the sum over the agents, since their reward is the group's sum.

Probe Observation Reward Correct answer Adds 1 Constant always 0 +1, one step value 1 value learning, reward delivery, episode end 2 Observation ±1, random per agent the agent's observation value = observation the observation reaches the value network 3 Discount 0, then 1 +1 only at the end of 2 steps V(0) = γ, V(1) = 1 (γ = 0.5) time, discounting, episode boundaries 4 Action always 0 \(1 - (a_i - t_i)^2\), targets −0.6, 0, 0.6 action = \(t_i\) the policy gradient, each agent's own reward 5 Obs → action ±1, random per agent \(1 - (a_i - o_i/2)^2\) action = \(o_i/2\) the policy uses the agent's own observation 6 Agent order as 4, agent names agent_2, agent_10, agent_1 as 4 as 4 agents stay matched when names sort differently

"Observation always 0" means each agent receives the number 0: the network still gets an input, but it carries no information, so the problem becomes "learn one constant". That removes input processing from the list of suspects.

Measurements.

  • The learned networks are read directly (probe.py): after training, the learner's value and action outputs are queried in the probe's states and compared with the correct answer (tolerance 0.15; values 0.15 times the size of the answer). Return curves are not used to judge a probe; they mix in exploration noise.
  • Which networks training changes: each group of parameters is copied before training and compared after. A network that does not move is not being trained.
  • Learner health, as Jones recommends: entropy, KL between old and new policy, policy and value loss, and whether any loss is NaN or infinite (local.py).

Controls. DTDE uses RLlib's own network for each agent, so it is the control group: a probe that DTDE passes is solvable with these settings and this budget, and a paradigm that fails it fails because of MARLEM's code. Probes 1-3 passing in a grouped paradigm clears the grouping (rewards, observations, episode ends) before its policy is examined.

Settings. PPO with the original's settings except the learning rate (3e-4, the usual PPO value; the original starts at 1e-5 and relies on population-based training to raise it), 1000 environment steps per iteration, 10 iterations for probes 1-3 and 20 for 4-6. Training runs in one process with the trainer's own algorithm configuration (build_local), not through Ray Tune; the Tune path is not tested yet.

Results (probe_paradigms.ipynb):

Probe DTDE CTCE CTDE 1 Constant pass pass (3.04 for 3) pass (2.98 for 3) 2 Observation pass pass, but the loss went NaN (R-02) pass 3 Discount pass pass pass 4 Action pass fail: −0.80, 0.01, 0.73 fail: −0.01, 0.19, 0.11 5 Obs → action pass fail: largest error 0.18 fail: largest error 0.67 6 Agent order pass pass fail: largest error 0.50

A second notebook, validate_rl.ipynb, trains the three paradigms on two slightly larger tasks with known best returns and gives the same picture: DTDE learns, CTCE learns slowly, CTDE does not learn.

docs.title: What the tests confirm works
docs.text:
Not every check found a problem. These parts behave correctly in every paradigm:

What Shown by Rewards reach the learner; the grouped reward is the sum over agents ([P2] eq. 17) Probe 1: grouped value 3.04 and 2.98 for 3 agents Each agent's observation reaches the value network, and the critic tells agents apart Probe 2, including the mixed state (+1, −1, +1 → 1) Episodes end where they should; discounting uses the configured γ Probe 3 with γ = 0.5 DTDE trains each agent's own policy on its own reward and observation Probes 4-6 CTCE keeps observations, actions and rewards matched to the right agent, also when agent names sort differently Probes 4-6 (direction and order right), probe 6 CTDE's acting networks each read only their own agent's observation (decentralised execution is wired correctly) Probe 5: each agent's output depends only on its own observation

docs.title: I-48: CTDE never trains the policies that act
docs.text:
Fidelity · Tested

src/environment/ctde.py L46-L57

# Centralized training: encoder and policy heads for centralized actor, and value head for centralized critic
self.pi_encoder = self._get_encoder_network(concat_obs_dim, embeddings_dim)
self.pi = self._get_head_network(embeddings_dim, concat_act_dim * 2)
self.vf_head = self._get_head_network(embeddings_dim, 1)

# Decentralized execution: each agent gets its own separate policy heads
self.pi_heads  = torch.nn.ModuleDict({
    agent_id: self._get_network(input_dim=tuple_obs_space[i].shape[0],
                                output_dim=tuple_act_space[i].shape[0] * 2,
                                embedding_dim=embeddings_dim)
    for i, agent_id in enumerate(self.agents_id)})

src/environment/ctde.py L86-L89, L104

# _forward_inference: used to act, during training and after it
obs_tuple = batch[Columns.OBS]["grouped_agents"]
action_logits = [self.pi_heads[agent_id](obs_tuple[i]) for i, agent_id in enumerate(self.agents_id)]
return {Columns.ACTION_DIST_INPUTS: torch.cat(action_logits, dim=-1)}

# _forward_exploration: used to collect training data
return self._forward_inference(batch, **kwargs)

src/environment/ctde.py L121-L128

# _forward_train: what the loss is computed from
concat_obs = torch.cat(batch[Columns.OBS]["grouped_agents"], dim=-1)
central_embeddings = self.pi_encoder(concat_obs)
central_action_logits = self.pi(central_embeddings)

fwd_out = {Columns.ACTION_DIST_INPUTS: central_action_logits,
           Columns.EMBEDDINGS: central_embeddings}

Why it is wrong. The module holds two actors. The agents act with pi_heads, one network per agent on its own observation, in data collection, evaluation and inference. The loss is computed from pi, a central actor on all observations. Nothing connects the two: pi_heads appear nowhere else except the target-network bookkeeping, so no gradient ever reaches them, and every CTDE run acts with randomly initialised networks, however long it trains.

[P1] §3.7.1 and [P2] §3.4.2 describe CTDE correctly: a centralised critic during training, and "each agent i retains an independent policy network \(\pi_{\theta_i}(a_i \mid o_i)\)", updated by [P2] eq. 18,

\[\nabla_{\theta_i} J(\theta_i) = \mathbb{E}\left[\nabla_{\theta_i} \log \pi_{\theta_i}(a_i \mid o_i)\; Q_\phi(s, a_1, \dots, a_I)\right].\]

The gradient is taken with respect to \(\theta_i\), the parameters of the network that acts. The code instead takes it with respect to the central actor's. The comments show the mix-up: "centralized training" was implemented as "train a central actor", while in CTDE "centralized" refers only to what the critic may see.

The PPO update of the central actor is itself distorted. PPO's ratio compares the new and old probability of an action under the same policy; here the actions were sampled by the heads, so the ratio compares two different networks, starts far from 1 and is mostly clipped.

The defect is in _forward_train, which PPO, APPO and SAC all use, so all three CTDE combinations are affected. Inference acts through the same heads.

Test.

  • Hypothesis. If the acting networks are never trained, CTDE passes the value probes (the critic is trained) and fails every policy probe, its actions do not move toward the answer, and the pi_heads parameters do not change at all.
  • Test. Probes 1-6, plus the change of each parameter group over training.
  • Result. CTDE passes probes 1-3 and fails 4-6. In probe 4 it outputs −0.01, 0.19 and 0.11 for targets −0.6, 0 and 0.6. Over two iterations the parameters change by: pi_encoder 0.150, pi 0.114, vf_head 0.168, pi_heads 0.000. On the toy task (validate_rl.ipynb) CTDE ends at −26.3, worse than always acting 0 (−10.1).
  • What it tells us. The behaviour (policy probes fail, value probes pass), the mechanism (zero change in exactly the acting networks) and the code (heads not on the loss's path) agree. The defect is confirmed and fully explained. Only PPO was run; APPO and SAC follow from the code, not from a test.

docs.title: I-60: CTCE is a centralised-information baseline, not an upper bound
docs.text:
Paper · Tested

src/environment/train.py L676-L687

def step(self, action_dict: MultiAgentDict) -> Tuple[...]:
    obs, rewards, terminateds, truncateds, infos = self.env.step(action_dict)
    grouped_obs = {k: tuple(v) for k, v in obs.items()}
    # The reward for the group is the sum of individual rewards
    grouped_reward = sum(rewards.values())
    return grouped_obs, grouped_reward, terminateds["__all__"], truncateds["__all__"], infos

Why it is wrong. [P1] §3.7.1 calls CTCE "a theoretical upper bound for system performance" and [P2] §3.4.1 "the theoretical upper bound for coordination quality", and [P2] reports DTDE as a percentage of it ("91.7 % relative to the theoretical centralized benchmark"). CTCE sees everything, so it can represent the best joint policy, but it is trained by the same approximate learner on a harder problem: one network outputs every agent's action and learns from the sum of all rewards. The learning signal for agent i's action carries every other agent's reward noise, the classic credit-assignment problem that [P1] itself names as CTDE's motivation. With a finite budget, CTCE can end below the decentralised paradigms; "upper bound" holds at best in the limit.

Test.

  • Hypothesis. With individual rewards, CTCE learns the same policy as DTDE but more slowly, because its gradient for each agent is noisier; it is not broken.
  • Test. Probes 4-6 and the toy tasks, with the same settings and budget as DTDE.
  • Result. On probes 4 and 5 CTCE moves every action in the right direction and order, and its entropy falls steadily (4.06 → 0.07 over 3 dimensions), but after 20 iterations it is still up to 0.20 off (DTDE: 0.06). It passes probe 6. On the toy task it reaches −17.3 where DTDE reaches −3.7; on the team-reward task it is close to DTDE (−2.1 against −1.8). Clipping actions to [−1, 1] explains at most 0.04 of the error at CTCE's final spread (computed).
  • What it tells us. Consistent with "slow, not broken", but not proven: a longer CTCE run on probes 4 and 5 should pass if the hypothesis is right. That run is prepared and has not been run yet. Either way, [P2]'s percentages "of the CTCE benchmark" depend on how long CTCE was trained, not only on the paradigms.

docs.title: I-73: returns of the paradigms are compared across different scales
docs.text:
Paper · Judgment

Same lines as I-60.

Why it is wrong. CTCE and CTDE optimise the sum of all agents' rewards ([P2] eq. 17); DTDE optimises each agent's own return (eq. 19). [P2] Table 9 ranks the nine combinations by one "mean episode reward". RLlib's reported episode return for a multi-agent run is also the sum over agents, so the numbers may well be on the same scale, but the papers do not say which number Table 9 shows, and a per-agent mean would be smaller by the number of agents. The comparison needs one stated team score, computed from the raw rewards the same way for every paradigm.

How to settle it. Decide the team score (sum or mean over agents, from raw environment rewards) and report it alongside per-agent returns for every paradigm.

docs.title: R-03: the paradigms train different networks
docs.text:
Code · Read

src/environment/train.py L337-L341

# DTDE: RLlib's default module for each agent, default model config
agents_rl_module = {agent_id: RLModuleSpec(module_class=self.algorithm.get_module_class(),
                                           observation_space=agents_policy[agent_id].observation_space,
                                           action_space=agents_policy[agent_id].action_space)
                    for agent_id in self.env.agents_id}

src/environment/ctce.py L290-L306

# CTCE and CTDE: custom encoder, embeddings_dim = 128 (train.py L166)
return torch.nn.Sequential(torch.nn.Linear(input_dim, embedding_dim, bias=bias),
                           torch.nn.ReLU(),
                           torch.nn.Linear(embedding_dim, embedding_dim, bias=bias),
                           torch.nn.ReLU())

Why it is wrong. DTDE uses RLlib's default network: two hidden layers of 256, tanh, and a limit on the action spread. CTCE and CTDE use a custom network: two layers of 128, ReLU (CTDE's acting heads add a third), and no limit on the spread (R-01). A difference in results between paradigms is therefore partly a difference in network size, activation and safeguards. [P2] attributes its 3 × 3 differences to the paradigms and algorithms alone.

How to test it. Give all paradigms the same network and safeguards (or record the difference as part of the paradigm), then repeat the comparison.

docs.title: I-59: grouped spaces are in name order, grouped data in environment order
docs.text:
Code · Read

src/environment/train.py L646-L648, L702-L705

# GroupedLEM.__init__: RLlib packs the agents' data in env.agents_id order
self.env = env.with_agent_groups(groups={"grouped_agents": env.agents_id},
                                 obs_space=_tuple_obs_space,
                                 act_space=_tuple_act_space)

# _dict_to_tuple_space: the spaces are put in sorted name order
sorted_keys = sorted(dict_space.keys())
tuple_of_spaces = tuple(dict_space[key] for key in sorted_keys)

Why it is wrong. The k-th entry of the grouped observation and action is agent agents_id[k], but the k-th grouped space belongs to the k-th name in alphabetical order. They differ whenever the names do not sort in environment order, e.g. agent_1 … agent_10 (alphabetically agent_1, agent_10, agent_2, …).

Where the spaces have the same shape, data still lands in the right place, but RLlib uses the action bounds: by default (normalize_actions=True) it rescales each policy output from [−1, 1] to its space's [low, high]. In the market, each agent's quantity bound is its own capacity (action.py L35-L44). With such names, in CTCE and CTDE an agent's bid would be scaled to another agent's capacity.

Test so far. Probe 6 (agents named agent_2, agent_10, agent_1) passes for DTDE and CTCE: observations, actions and rewards stay matched. But all probe agents have identical bounds, so the probe cannot show the wrong scaling.

How to test it. Probe 6 with different action bounds per agent: the correct action of each agent is known in its own units, so a scaling with another agent's bounds shows as a wrong answer.

docs.title: R-01: the CTCE and CTDE action spread has no limit
docs.text:
Code · Tested

src/environment/ctce.py L45, L309-L322, L365

self.pi = self._get_head_network(embeddings_dim, concat_act_dim * 2)  # mean + log_std

# _get_head_network
return torch.nn.Linear(embedding_dim, output_dim, bias=bias)

# _get_distribution_class
child_dist_cls = TorchDiagGaussian

src/environment/ctde.py L360-L364 (the per-agent heads end the same way)

Why it is wrong. For each action the policy outputs a mean and a log standard deviation \(\log\sigma\), and the action is drawn from a Gaussian. Its entropy per dimension is \(1.42 + \log\sigma\), and PPO's loss rewards entropy (coefficient 0.01). Where the reward does not depend on the action, the reward gradient averages to zero and the entropy bonus is the only steady force on \(\log\sigma\), so it grows for as long as training runs. RLlib's own networks clip \(\log\sigma\) to ±20 (its PPO default, log_std_clip_param = 20). MARLEM's custom heads are a plain linear layer feeding TorchDiagGaussian, which does not clip, so \(\log\sigma\) can grow until \(\sigma^2\) overflows the float32 range. In the market, a step where an agent's bid cannot change its reward (no counterparty, a full battery) creates exactly this condition.

Test.

  • Hypothesis. In probe 2 (reward independent of the action) DTDE's entropy stops where RLlib's clip sits, while CTCE's and CTDE's grows without limit until it overflows.
  • Test. Probe 2, with the learner's entropy and KL logged every iteration.
  • Result. DTDE's entropy ends at 21.42, exactly \(1.42 + 20\), RLlib's clip. CTCE reaches 147.9 and CTDE 151.3 over 3 dimensions, about \(\log\sigma \approx 48\) per dimension; \(\sigma^2\) exceeds float32, and the KL between old and new policy becomes infinite. At the original learning rate (1e-5) CTCE did not diverge within 6 iterations; at 3e-4 it diverged within 4.
  • What it tells us. The missing clip is confirmed, and RLlib's clip is the exact difference. The speed depends on the learning rate and the entropy coefficient, both of which the original's population-based training raises (I-49). In CTDE the network that diverged is the central actor, which never acts (I-48); once the heads are trained, they have the same unbounded output.

docs.title: R-02: kl_coeff = 0 does not switch off the KL term, and a NaN loss goes unnoticed
docs.text:
Code · Tested

src/environment/train.py L216-L226

return (PPOConfig()
        .training(lr=1e-5,
                  # ...
                  num_epochs=30,
                  minibatch_size=128,
                  kl_coeff=0.0,
                  entropy_coeff=0.01,
                  clip_param=0.2,
                  grad_clip=0.5))

Why it is wrong. Setting kl_coeff=0.0 looks like it removes PPO's KL penalty. In RLlib it does not: use_kl_loss stays on by default, so the learner still computes the KL between the old and new policy and adds \(0 \cdot \text{KL}\) to the loss. When the KL is infinite (R-01), \(0 \cdot \infty\) is NaN in floating point, and the whole loss is NaN. RLlib's default response (torch_skip_nan_gradients = False) is to replace NaN gradients with zero, log a warning and step on, warning itself that this "can corrupt the internal state of the optimizer". Training continues, metrics keep arriving, and the policy has stopped learning. The value network does not depend on the KL and keeps learning, so value metrics look healthy.

Test.

  • Hypothesis. In the iteration where the KL becomes infinite, the total loss is NaN while the policy loss is still finite (the NaN comes from \(0 \cdot \infty\), not from the policy itself), and the value network keeps learning afterwards.
  • Test. Probe 2 with CTCE, logging total loss, policy loss and KL each iteration.
  • Result. At iteration 4 (learning rate 3e-4): KL = ∞, total loss NaN, policy loss 0.005. From the next iteration on the policy loss is NaN too. The value check of probe 2 still passes (error 0.001). RLlib's log fills with "Gradients … contain nan/inf values" warnings (about 200 MB of them in the notebook).
  • What it tells us. The mechanism is confirmed: a divergence that should stop a run instead degrades it silently. Any run of the original should be checked for NaN losses before its results are read.

docs.title: R-04: SAC in CTCE and CTDE uses an unsquashed Gaussian
docs.text:
Code · Read

src/environment/ctce.py L358-L373

def _get_distribution_class(self) -> TorchMultiDistribution:
    tuple_space = self.action_space["grouped_agents"]
    child_dist_cls = TorchDiagGaussian
    # ... one TorchDiagGaussian per agent, for every algorithm

Why it is wrong. RLlib's SAC uses a tanh-squashed Gaussian for bounded actions (TorchSquashedGaussian), so that sampled actions stay in bounds and the log-probabilities and entropy in SAC's loss ([P2] eq. 15) are those of the actions actually taken. The custom modules give SAC the same plain Gaussian as PPO, for both CTCE and CTDE, while SAC-DTDE uses RLlib's squashed one. So SAC differs between paradigms in its action distribution, and in CTCE and CTDE the entropy target (\(-\sum \dim A_i\), train.py L240) applies to an unbounded distribution whose samples are clipped afterwards. [P2] attributes SAC's very different results across paradigms ("excellent in CTCE and CTDE … failing in DTDE") to the paradigms.

How to test it. Probes 1-6 with SAC in each paradigm. SAC has no value function, so its value probes check the Q-values instead.

docs.title: R-05: SAC's actor in CTCE and CTDE gets no gradient from the critic
docs.text:
Code · Read

src/environment/ctce.py L132-L146 (ctde.py L143-L157 is the same)

# SECOND PASS: Compute Q-values for actions sampled from current policy to train the actor
curr_action_dist = self.action_dist_cls.from_logits(action_logits)
curr_actions_resampled = curr_action_dist.sample()
# ...
fwd_out["q_curr"] = torch.min(self.qf(curr_qf_embeddings).squeeze(-1),
                              self.qf_twin(curr_qf_twin_embeddings).squeeze(-1))
fwd_out["logp_resampled"] = curr_action_dist.logp(curr_actions_resampled)

Why it is wrong. SAC trains its actor on \(L_\pi = \alpha \log\pi_\theta(\tilde a \mid s) - \min_j Q_j(s, \tilde a)\) ([P2] eq. 15). The second term is how the actor learns from the critic: \(\tilde a\) must be a reparameterised sample, \(\tilde a = m_\theta(s) + \sigma_\theta(s)\,\varepsilon\), so that the gradient flows through \(\partial Q / \partial \tilde a\) into \(\theta\). RLlib's own SAC module does this with rsample() (default_sac_torch_rl_module.py L155). The custom modules call sample(), which draws without a gradient (checked: sample() returns a tensor with requires_grad=False, rsample() one with True). The \(Q\) term is then a constant for the actor, and \(\partial L_\pi / \partial\theta\) comes from \(\alpha \log\pi_\theta\) alone: the actor is trained only to raise its entropy, never toward higher Q-values. The critic still learns, so Q metrics look healthy.

So SAC-DTDE (RLlib's module) is SAC, but SAC-CTCE and SAC-CTDE are not: their policies drift toward maximum spread regardless of the reward. In CTDE this adds to I-48 (the trained actor does not even act). [P2] reports SAC as "excellent in CTCE and CTDE … failing in DTDE".

How to test it. Probe 4 with SAC-CTCE: the action means should stay where they start while the entropy rises; with rsample() they should move to the targets. Directly: one SAC loss on a batch, then check that the actor's parameters receive a gradient from the \(Q\) term (zero now).

docs.title: I-49: population-based training jumps the learning rate and reaches entropy 10
docs.text:
Code · Read

src/environment/train.py L178-L189

if self.algorithm == RLAlgorithm.PPO:
    hyperparam_mutations = {"lr": loguniform(0.0001, 0.01),
                            "entropy_coeff": loguniform(0.01, 10.0),
                            "lambda_": loguniform(0.8, 0.99),

Why it is wrong. Training starts at lr=1e-5 (L216), but the mutation domain starts at 1e-4, so the first resample jumps the learning rate by 10-1000×. The entropy coefficient can reach 10, a thousand times its starting value; at that size the entropy bonus outweighs the reward in the loss. Together with R-01, the search space contains exactly the settings that make CTCE and CTDE diverge, and with R-02 those trials keep running with a NaN loss. [P2] ran 10 trials per combination with these mutations (§4.2).

How to test it. Probe 2 with CTCE and CTDE at entropy coefficients across the domain (0.01, 0.1, 1, 10): the iteration at which the KL becomes infinite should fall as the coefficient rises.

docs.title: I-62: training configuration defects
docs.text:
Code · Read

src/environment/train.py L116, L285-L293, L426-L458

# _check_init
if not (isinstance(self.evaluation_duration, str) and self.evaluation_duration == "auto") or (isinstance(self.evaluation_duration, int) and self.evaluation_duration <= 0):
    raise ValueError(...)

# _setup_extra_config
.env_runners(num_env_runners=self.cpus, sample_timeout_s=None)
# ...
.evaluation(evaluation_interval=self.evaluation_interval,
            # ...
            evaluation_num_env_runners=self.cpus,
            evaluation_parallel_to_training=True,

# train
if not ray.is_initialized():
    ray.init()
tuner = Tuner(..., scheduler=PopulationBasedTraining(...), ...)
results = tuner.fit()
# ...
ray.shutdown()

Why it is wrong.

  • A positive evaluation length is rejected. not A or B is read as (not A) or B, so any integer, positive or not, raises. Only "auto" works.
  • CPUs are counted twice. cpus sampling workers and another cpus evaluation workers run in parallel, each loading PyTorch. The default cpus = cpu_count() − 4 (L154) gives 16 worker processes on a 12-thread machine. On this machine the workers failed with "The paging file is too small" when memory was short.
  • Population-based training is always on, also for a single trial, so a plain run with fixed hyperparameters is not possible.
  • ray.shutdown() is not in a finally, so a failed run leaves Ray running.

How to test it. Each is checkable directly: build the trainer with evaluation_duration=5; count the worker processes of a run; run a trial that raises and check whether Ray is still up.

docs.title: R-06: APPO's lambda_ has no effect
docs.text:
Code · Read

src/environment/train.py L186-L189, L229-L235

elif self.algorithm == RLAlgorithm.APPO:
    hyperparam_mutations = {"lr": loguniform(0.0001, 0.01),
                            "entropy_coeff": loguniform(0.01, 10.0),
                            "lambda_": loguniform(0.8, 0.99)}
# ...
return (APPOConfig()
        .training(lr=1e-5,
                  vtrace=True,
                  lambda_=0.95,

Why it is wrong. APPO computes its targets with V-trace, and RLlib's V-trace takes no λ (vtrace_torch_v2.py L72-L81); nothing in APPO's learner reads lambda_ (appo_torch_learner.py L141-L150). The setting is ignored, and one of the three hyperparameters population-based training searches for APPO searches nothing: trials that differ only in lambda_ are identical, and a "best lambda_" read from the results is noise. [P2] does not mention λ for APPO.

How to test it. Two APPO runs with the same seed and lambda_ 0.8 and 0.99: their losses should match step for step.

docs.title: I-50: the budget is counted in iterations, the paper in episodes
docs.text:
Paper · Judgment

src/environment/train.py L440

stop={TRAINING_ITERATION: self.iters if _iters is None else abs(int(_iters)),

Why it is wrong. [P2] §4.2 trains "for a total of 10 000 episodes". The trainer stops after a number of training iterations, each of which collects a batch of environment steps (4000 by default for PPO, 166 market days of 24 steps). 10 000 iterations and 10 000 episodes differ by two orders of magnitude, and the papers do not say which was meant. Budgets also matter for the paradigm comparison (I-60): CTCE needs more data than DTDE to reach the same policy.

How to settle it. State the budget in environment steps, the same for every paradigm and algorithm.

docs.title: I-61: standalone inference does not act like training
docs.text:
Code · Read

src/environment/inference.py L159-L174

# The model outputs mean + log_std for each action dimension
means = action_dist_params[..., :action_dim]
# ...
else:
    sampled_actions = means

# Clip actions to valid range
actions[agent_id] = np.clip(sampled_actions,
                            a_min=action_space.low,
                            a_max=action_space.high)

src/environment/inference.py L229-L232, src/environment/lem.py L486

# inference: market metrics read from the top level of info
if info and isinstance(info, dict):
    price_history.append(info.get("market_price", 0.0))

# lem.step: info is keyed by agent
infos = {agent_id: self.info for agent_id in self.agents_id}

Why it is wrong.

  • Actions are not rescaled. In training, RLlib treats the policy's output as a value in [−1, 1] and rescales it to the action's bounds (low + (a + 1)(high − low)/2, normalize_actions=True by default). Inference takes the policy's mean as the action itself and only clips it. A trained output of 0.5 for the bid price means 75 % of the price range in training, but a price of 0.5 in inference. Inference evaluates a different policy from the one trained.
  • The market metrics are always 0. The environment returns one info dict per agent, so info.get("market_price") never finds the key, and the mean price, volume and grid balance reported by inference are 0.
  • CTDE inference acts with the untrained heads (I-48).

How to test it. Run a trained DTDE probe policy through RLInference and through RLlib's own evaluation, and compare the actions sent to the environment.

docs.title: I-64: no baselines, no seeds, no record of a run
docs.text:
Code · Read

Why it is wrong. The trainer has no way to evaluate a random or untrained policy on the same scenario, runs one seed per trial, and saves no manifest of versions and settings. A result such as "SAC-CTDE reaches 3158" cannot be compared with what an untrained policy reaches, which is exactly the comparison that would have exposed I-48. The probe notebooks report each result against fixed baselines (best, always 0, random) for this reason.

How to test it. Not a test: a capability to add (random and untrained baselines on held-out seeds, several training seeds, a run manifest).

docs.title: I-72: [P2]'s evaluation protocol cannot show generalisation or variance
docs.text:
Paper · Judgment

src/environment/train.py L285-L293

Why it is wrong. [P2] fixes one global seed ("environmental conditions are identical across all experimental runs"), evaluates on the training scenario, and ranks by the shaped reward the agents were trained on. That shows how well each combination fits one scenario, not how it generalises, and with one seed there is no variance to compare. The ranking of Table 9 cannot separate a real difference from seed luck.

How to settle it. Decide the protocol: held-out days or seeds for evaluation, several training seeds per combination, and a score that is not the training reward alone.

docs.title: I-52: the trainer's test checks that it runs, not that it learns
docs.text:
Code · Read

tests/test_trainer.py L35-L44, L144-L145

trainer = RLTrainer(env_config=env_config,
                    algorithm=...,
                    training=...,
                    iters=5,
                    # ...
results, training_metrics = trainer.train()   # then prints metrics

# run_tests
test_trainer(algo="ppo",  # ppo, appo, sac
             mode="dtde")  # ctce, ctde, dtde

Why it is wrong. The test trains 5 iterations and prints the metrics; it asserts nothing about learning, and by default it runs only PPO-DTDE. A smoke test like this cannot catch a learning defect: a CTDE run executes without errors, logs moving losses (the central actor is being trained) and saves checkpoints. I-48 passes it. The register's I-52 covers the whole test suite; this is its RL part.

What replaces it. The probe notebooks are the first learning tests: each probe has an exact answer, and the parameter-change check fails a frozen actor. They are notebooks, not yet automated tests.

docs.title: Problems in the papers' RL method
docs.text:
What the papers leave wrong or open, whatever the code does. Each needs a recorded decision.

Topic The problem in [P1] / [P2] Issues CTCE as upper bound Called a theoretical upper bound, but trained by the same approximate learner on the summed reward; it learns more slowly I-60 Comparing returns One "mean episode reward" across paradigms whose objectives are a group sum (eq. 17) and per-agent returns (eq. 19); the score is not defined I-73 CTDE critic Eq. 18 uses a joint-action critic \(Q_\phi(s, \mathbf{a})\); PPO and APPO learn a state-value critic \(V(s)\). "CTDE" names a family, not one method I-48 Budget "10 000 episodes"; the code counts iterations I-50 Evaluation One seed, evaluation on the training scenario, ranking by the training reward I-72 Network design Not described; the paradigms use different networks (R-03) and the custom ones lack RLlib's safeguards (R-01, R-04) R-03

docs.title: What this means for the published results
docs.text:
[P1] is not affected. Its results use zero-intelligence agents (random bids); it states that "full MARL training is deferred to future work". The defects above affect the framework [P1] presents, including its highlight of "the first true, like-for-like comparison of … CTCE, DTDE and CTDE", not its numbers.

[P2] trains the 3 × 3 matrix. Its hyperparameters (Table 8: learning rate 1e-5, entropy 0.01, clip 0.2, gradient clip 0.5, minibatch 128, buffer 1000) are the original code's. If its runs used this code, which cannot be confirmed independently:

  • Every CTDE result comes from untrained policies (I-48). PPO-CTDE (mean 3004.8), APPO-CTDE and SAC-CTDE (mean 3158.2) acted with the heads' initial weights. [P2] reads SAC-CTDE's low standard deviation (42.5) as "the centralized critic successfully guided the local actors"; a policy that never changes also varies little. That untrained policies score close to CTCE (3099-3144) also says the reward hardly separates trained from untrained behaviour, a question for the connection document.
  • CTCE and CTDE trials may have run with NaN losses (R-01, R-02, I-49). With population-based training raising the entropy coefficient toward 10, trials of the grouped paradigms are exactly the ones whose spread can diverge, and the original would keep reporting them.
  • SAC-CTCE and SAC-CTDE policies were never steered by their critics (R-05). Their actors only gained entropy, so [P2]'s SAC results in the grouped paradigms ("excellent in CTCE and CTDE") come from policies that did not learn from the reward.
  • APPO's λ search found nothing (R-06): lambda_ has no effect in APPO.
  • The ranking mixes paradigm with network (R-03, R-04) and with training length (I-60), on one seed (I-72).

So [P2]'s conclusions about CTDE ("a robust middle ground", "the optimal choice" for SAC) are not supported by the original code, and its comparisons between paradigms need the fixes above before they can be repeated.

core.grid.contract · source on GitHub

Technology-neutral grid contract: what crosses the grid seam.

Plain, frozen data only: no pandapower, SimBench or NetworkX objects cross this seam. The pandapower adapter (core/grid/simbench.py) produces these records; the market, the services and the Studio consume them.

The catalog records are used by the Studio's Inspect page. ParticipantInjection and GridModel are the step-time contract and have no implementation yet.

def reset(self) -> None:
    """Load a fresh copy of the network for the configured day."""
    net = simbench._working_copy(self.ref)
    self._net = net
    self._graph = None
    self._zones = {}
    self._bus_index = {name: i for i, name in simbench._bus_ids(net).items()}
    self._loads = {}
    wanted = {e for ids in self.owned.values() for e in ids}
    self._owned_rows = {
        table: [
            int(i)
            for i, row in net[table].iterrows()
            if _element_id(row, table, i) in wanted
        ]
        for table in ("load", "sgen", "storage")
    }
    self._static = {
        (t, c): net[t][c].copy()
        for t in ("load", "sgen", "storage")
        for c in ("p_mw", "q_mvar")
        if c in net[t]
    }

docs.title: assess
docs.text:
assess(
    step: int, injections: Sequence[ParticipantInjection]
) -> GridAssessment

Run the power flow for step with the participants' injections. A flow that does not converge is reported as such, not raised.

Source code in core\grid\powerflow.py 
def assess(
    self, step: int, injections: Sequence[ParticipantInjection]
) -> GridAssessment:
    """Run the power flow for ``step`` with the participants' injections. A flow
    that does not converge is reported as such, not raised."""
    import pandapower as pp

    if self._net is None:
        self.reset()
    net = self._net
    self._apply_background(step)
    for inj in injections:
        if inj.bus_id not in self._bus_index:
            raise ValueError(f"{inj.participant_id}: no bus {inj.bus_id!r}")
        p_mw = -inj.net_injection_kw / 1000.0  # a negative load injects
        index = self._loads.get(inj.participant_id)
        if index is None:
            index = int(
                pp.create_load(
                    net,
                    self._bus_index[inj.bus_id],
                    p_mw=p_mw,
                    q_mvar=0.0,
                    name=f"injection {inj.participant_id}",
                )
            )
            self._loads[inj.participant_id] = index
        net.load.loc[index, "p_mw"] = p_mw
        net.load.loc[index, "q_mvar"] = 0.0
    try:
        pp.runpp(net, algorithm="nr", recycle=self.recycle)
    except pp.LoadflowNotConverged:
        return simbench._not_converged(step, [])
    return simbench._assessment(net, step, self.setup.step_hours, [], self.limits)

path(bus_a: str, bus_b: str) -> GridPath

The shortest way between two buses along the lines: its length d_ij ([P1] §3.5.1), the lines on it (for the congestion of [P1] eq. 8a) and the zone of each end ([P1] §3.5.4, for the zone bonus of eq. 8e).

Source code in core\grid\powerflow.py 
def path(self, bus_a: str, bus_b: str) -> GridPath:
    """The shortest way between two buses along the lines: its length d_ij
    ([P1] §3.5.1), the lines on it (for the congestion of [P1] eq. 8a) and the
    zone of each end ([P1] §3.5.4, for the zone bonus of eq. 8e)."""
    import networkx as nx

    graph = self._topology()
    a, b = self._bus_index[bus_a], self._bus_index[bus_b]
    nodes = nx.shortest_path(graph, a, b, weight="weight")
    return self._along(graph, nodes)

docs.text:
path_upstream(bus: str) -> GridPath

The way from a bus to where the upstream grid feeds the network: the nearest transformer's low-voltage busbar (or the external grid bus). The route of energy bought from or sold to the DSO.

Source code in core\grid\powerflow.py 
def path_upstream(self, bus: str) -> GridPath:
    """The way from a bus to where the upstream grid feeds the network: the
    nearest transformer's low-voltage busbar (or the external grid bus). The
    route of energy bought from or sold to the DSO."""
    import networkx as nx

    graph = self._topology()
    a = self._bus_index[bus]
    if not self._roots:
        return GridPath(0.0, (), self._zones[a], self._zones[a])
    _, nodes = nx.multi_source_dijkstra(graph, self._roots, a, weight="weight")
    return self._along(graph, nodes[::-1])

core.grid.simbench · source on GitHub

pandapower adapter for SimBench and the pandapower built-in networks.

The only module that imports pandapower and simbench. Everything it returns is plain contract data from core/grid/contract.py; no pandapower object leaves it.

It lists networks, loads them once per process (with a disk cache), summarises them, builds a topology view, lists their elements and profiles, and runs one power flow on the unmodified network for a chosen day and hour. The step-time power flow is core/grid/powerflow.py.

Heavy imports happen inside the functions, so importing this module is cheap.

def simbench_label(code: str) -> tuple[str, str]:
    """``(label, voltage level)`` from a SimBench code, e.g. ``1-LV-semiurb4--0-sw``."""
    parts = code.split("-")
    level, kind, lv_part, scenario, switches = (
        parts[1],
        parts[2],
        parts[3],
        parts[4],
        parts[5],
    )
    base = kind.rstrip("0123456789")
    number = kind[len(base) :]
    name = SIMBENCH_TYPES.get(base, base) + (f" {number}" if number else "")
    if lv_part and lv_part != "all":
        name += f", LV {lv_part}"
    elif lv_part == "all":
        name += ", all LV"
    sw = "with switches" if switches == "sw" else "no switches"
    return f"{level} {name} · scenario {scenario} · {sw}", level

def list_networks(
    source_type: str | None = None, level: str | None = None
) -> list[NetworkInfo]:
    """Catalog entries. Counts are filled only for networks already loaded."""
    refs: list[tuple[NetworkRef, str, str]] = []
    if source_type in (None, "simbench"):
        for code in _simbench_codes():
            label, lvl = simbench_label(code)
            refs.append((NetworkRef("simbench", code), label, lvl))
    if source_type in (None, "pandapower_builtin"):
        for name, (label, lvl) in BUILTIN_NETWORKS.items():
            refs.append((NetworkRef("pandapower_builtin", name), label, lvl))
    out = []
    for ref, label, lvl in refs:
        if level and lvl != level:
            continue
        loaded = ref in _LOADED
        info = _info(ref, label, lvl) if loaded else NetworkInfo(ref, label, lvl)
        if ref.source_type == "simbench":
            category, scenario, switches = simbench_facets(ref.code)
            info = replace(
                info, category=category, scenario=scenario, switches=switches
            )
        out.append(info)
    return out

def cache_coverage() -> dict[str, tuple[int, int]]:
    """How much of the catalogue is cached: ``{group: (cached, total)}``.

    One group per SimBench voltage level, in catalog order, and ``"built-in"`` for
    the pandapower networks. Only files of the current pandapower and SimBench
    versions count. Empty without a cache.
    """
    if _CACHE_DIR is None:
        return {}
    groups: dict[str, list[NetworkRef]] = {}
    for code in _simbench_codes():
        groups.setdefault(simbench_label(code)[1], []).append(
            NetworkRef("simbench", code)
        )
    groups["built-in"] = [NetworkRef("pandapower_builtin", n) for n in BUILTIN_NETWORKS]
    folder = _cache_path(NetworkRef("simbench", "x")).parents[1]
    cached = (
        {(p.parent.name, p.stem) for p in folder.rglob("*.pkl")}
        if folder.exists()
        else set()
    )
    return {
        group: (sum((r.source_type, r.code) in cached for r in refs), len(refs))
        for group, refs in groups.items()
    }

def warm_cache(
    levels: Sequence[str], progress: Callable[[int, int], None] | None = None
) -> int:
    """Build the cache files of every SimBench network of ``levels`` not yet cached.

    The networks are not kept in RAM. Safe to run in a background thread.

    Args:
        levels: Voltage levels, e.g. ``["LV", "MV"]``.
        progress: Called with (done, total) after each network.

    Returns:
        The number of networks built.
    """
    if _CACHE_DIR is None:
        return 0
    refs = [
        NetworkRef("simbench", c)
        for c in _simbench_codes()
        if simbench_label(c)[1] in set(levels)
    ]
    todo = [r for r in refs if not is_cached(r)]
    for i, ref in enumerate(todo, start=1):
        _read_or_build(ref)
        if progress:
            progress(i, len(todo))
    return len(todo)

def provide(ref: NetworkRef, net: "pp.pandapowerNet | None") -> None:
    """Use ``net`` for ``ref`` instead of loading it (``None``: load it again).

    The seam for tests and for networks built in memory: a small hand-made
    pandapower net registered under any reference works with every function of
    this module, and with the services above it, without SimBench.
    """
    for cached in (_load_cached, _absolute_profiles):
        cached.cache_clear()
    if net is None:
        _PROVIDED.pop(ref, None)
        _LOADED.discard(ref)
    else:
        _PROVIDED[ref] = net
        _LOADED.add(ref)

def topology_view(ref: NetworkRef) -> TopologyView:
    """The network's shape as plain records: buses and branches.

    Branches are lines, transformers and bus-to-bus switches. A branch that is out
    of service or behind an open switch has ``closed=False``. Networks without
    geodata get a generated radial layout (``coordinates="generated"``).

    Args:
        ref: The network.
    """
    net = _load(ref)
    ids = _bus_ids(net)
    coords, how = _coordinates(net)
    kinds = _bus_kinds(net)
    buses = tuple(
        BusView(
            id=ids[int(b)],
            x=coords[int(b)][0],
            y=coords[int(b)][1],
            kind=kinds[int(b)],
            vn_kv=float(net.bus.vn_kv[b]),
        )
        for b in net.bus.index
    )
    open_lines = set()
    if len(net.switch):
        mask = (net.switch.et == "l") & ~net.switch.closed.astype(bool)
        open_lines = {int(e) for e in net.switch.element[mask]}
    branches = [
        BranchView(
            id=str(row["name"]) if isinstance(row["name"], str) else f"line {i}",
            from_bus=ids[int(row.from_bus)],
            to_bus=ids[int(row.to_bus)],
            kind="line",
            closed=bool(row.in_service) and int(i) not in open_lines,
        )
        for i, row in net.line.iterrows()
    ]
    branches += [
        BranchView(
            id=str(row["name"]) if isinstance(row["name"], str) else f"trafo {i}",
            from_bus=ids[int(row.hv_bus)],
            to_bus=ids[int(row.lv_bus)],
            kind="trafo",
            closed=bool(row.in_service),
        )
        for i, row in net.trafo.iterrows()
    ]
    if len(net.switch):
        for i, row in net.switch[net.switch.et == "b"].iterrows():
            branches.append(
                BranchView(
                    id=str(row["name"]) if isinstance(row["name"], str) else f"sw {i}",
                    from_bus=ids[int(row.bus)],
                    to_bus=ids[int(row.element)],
                    kind="switch",
                    closed=bool(row.closed),
                )
            )
    ext = [ids[int(b)] for b in net.ext_grid.bus]
    return TopologyView(buses, tuple(branches), ext[0] if ext else None, how)

def elements(ref: NetworkRef, bus: str | None = None) -> list[ElementRecord]:
    """Loads, static generators and storage units of a network.

    Args:
        ref: The network.
        bus: Bus ID as in the topology view; ``None`` for all elements.
    """
    net = _load(ref)
    ids = _bus_ids(net)
    out = []
    for table, kind in (("load", "load"), ("sgen", "sgen"), ("storage", "storage")):
        df = net[table]
        for i, row in df.iterrows():
            name = row.get("name")
            profile = row.get("profile") if "profile" in df else ""
            rated_mw = row.p_mw if kind == "load" else row.get("sn_mva", row.p_mw)
            if rated_mw is None or (
                isinstance(rated_mw, float) and math.isnan(rated_mw)
            ):
                rated_mw = row.p_mw
            out.append(
                ElementRecord(
                    id=str(name) if isinstance(name, str) else f"{kind} {i}",
                    element_type=kind,
                    bus=ids[int(row.bus)],
                    profile_type=str(profile) if isinstance(profile, str) else "",
                    rated_kw=round(float(rated_mw) * 1000, 2),
                    energy_kwh=(
                        round(float(row.max_e_mwh) * 1000, 2)
                        if kind == "storage"
                        else 0.0
                    ),
                )
            )
    return [e for e in out if bus is None or e.bus == bus]

def profile_catalog(ref: NetworkRef) -> list[ProfileRecord]:
    """Every profile the network ships, with how many elements use it.

    Networks without profiles (pandapower built-ins, most files) return ``[]``.
    """
    net = _load(ref)
    out = []
    for (table, name), columns in _profile_columns(net).items():
        values = net.profiles[table][columns.get("p", next(iter(columns.values())))]
        users = getattr(net, PROFILE_USERS[table])
        count = int((users["profile"] == name).sum()) if "profile" in users else 0
        out.append(
            ProfileRecord(
                name=name,
                table=table,
                quantities=tuple(q for q in ("p", "q") if q in columns),
                elements=count,
                mean=round(float(values.mean()), 4),
                peak=round(float(values.max()), 4),
            )
        )
    return sorted(out, key=lambda r: (PROFILE_TABLES.index(r.table), r.name))

def profile_series(
    ref: NetworkRef,
    names: Sequence[str],
    start: str,
    days: int,
    resolution: str = "hourly",
    quantity: str = "p",
) -> tuple[list[str], dict[str, list[float]]]:
    """Values of the given profiles over a time window, as factors of rated power.

    Args:
        ref: The network.
        names: Profile names (as in ``profile_catalog``).
        start: First day, ``YYYY-MM-DD`` in the profile year.
        days: Number of days; clipped at the end of the year.
        resolution: ``"15min"`` (raw), ``"hourly"`` or ``"daily"`` (means).
        quantity: ``"p"`` or ``"q"`` (only loads have ``q``).

    Returns:
        Time labels (standard time, counted in 15-minute rows from 1 January) and,
        per profile name, its values (factors of rated power).
    """
    d, first, last, step = _window(start, days, resolution)
    net = _load(ref)
    columns = _profile_columns(net)
    values: dict[str, list[float]] = {}
    for table, name in columns:
        if name in names and quantity in columns[(table, name)]:
            column = net.profiles[table][columns[(table, name)][quantity]]
            values[name] = [round(v, 4) for v in _aggregate(column, first, last, step)]
    count = len(next(iter(values.values()), []))
    return _labels(d, count, step, resolution), values
